But with a great cry 'What madness is this, Eurymedon?' she sounded with lamentation, and, deceived by the marks of the twin shape, the mother called back the deaths with the name exchanged, until, the steel driven through her trembling breast, then too she fell, unknowing, over her ambiguous sons.

Who could unfold and command in tears the dire disasters of the city and the deeds to be praised, the punishments of Faith, and the sad fates of the pious? Scarcely would the Punic camp have ceased from weeping, and the foe that knows not to pity. The city, long inhabited by Faith, claiming heaven as the parent of its walls, falls amid the perfidious weapons of the Sidonian race and the monstrous deeds of its own people, neglected by the unjust gods: sword and fire rage, and where there is no flame, there is room for crimes. The pyre raises a cloud, blackening with dark smoke, to the high stars. On the lofty summit of a tall mountain there burns the citadel, untouched before by wars (from here the Punic camp and the shores and all Saguntum they were wont to behold), the houses of the gods burn. The sea shines back with the image of the flame, and the fires quiver in the trembling deep. Behold, in the midst of the frenzies of slaughter, Tiburna, her right hand armed with the gleaming blade of her husband and, unhappy, brandishing in her left a blazing torch, her squalid hair erect, and showing her breasts livid with beating, savage, her arms bared, to the mound of Murrus is borne over the very corpses: as, when the hall of the infernal parent thunders dread, and royal wrath plies the troubled shades, Alecto, before the throne and the dread seat of the god, serves Tartarean Jove and ministers his punishments. The arms of the man, lately defended with much blood, she places, weeping, on the mound, and, having prayed the shades to receive her, sets the blazing torch beneath. Then, snatching death, 'For you I bring these, O best of husbands, to the shades, behold, I myself,' she said; so, the sword taken back, she rushes upon the arms and invades the flames with open mouth.

Half-burnt, with no distinction, everywhere lies the unhappy throng, dead in mingled death: as, when, hunger goading, the lion at last, a victor, has assailed the sheepfolds with dry jaws, he chews the unwarlike flock with gaping mouth, roaring, and from his open throat overflows the gore he has belched in plenty: he broods on the dark heaps of the half-eaten slaughter, or with panting murmur, gnashing, he ranges among the mangled piles: far and wide lie scattered the sheep and the Molossian watchdog and the band of shepherds and the master of stall and flock, and the whole encampment, the huts laid waste, dispersed. The Carthaginians burst into the citadel, emptied by so many disasters. Then at last, the office accomplished, the Fury, to the shades, praised by Juno, returns, and, proud, exults, snatching with her the great throng down to Tartarus.

But you, starry souls, whom no age shall equal, go, glory of the lands, venerable multitude, adorn Elysium and the chaste seats of the pious. But to whom an unfair victory has given a name — (hear, O nations, and break not the bonds of peace, nor set faith below kingdoms!) — a wandering exile in the world he will stray over the whole earth, cast out from his fathers' shores, and trembling Carthage will see him turning his back. Often, his sleep terrified by the Saguntine shades, he will wish to have fallen by his own hand, and, the sword denied, once unconquered, a warrior to the Stygian waves he will bear his limbs disfigured by livid poison.

After faith had been broken with the Tyrians and the walls of chaste Saguntum overthrown, the father of the gods being unjust, at once the victor visits the peoples set at the fixed boundary of the world, and Gades, his kindred home. Nor did he cease to stir the minds of the seers and their foreseeing hearts about his empire: swiftly Bostar is bidden to set sail over the sea and learn beforehand the fates of things. An ancient worship is kept in the shrine from a long age, where, sitting on high, a rival of the Cirrhaean caves, among the panting Garamantes, horned Hammon unfolds the coming ages in his prophetic grove. From here he sought to know an omen for his enterprise and the chances to come before their day, and to learn the turns of the war.

Then, having venerated the altars of the club-bearing deity, he loads them with captured gifts, which lately from the citadel the victor had snatched, half-burnt, from smoking Saguntum. It is reported, and the belief is not idle, that from the founding of the shrine the set-up beams endure, and that through the age they have known only the hands of the builders. Hence they are glad to believe that the god has settled there and keeps age away from the temples. Then those to whom it is right and an honour to know the inmost parts of the shrine forbid women's steps, and take care to keep from the threshold the bristly swine. Nor is the dress before the altars different for any man: their bodies are veiled in linen, and the head gleams with the thread of Pelusium. It is the custom for the ungirt to offer incense, and, by the law of their fathers, to mark the sacrificial robe with a broad stripe: bare foot, shorn hair, and a chaste couch. Unextinguished flames keep watch on the hearths of the altars, but no image or familiar likeness of the gods has filled the place with majesty and sacred awe.

On the doors is the labour of Alcides: the Lernaean Hydra lies with its serpents cut off, and, crushed in his grip, the jaws of the Cleonaean lion are engraved with wide-open maw. But the Stygian doorkeeper, terrifying the shades with his savage baying, then for the first time dragged from his eternal cave, resents his bonds, and Megaera fears the chains. Beside them are the Thracian horses, and the Erymanthian plague, and the high branches of the bronze-footed stag, and his horns overtopping them. Nor lighter to be conquered is the nursling of the Libyan land upon his mother, and the deformed race, the laid-low double-membered Centaurs, and the Acarnanian river, now lessened by a horn. Among these Oeta gleams with consecrated fires, and the flames carry the mighty soul up to the stars.

When he had filled his eyes with the varied image of valour, then he beholds wonders: a sea that swept in suddenly upon the land with the mass of the rising deep, and no shores around, and the fields flooded with the poured-in waters. For where Nereus rolls forth from his blue caves and whirls the waters of Neptune from the deepest bottom, the burst-forth sea overflows, and, loosing its blind springs, Ocean comes on with its rushing waves. Then the shoals, as if stirred deeply by the savage trident, struggle to set the swollen sea upon the land. Soon the flood returns, and slips back as the tide is drawn off, and the ships, robbed of the deep, are left deserted on the fields, and the sailors, sprawled over their thwarts, await the waters. The Moon stirs these realms of wandering Cymothoe and the labours of the sea, the Moon, her chariot sent through the blue, and carries and carries back the strait, and Tethys follows, turned again and again.

These things were swiftly viewed by the leader; for many cares weary him. The first of his cares troubles him: to withdraw from the war the partner of his bed and the small son at her breast. His wife had imbued the young man with the maiden torches and his first wedding, and held him in mindful love. But the boy, begotten in the face of besieged Saguntum, had not yet completed twelve circuits of the Moon. When it was resolved to set these aside and separate them from arms, the leader speaks: 'O hope of high Carthage, my son, and not the lesser fear of the sons of Aeneas, be greater, I pray, in your fathers' glory, and found yourself a name by deeds by which, a warrior, you may surpass your grandsire; and already, sick with fear, Rome counts your years, to be wept for by mothers. Unless my prophetic heart deceives my senses, a great labour grows here for the lands: I recognize the face of my father, and your eyes threatening grim beneath your brow, and your heavy wailing, and the elements of my own wrath. If some god should chance to cut short such great deeds that he break off, with my death, the beginnings of things, strive, my wife, to preserve this pledge of war. And when he is given to speak, lead him through our cradle-shrines: let him touch the altars of Elissa with his boyish palms and swear to his father's ashes the wars of Laurentum. Then, when his stronger age comes of age with new flower, let him dart out to war and, the treaty trodden underfoot, victorious, on the Capitoline citadel claim my tomb for me. But you, whom the glory of so great a birth, happy, awaits, venerable in faith, depart from the perils of uncertain war and leave the hard labours. Crags shut in by snows and rocks set under the sky await us, and the labour Alcides sweated at, his stepmother marvelling, and, a labour fiercer than wars, the Alps. But if Fortune turn aside her promised favour and be sinister to my undertakings, I would wish you to stand in a long old age and to have prolonged your span; yours is the juster life, for whom the unhurrying sisters may draw the thread beyond me.'

So he. But in answer Imilce, the blood of Cirrhaean Castalius, who, named from her mother's name (Castulo keeps the surname of the Phoebean seer), likewise traced her parents from a consecrated stock. At the time when Bacchus was subduing the Iberian peoples, shaking Calpe with his thyrsus and his armed Maenad, Milichus, begotten of a wanton Satyr and the nymph Myrice, had reigned far and wide on the native shores, lifting a horned brow in his father's likeness. From him Imilce traced her country and her illustrious race, the name a little corrupted by the barbarian tongue. She then thus begins, her tears flowing little by little: 'Do you refuse me, forgetful that ours hangs on your safety, as a companion of your undertakings? Are these the bonds known to me, and the first-fruits of our marriage — that I, your wife, should fail to climb the icy mountains with you? Trust the vigour of a woman. No labour overcomes a chaste love. But if I am regarded only by my sex, and it is fixed that I be left, I yield indeed, nor do I delay the fates; may the god grant it, I pray: go, happy, go with favouring powers and vows, and amid the battle-lines and the blazing arms remember to keep care of the wife you have left, and of your son. For neither the Ausonians so much, nor weapons, nor fires do I fear, as I fear you: keen, you rush upon the very swords and thrust your head against the spears, nor does any valour sate you with a fortunate issue, for you alone glory knows no end, and you believe it an ignoble death for warlike men to die in peace. A tremor binds my limbs, nor do I shudder at any man who will come against you alone. But you, begetter of wars, have pity, and turn aside the outrage, and keep your head inviolable for the Teucrians.'

And now they had gone out and stood on the first shore, and the ship, run forward, the sailors hanging from the mast, was fitting little by little its sails to the driving wind, when Hannibal, hastening to soothe her fears and to lighten her mind, sick with stunned cares, thus began: 'Spare your omens and your tears, most faithful wife. In peace and in war a fixed term of life stands for all, and the first day brought with it the last; to pass from mouth to mouth in a name everlasting a fiery spirit grants to few, whom the father destines for the heavenly shores of the gods. Or shall I endure the Roman yoke and the citadels of Carthage enslaved? The ghosts goad me, and my father, chiding me through the shades of night, the altars stand and the dread rites before my eyes, and the changeable brevity of the hour forbids to put off the day. Should I sit still, that Carthage alone should know me, and that all the race of men should not know who I am, and that for fear of death I should leave high honours behind? For how far does the silence of life differ from death? Yet do not shudder at my reckless frenzies for praise. For us too there is an honour in light, and glory rejoices in old age, when it is celebrated by titles through a long age. You too the great rewards of an undertaken war await. Only let the gods grant themselves, all Thybris will serve you, and the brides of Ilium, and the Dardan rich in gold.' And while they pray these things with their weepings mingled together, the helmsman, trusting the sea, from the high stern rouses the lingerer. She is snatched away, torn from her husband. Their fixed faces cling, and they keep watch on the shores, until, as the winged keel snatched away the liquid path, the sea consumed their sight and the land receded.

But the Carthaginian prepares to turn away love with the cares of war, and seeks again the walls with hastened step. And while he surveys them and goes over all with frequent gaze, at last the hard strength yielded to anxious toil, and it is granted to compose his warlike mind in sleep.

Then the almighty father, meaning to exercise the Dardan race with perils and to raise the fame of savage wars to the stars and to bring back the labours of old, hastens the man's counsels, and terrifies his sluggish rest and breaks his sleep with fear sent upon him. And now through the moist shade of night the Cyllenian was carrying his parent's commands in winged flight. No delay. As the young man soothes his limbs in untroubled slumber, he approaches and assails him with bitter warnings: 'Shameful for a leader to consume the whole night in sleep, O ruler of Libya. Wars stand firm with a wakeful master. Soon you will see the seas troubled with poured-out ships and the Latin youth flit over all the deep, while you, sluggish in your undertaking, delay in the Iberian land. Is this enough of honour, forsooth, and a valour to be remembered, that Greek Saguntum fell with so great an effort? Come, then, if there is in your mind anything to match brave daring, bear your nimble steps with me and follow me who call (I forbid to look back: that father of the gods warns this): I will set you, a victor, before the walls of lofty Rome.'

And now he seemed to lay his right hand upon him and, with quickened step, to draw the glad man into the realms of Saturn, when a sudden crash around, and hisses brandished through the air from behind with savage tongues, terrify him, and from the man, fearing with a great terror, the precepts of the god slipped away, and, troubled, he turns his eyes. Behold, snatching forests and oaks from the ridges, twisted in its vast embrace, and the crags dragged through the pathless ways, a black serpent was hissing with a death-bearing whirl. As great as the Snake that ranges the unequal Bears with its bends and binds round the twin constellation with its gliding, so great it opens its jaws with a monstrous gape and, raising its head, makes it level with the cloud-bearing mountains. The violence of the riven sky redoubles the crash and whirls a rain-bringing storm mingled with hail. Trembling at this portent (for neither that slumber nor the force of deep night was upon him, and the god, with his wand that puts darkness to flight, had mingled light with sleep), he asks what the steep plague may be, and whither it bears the limbs that press upon the lands, and what peoples it claims with its gape. To him the one born in the cold caves of kindly Cyllene: 'You see the wars you wished for. The greatest wars, the slaughter of forests, the storm troubled with the moved sky, the killing of men and the great ruins of the Idaean race and tearful fates follow you. As great as the serpent that, the mountains laid waste, hurls the forests driven across the plains, with its squalid hide, and far and wide wets the lands with foaming venom, so great, running down from the mastered Alps, in black war you will enwrap Italy, and with so great a crash you will lay low towns torn up, their walls shattered.' With these goads the god and the slumber left the sick man. A cold sweat goes over his limbs, and with glad fear he unrolls the promises of his dream and goes back over the night. And now to the king of the gods and to Mars, under a favouring omen, honour was renewed, and before all, with a snowy bull, the Cyllenian warner appeased at deserving altars. At once he proclaims the standards to be torn up, and suddenly a clamour dissonant with mingled tongues shakes the camp.

Set forth, Calliope, to fame what peoples the dread enterprise stirred up and bore into the realms of Latinus, and what cities it armed among the untamed Iberians, and what squadrons it massed on the Paraetonian shore, when Libya dared to demand for herself the reins of empire and to change the yoke of the lands. No storm, never, goes more savage, driven by fierce gales, nor did war so dire, with a thousand keels burst forth, roar more keenly and terrify the trembling world.

First the youth bore the standards from Tyrian Carthage, light of limb and cheated of the proud grace of a tall body, but apt at deceiving and never slow to weave hidden wiles. Their shield was then rude, and with a short sword they fought; but bare were their footprints, and to gird their loins they were unaccustomed, and in the covering of a red garment their art in battle was to hide the blood they had shed. Among these their ruler, gleaming in purple, higher than all, the brother of Hannibal shines, and with welcome tumult Mago shakes the chariot and breathes his brother in arms.

Next, Utica was poured out among the Sidonian companies, ancient in its decay, founded before the citadel of old Byrsa. Then Aspis, which girded its shores with a Sicilian wall, its towers curved into the likeness of a shield. But the leader Sychaeus had turned faces upon himself, the offspring of Hasdrubal, whose heart his mother's race filled with a vain swelling, and his uncle Hannibal he never ceased to sound on his proud lips. There was present the soldier born of wave-washed Berenice, nor, though armed with the rounded pike for battle, did parched Barce fail, with its thirsting veins. And Cyrene, of the stock of the Pelopian grandson, goaded into arms the Battiadae, crooked in faith. These Ilertes leads, praised once by ancient Hamilcar, green in counsel, but late for war. Then Sabratha sent the Tyrian crowd, and Sarranian Leptis, and Oea, with Trinacrian settlers mingled with Africans, and Lixus sent Tingis from its rapid sea. Then Vaga, and Hippo, dear to the ancient kings, and Ruspina, which afar warded off the uneven waves, and Zama, and Thapsus, now richer with Rutulian blood. So many peoples he leads, huge in body and in arms, keeping the Herculean fame in deeds and in name, Antaeus, and lifts his lofty head above the lines. The Ethiopians came, a race not unknown to the Nile, who cut the magnet: theirs is the sole honour, to draw with a neighbouring stone the untouched steel from the metal. With these, witnessing by their bodies the pitiless sun, came the scorched Nubians. No brazen helmet nor cuirass stiffens with iron for them, no bow is bent: their custom is to defend their temples with manifold linen and to fortify the side with linen, and to aim darts wicked with juices, and to disgrace the iron with poison. Then for the first time in the Phoenician fashion to pitch in camp the Cinyphian Macae learned. Their faces are squalid with beard, and they cover their shoulders with the hide of a bristly goat; their hand is armed with the curved cateia. Against them are the parti-coloured shield and the sword curved by craft of the Adyrmachidae, and coverings on the left leg. But the people are harsh in their meals and grudging in their fare: for their gloomy feasts are roasted on the hot sand. Moreover the Massylians bore gleaming standards, the home, the last of the lands, that comes from the groves of the Hesperides. Over them was set, his twisted hair hanging from his crown, fierce Bocchus, who on the shore had seen the consecrated woods and, among the leaves, the gold growing green again. You too go from your deserted huts into the camp, Gaetulia, wont to mingle with the herds of wild beasts and to speak to the untamed, and to soothe the wrath of lions. No house: they dwell in wagons; to migrate over the fields is their custom, and to carry their wandering household gods about. Hence a thousand winged squadrons (the steed swifter than the East winds and taught the switch) rushed into the camp: as, when the nimble Spartan hunter fills the dense thickets with roving baying, or the keen-nosed Umbrian drives the beasts by scent from the path, the swift stags, terrified far and wide, hurl their lines headlong in fear. These Acherras drives, with no glad face nor serene brow, the brother of Asbyte lately slain. The Marmaridae, a healing crowd, clamoured in their troops, at whose chants the serpent forgot its venom, at whose touch the horned vipers lay tame. Then, poor in steel, the raw youth of the Baniurae, content to have hardened their spear-shafts with a sparing flame, mingled, eager, savage murmurs with their fierce tongues. And the Autololes too, a race fiery on their light feet, to whom the steed in its course, to whom the swift river would yield, so great is their flight: they vie with wings, and when in their flying they have snatched the plain away, you would seek the prints of their feet in vain. Conspicuous in the camp were those whom the tree noble in its juice and the lotus, too hospitable, feeds with its sweet berry, and the Garamantes, who in their immense sands shudder at the raging dipsads that seethe with black venom. Report teaches that, when Perseus snatched the head of the slain Gorgon, the dire blood flowed into Libya: hence the land overflowed with Medusan water-snakes. Over these thousands was the leader Choaspes, proved in war, born in Neritian Meninx, whose javelin always armed his lightning right hand, a renowned missile. Hither gathers the sea-faring Nasamon, bold to assail shipwrecks in the flood and to tear plunder from the sea, hither those who dwell by the deep pools of the Tritonian marsh, where the warrior maiden, as report says, born from the water, poured the first oil over Libya at the olive she had found.

And the whole West too is present, and the far-off peoples. The Cantabrian before all, unconquered by winter and heat and hunger, and bearing off the palm from every labour. A wondrous love is in that people: when sluggish age grows white, to anticipate, long since, their unwarlike years with a stone, and not to endure life without war. For all the cause of their light is set in arms, and they condemn living to peace. There came too, bedewed with the tears of Aurora — when into the world opposite she fled, an exile from her native shores — the armour-bearer of Eastern Memnon, ill-starred Astyr. For these there is a small steed, not born for Mars, but the same either gathers its footprints with unshaken back or, gentle, swiftly draws the soft chariot with pliant neck. Cydnus drives them, keen to measure the ridges of Pyrene in hunting, or to extend the battle with the Moorish javelin. The Celts too came, joining their name to the Iberians. For these it is glory to have fallen in battle, and to burn the body such a sin: they believe that to heaven and the gods above one is restored if the unfed vulture plucks the lying limbs. Of fibres and of feathers and of the divining flames rich Callaecia sent its wise youth, now howling barbarous songs in their native tongues, now, the earth struck by the alternate beat of the foot, rejoicing to clash their resounding shields to the measure. This is rest and sport for the men, this their sacred delight. The rest a woman's toil accomplishes: to add to the furrow the seed and to turn the earth with the pressed plough is base for the men. Whatever is to be done without hard war, the wife of the Callaecian husband performs, unresting. These Viriathus drives, drawn from the remote lairs of Lusitania, Viriathus in his early age, a name made soon famous by Roman losses. Nor did the Cerretani, once a Tirynthian camp, or the Vascon unused to bear the arms of the helmet, delay, nor Ilerda, which afterward saw the Dardan frenzies, nor you, Concanian, who, showing your Massagetan parent in your fierceness, sate yourself with the poured-out vein of a horn-hoofed steed. And now Phoenician Ebusus moves, Arbacus moves to arms, a fighter to press on with the aclys or the slender dart, now one whose founder was Tlepolemus and whose origin Lindus, the Balearic bearing wars with the sling and winged lead, and those whom now, with the name of the Greeks profaned, the houses of Oeneus and Aetolian Tyde sent as Gravii. Carthage gives men, founded by old Teucer, the Phocaean Emporiae give them, Tarraco gives its youth, vine-bearing, and to yield only to the Latin Lyaeus. Among these shone, in the bright light of its breastplate, the Sedetan cohort, which Sucro with its stiff waters and Saetabis, its nurse, sent from its lofty citadel, Saetabis, proud to have scorned the webs of the Arabs and to set its thread against the linen of Pelusium. Mandonius and Caeso, conspicuous tamer of horses, command the peoples, and the camp stands by their shared toil. But Balarus proves the squadrons of the Vettones in the open plain, here indeed, when the spring is calm and the breezes grow warm, the herd of mares, keeping their silent unions, stands fast and conceives a hidden Venus from the breeze that begets. But that breed has not many days, and old age hastens, and the seventh summer is the longest reckoned for those stables. But Uxama, raising its Sarmatian walls, does not skirmish on such light horses: hence comes to war a steed not frail in age, and harsh with raw vigour to bear the bridle or to obey its commanding masters. Rhyndacus is their leader, the spear their javelin; with the faces of beasts and gaping jaws they make their helmets dreadful. In hunting their life is passed, or, after the manner of their fathers, they live by violence and plunder.

Parnassian Castulo gleams with conspicuous standards, and Hispal, famed for its Ocean and its alternate tides, and Nebrissa, conscious of the Nysaean thyrsi of the god, which the light Satyrs cultivated, and the nightly Maenad, wreathed in the sacred fawnskin and the secret Lyaeus. Carteia arms the grandsons of Arganthonius. Their king was, of his forefathers, the richest in human life, a warrior who had measured ten times thirty years. Tartessos arms, conscious of stabling Phoebus, and Munda, to bring forth Emathian labours for the Italians. Nor did the glory of the gold-bearing land of Corduba fail. These men led Phorcys with his yellow crown and Arauricus, a heavy warrior on the corn-bearing shores, equal in age, whom on a fertile bank Baetes begot, his horns shaded with the bough of Pallas.

Such lines through the fields the Sidonian leader, blackening with dust, hurries, and surveying them under arms, as far as the eye could take them in, the gleaming standards he went rejoicing, and drew his shadow over the long land. Not otherwise, as often as Neptune glides over the waters in his car and seeks farthest Tethys, the couch of Phoebus, with his bridled horses, the whole chorus of the Nereids flows from their caves, and in their wonted contest of swimming they turn their white arms in the clear sea.

But the Carthaginian, the peace of the lands being troubled, was making for the leafy summits of the Pyrenaean mountain. Pyrene, from the high citadel of its cloudy summit, looks out far upon the Iberians divided from the Celts and holds an eternal division between great lands. The hills drew their name from the Bebrycian maiden, the crime of his host Alcides, who, when by the lot of his labours he sought the long fields of three-bodied Geryon, possessed by Bacchus in the savage hall of Bebryx, left Pyrene, her maidenhood lost, to be mourned for her beauty, and the god, if it is right to believe it, was the cause of the wretched girl's death — the god. For when from her womb she brought forth a serpent and shuddered at her father's wrath, at once, troubled, she left her sweet home. Then in lonely caves she bewailed the night of Alcides and told of the man's promises to the shady woods, until, as she mourned the ungrateful love of her ravisher and stretched out her hands and called for the arms of her host, the wild beasts tore her apart. The Tirynthian, her mangled limbs, as he returns a victor, drenched with tears, and, beside himself, grew pale at the found face of the beloved maiden. But the summits of the mountain, struck by the Herculean voice, trembled on their ridges: with a mournful cry he called on Pyrene, and all the crags and the lairs of beasts resound Pyrene. Then he lays her limbs upon a mound, weeping for the last time, nor did the honour perish with age, and the mountains hold the wept-for name through the ages.

And now through the hills and the groves dense with fir the Carthaginian had crossed the borders of the Bebrycian hall. Then, fierce, the way sought by arms through the inhospitable country of the Volcae, he lays waste, and approaches the threatening banks of the swollen Rhone with hurried soldiery. With its Alpine ramparts and its snowy rock the Rhone thrusts its head out toward the Celts and draws forth its mighty stream, cleaving the fields with its foaming flood, and rushes swiftly toward a bridge in its broad channel. The Arar, mingled with it, like one standing still and with silent water, adds to its wealth, and the Rhone, embracing it with its panting eddies, plunges the lingerer in the sea and, snatched through the fields, forbids it to bear its native name to the neighbouring shores. They assail the hostile river eagerly with bridges: now with high head and shoulders they protect their arms, now the flood is broken in rivalry by their strong forearms. The steed is led, tied to a river-alder of wood, nor does the Libyan beast hold back, though slowed by fear. For by beams, the shoals and the thrown-on earth being found, they cover the joined beams and lead them little by little into the deep, the fastenings loosed from the bank's rampart. But the Rhone, terrified by the bellowing inrush of the herd, was afraid of the dark masses, and, its pools poured back, hurled its threatening murmurs from its sandy bottom.

And now the host advances within the Tricastine borders, now it passes the easy fields, now the Vocontian country. Here Druentia, turbid with trunks and stones, laid waste the leader's glad way. For, risen from the Alps, it is borne rolling with a roar, in its barking waves, ash-trees torn away and the fragments of the eaten-away mountain, and changes its treacherous shoals as its course is shifted, faithful to no foot-soldier, fair to no broad-beamed ship. And then, swollen lately by the poured-out rain, snatching up many bodies of men under arms, whirling them in its foaming summit, it plunged them, hideous with mangled limbs, to the bottom.

But now the Alps, seen nearer, took from the trembling men the will to remember the labours past beyond. All things, covered with frost and white with eternal hail, hold the ice that is as old as themselves: the steep face of the heaven-high mountain stiffens, and, facing the rising Phoebus, it knows not how to soften its hardened frosts with flames. As far as the Tartarean gulf of the pale realm opens from the upper earth to the lowest shades and to the pools of the black marsh, so far through the air the land is raised, and intercepts the sky with its shadow. No spring anywhere, and no honours of summer. Alone on the dread ridges deformed winter dwells and keeps its perpetual seats; it from every side drives the black clouds hither, and the storms mingled with hail. Now all the blasts and the winds have set their raging realms in the Alpine home. The gaze is dimmed upon the high rocks, and the mountains pass off into the clouds. Athos mingled with Taurus, and Rhodope joined to Mimas, and Ossa with Pelion, and Othrys with Haemus, would yield to them. The Tirynthian first approached the untried citadels. The gods above watched him cleave the clouds and break the steep of the mountain, and, with great force, tame the rocks unviolated by a step from their origin in the long ages.

But the soldier slows his footsteps with doubtful gait, as if they bore impious arms into sacred bounds throughout the world, Nature forbidding, and warred against the gods. Against this the leader — not he, troubled by the Alps nor by any terror of the place, but he cherishes the men's languid, sad hearts with exhortation and calls back their vigour: 'Is it no shame, after the glory of war and the battle-lines, in obedience to the gods, and weary in their favour, to turn your backs on the snowy mountains and, slack, to submit your arms to the crags? Now, O now, comrades, believe that you climb the walls of domineering Rome and the highest summit of Jove. This labour will give you Ausonia, and this will give Thybris into chains.' No delay. The host, moved by the rich promises, he raises onto the hill, and bids them leave the famous footprints of great Hercules and set their foot on the raw places and let the squadrons go out by a path of their own. He bursts the inaccessible approaches, and first surmounts the heights and from the topmost crag calls the cohorts. Then, where the slippery path on the hill hardened with frozen cold balks them on the whitening slope, he burns the ice, struggling with the steel: the loosened snow swallows the men with its gape, and from the high summit, headlong, the collapse, slipping down, buries the squadrons in its wet ruin. At times Corus, dreadful, drives the snows massed in an opposing whirl into the very faces with his dusky wings, or again, whistling, snatches the arms torn off by the monstrous gale from the bared men, and, rolling them through a circle, whirls the things on high into the clouds with its twisted blast. And the more they climb the ridge and, straining to escape, raise their step, the labour grows. Steep above opens out before the weary, and a second mass is born, whence it pleases them not to look back on the labours mastered and sweated through: such fear the levels repeated to their eyes inspire, and one face of the whitening frost, wherever it is given to send the gaze, is heaped before them. So, in mid-sea, the sailor, when he has left the sweet lands, and the idle canvas finds no winds upon the untroubled mast, looks out on the immense waters and, conquered by the deep seas, weary, renews his eyes upon the sky.

And now, above the disasters and the harshness of the places, in their filth and the squalor of their stiff hair, ever foul, half-wild men thrust their dreadful faces from the crags, and, poured forth from the hollow caves of the eaten-away pumice, the Alpine band attacks, and with their wonted vigour through the thickets and the familiar snows and the pathless ways, nimble, they harass the shut-in foe with their mountain-roving courses. The shape of the places now changes. Here, with much blood, the snows reddened, stained; here the ice, knowing not to be conquered, little by little yields, warmed by gore, and while the steed presses its footprints with hard hoof, its hoof stuck, gripped fast in the pierced frosts. Nor was the plague of the falls simple: cut-off limbs the frost leaves behind, and the harsh stiffness amputates the broken joints. Twelve suns, and through their wounds as many savage nights traversed, they sink upon the wished-for summit and hang their steep camp on the sheer rocks.

But Venus, her mind shaken with doubtful fear, addresses her father and, mournful, bursts into complaint: 'What measure of punishment or end of perishing, I pray, will there be for the sons of Aeneas, and when will you grant them, the lands and the strait measured out, to settle? Why does the Carthaginian prepare to drive my descendants from the city granted by you? He has set Libya upon the Alps and threatens an end to their empire. Already Rome fears the fate of Saguntum. Whither shall we bear the last ashes of Troy and the sacred ruin and the home of Assaracus and the secret things of Vesta? Grant a seat, father, and to lie safe. Is it too little to have sought our wandering exiles through the whole world? Or shall Pergamum be sought again, Rome captured?' Thus Venus, and in answer the father then declares: 'Drive away your fears, nor let the attempts of the Tyrian race have troubled you, Cytherea: your blood holds, and long will hold, the Tarpeian citadels. By this mass of war I prepare to test the men and to weigh them in battle. A race that endures iron and rejoices to master toils little by little grows unaccustomed to the ancient honour of its fathers, and that people, never sparing of blood for praise and ever thirsting for fame, by sitting still spends obscure times, rolling on a mute and inglorious age, that people sprung from our blood, and by the sweet venom of sloth its virtue, little by little overcome, grows old. It is a work of great labour, to be prepared with much toil, to demand among so many peoples a realm for itself alone. And now a time will come to you when Rome, greatest of things, will be nobler for her woes. Hence labour will bring back names not unworthy of our heaven, hence to you Paulus, hence Fabius, and Marcellus, dear to me for the spoils. These will bring forth so great a realm for Latium through wounds that their descendants, in luxury and with much-changed minds, yet cannot overthrow it. And now there is already born one who shall recall the Carthaginian to his country and, repulsed from Latium, strip him of his arms before the walls of his own Carthage. Hence, Cytherea, your line will reign through a long age. Then from Cures a heavenly valour will lift itself to the stars, and the warlike race nursed by the berry-bearing Sabine will increase the name of the sacred Julii. Hence the father will grant the conquest of unknown Thule and will first lead the lines into the Caledonian groves, will check the Rhine within its banks, will rule the Africans tirelessly, and, an old man, will master in war palm-bearing Idume. Nor will he hold the lakes of Styx and the realms widowed of light, but the seat of the gods above and our honours. Then a youth, excelling in the great strength of his mind, will take up the burden of his country, and, lofty, will be borne lifting his head to match his empire. He the savage wars of the Palestine race will blot out in his early age. But you, Germanicus, will surpass the deeds of your kin, already as a boy dreaded by the golden-haired Batavian. Nor will the fires of the Tarpeian summit have terrified you: amid the sacrilegious flames you will be kept for the lands. For a long partnership of our heaven awaits you. To him one day the Gangetic youth will lower their slackened bows, and Bactra will show its empty quivers. He too will drive his chariot from the Northern pole through the city and will lead Eastern triumphs, Bacchus yielding. He, a victor, will check the Hister, indignant at letting the Dardan standards cross, within its Sarmatian seats. Nay, he will surpass the descendants of Romulus in eloquence, those for whom there will be a glory won by speech. To him his own the Muses will bring their rites, and, better in his lyre — at which the Hebrus stayed and Rhodope came — he will speak things to be wondered at by Phoebus. He too, where you see our ancient palace stands, will set the golden Capitol on the Tarpeian rock and will join the summits of the temples to our heaven. Then, O child of gods, and about to give gods, rule with your father's sway the lands made blessed. A slow hospitality of heaven will receive your old age, and Quirinus will yield his throne, and your parent and your brother will set you in the midst: beside you the temples of your starry son will shine.'

While Jupiter unfolds the sequence of the age to come, the Agenorean leader, borne down by the unfair mounds, slipping with doubtful effort over the downward pathless ways, steadied his step and trod the wet rocks. No battle-line or foe holds him, but the sheer slopes with their threatening crag, and the rocks that meet him with their boulders, throw him into confusion. They stand shut in and mourn the delays and the hardships of the ways. Nor is it granted to refresh their numb limbs with rest: they join night to the work and hasten to bear the oaks on their forced shoulders, and the ash-trees snatched from the hills. And now, when they had stripped the densest wood from the mountains, they heaped up beams, and the crag, kindled in a ring with swift flames, is burned out: soon, broken down with iron, the rotten mass gives a groan as its weight is loosed, and opens to the weary the realm of ancient Latinus. By these chances at last, the unknown Alps crossed, the leader set his tents on the Taurinian fields.

Meanwhile, bearing the voices of Jove and his oracles, Bostar, glad, the sands of the Garamantes measured out, was present, and, as if he had seen the Thunderer, spurred their hearts: 'Greatest son of Belus, who with your right hand ward off servitude from your fathers' walls, we have penetrated the Libyan altars. The Syrtis, that drenches the stars, bore us up to the gods above, the land, more violent than the seas, almost swallowed us. To the edge of heaven from the middle of the world stretch the squalid plains. Nature has denied a mound in those immense spaces, save such as the whirlwind, twisting the hollow clouds, has built, massed of the dashed-on sand, or such as, when the African, having laid waste the lands, its prison broken, and Corus, scattering the sea over the air, fierce, have invaded the plain that takes their battles and in turn, the dust heaped on, have piled into mountains. These valleys we sailed over, watching the stars. For day confuses the way, and the foot-traveller, wandering in the deep plain and ever seeing the fields in the midst, the most faithful Cynosure guides for the Sidonian sailors. But when, weary, we came to the groves and the wooded realms of horned Jove and his gleaming temples, Arisbas, our host, leads us, received, into his dwelling. There stands, near the shrine, a water, new and memorable, which at the dawning day, which at the failing day grows warm, and which stiffens when the midday sun kindles Olympus, and the same again grows hot in the nocturnal shades. Then, the old man shows us the places full of the god, the rich clods without the ploughshare, and thus speaks with a glad mind: "These shadows of the groves and the summits joined to the sky and the groves trodden by Jove, adore, Bostar, with prayer. For to whom are the gifts of Jove not spread through the world, that twin doves sat in the lap of Thebes? Of these, the one that touched with its wings the Chaonian shores fills the Dodonian oak with prophetic murmur. But the one that, borne through the air over the Carpathian sea, swam across into Libya, of one colour with its snowy wings, this Cytherean bird founded this seat with a temple; here, where now you see the altar and the shady groves, the leader of the flock chosen — wonderful to tell — standing in the midst between the horns of the wool-bearing head, the bird sang responses to the Marmaric peoples. Soon a sudden wood and a grove of aged oak sprang up, and such oaks as now press upon the stars came from the first day: hence, from ancient awe, the tree holds a deity and is worshipped at the warm altars." And while we marvel at these things, with sudden creaking the doors, struck, opened dreadfully, and a greater light suddenly strikes the eyes. Before the altars stands the priest, gleaming in a snowy robe, and the peoples vie to run together. Then, when I poured from my breast the words entrusted to me, behold, the god suddenly enters the seer. Deep murmurs roll through the sounding grove, the beams dashed together, and now a voice greater than is known bursts out into the air: "You make for Latium and prepare to harry with war the offspring of Assaracus, you Libyans. I see the harsh enterprise and grim Gradivus now mounting his car, and the horn-hoofed steeds, raging, breathing a black flame upon the Hesperian flank, and the reins flowing with much blood. You, who demand the issues of battle and the ends of fate and, fierce, give your sails to a glorious labour, invade the Iapygian plain of the Aetolian leader. You will increase your Sidonian forefathers, and to none will you leave it to penetrate deeper into the vitals of the Ausonian race, until the Dardan realms, conquered, tremble before you. Nor will the Saturnian youth ever lay aside their care while Hannibal plucks the upper airs upon the earth."' Such oracles Bostar bore to the glad men, and had filled them with a love of the nearer fight.

Rumour scatters itself through the troubled cities of Ausonia, that the cloud-bearing mountains and the crags that threaten heaven have taken the yoke, that the Carthaginians have been carried over trackless ways, and that their leader, boasting deeds to rival the labour of Hercules, has come down upon them. Wicked Rumour sings of dreadful upheavals, and swells as she goes, swifter than the winged East Wind, and shakes the stunned strongholds with terrifying reports. Docile fear feeds the people's rumour upon what it hears, piling emptiness on emptiness: men rush into the bitter cares of war in haste, and suddenly throughout all Ausonia Mars roars and rouses arms and men. They forge new javelins, and the steel's fierce gleam, its rust scoured off, is donned again; they restore to laid-by helmets the snow-white glory of the crest; the spear is fitted with its thong, and from a fresh forge the axes are called back. The breastplate is woven, impenetrable guard of the flanks, fated to bear many a blow and many a wound made vain. Some watch over the bow, some break with the lash the panting horse into its circles, and whet the sword on the stone. Nor do they delay to bring help to the walls with which old age has wrestled; they haul up stones and pull back the hollow towers that length of years has eaten away. From these the strongholds take their weapons, and they strive to bring oak for the gates and trusty bars from the forest, and they ring them with ditches. The taskmaster Fear, no sluggard, hurries all things on, and the broad fields are loud with alarm. They have abandoned the hearth: stunned, they carry on their shoulders their ailing mothers, and the aged old men, who draw out their last thread of life, are snatched away; then with hair unbound the wife is driven before them, and to right and left are dragged the little children, keeping no even order as they go. So the crowd; and fear is passed from hand to hand, no source is asked. But the senators, though the monstrous undertaking terrifies them, and war in their very bosom, and the Alps and their passable rocks have failed them, still raise against these hardships a stern, unbroken mind, and lift up their great spirits. It is their joy to go through dangers to glory and to found by the right hand a name worth remembering, such as Fortune never gave to men in her favouring moods.

But the leader of Libya cherishes his troops behind a safe rampart, weary of march and numb in their sinews from much frost, and, by way of comfort, points out to them, glad, that a road still remains across the plains to the city, and Rome within his reach. Yet he does not think it good to let the cares of state and the counsels of war stand idle, nor can he alone endure repose. In ancient times, among the old ages, warlike nations once invaded the side of Ausonia and won themselves blessed seats and made themselves feared by the hand of arms. Then impious wars the Tarpeian father and the captured Quirites felt. While he stirs them with gifts, and warms their empty hearts and their nation loose in its ways, and joins their arms to his, already the consul, sailing past the shores in a swift fleet, Scipio was bringing himself back from the Phocaean coast, and the mighty leaders, having measured out the toil of sea and of land in opposite ways, were now drawing nearer to dangers closer to the rampart, and the first beginnings of a great disaster were at hand. For when, the camps drawn together as the consul advanced, Fortune had taken away delay, and the cohorts, kindled at the sight of the foe, demanded the signal for their fury, the Tyrian leader, in a great voice, sounds through his numerous columns that all is conquered far and wide, whatever bears the name of Iberian: that neither the Pyrenees nor the fierce Rhone spurned his orders, that Rutulian Saguntum smoked in ashes, that his march was forced through the Celts, and that where it had been a labour for the son of Amphitryon to set his step, there under arms the Carthaginian squadrons had gone, and the horseman, borne over the heights, had trampled the ridge, and the Alps had echoed with neighing.

Against him the consul calls his own men to noble trial: "You have, soldier, a foe broken and scorched by the snowy crags, dragging along with difficulty his numbed limbs. Come now, let him who leaped across the sacred mountains and the deep cliffs learn how much more loftily our rampart stands than the Herculean height, and whether it is more to scale the hills or to break your ranks. Let him grant rumour its empty boast, so long as, when the battle is poured out and he rushes back the way he came, the Alps stand in his path. Over the heights the gods have driven him on and led him here, that he might dye the bounds of Latium with his blood, and that a hostile land might hide his bones. I would gladly learn whether now a new and second Carthage sends out this war against us, or the same that lies sunk beneath the sea, buried in the vast deep among the Aegates." This he says, and turns his column toward the waves of Ticinus. Clear Ticinus keeps its waters sky-blue and its pools, with their shallow bed, never knowing to be stirred, and slowly draws its bright liquid in a green stream. You would scarcely believe it glides: so gentle between its shady banks, amid the tuneful rivalry of the birds' song, it leads its sleep-bringing water in a shining flood.

And now, as the shadows fled at the very edge of night, the light was at hand, and Sleep had finished out his hours. The consul was preparing to explore the ground, the nature of the neighbouring hill, and what kind of soil the plains might have. Equal zeal was in the Carthaginian, and like cares in his breast. And so they were at hand, with swift wings of cavalry attending them. But when the clouds of stirred-up dust had shown that the foe was advancing, and nearer and nearer the ground groaned with the ringing horn of hooves, and at the same time the keen neighing of the conquering horses raged louder than the trumpets, "To arms, men, seize your arms, men! Both leaders press on!" In both was swift valour and a twin desire for praise, and a madness for battle and war alike resolved. No delay. Now only so much field divided them from striking range as a hurled lance, driven by its thong, can reach, when suddenly, from a clear sky with no clouds at all, an omen turned their minds and eyes toward the stars. A hawk, holding its way from the mid-path of the sun, was violently troubling the birds beloved of Venus and famed for the honour of Dione, and with talons, now with beak, now with hard buffets of the wing, it had given fifteen of them to death amid its cruel wounds. Nor was there end or surfeit, but a thirst for new blood kept swelling, and now it pressed the dove, trembling at the slaughter of those before, and uncertain in her flight as the feathers slipped, until the bird of Jove, coming from the eastern source of Phoebus, forced it at last to turn its back into the thin clouds. Then victorious it turned its glad flight toward the Roman standards, and where the fair son of the leader, young Scipio, was brandishing arms with his boyish arms, it gave its cry twice and three times, and grazing with its beak the gleaming crest of his helmet, returned itself to the stars.

Liger cried out (his was the art of feeling the gods' warnings and of showing things to come, the bird his teacher): "Carthaginian, for twice eight years within Italy's bounds, like the bold bird, you will hunt the youth of Ausonia, and carry off much plunder with blood. But check your threats: the armour-bearer of Jove, see, denies you the realm of Daunus. I know you, highest of the gods: be at hand, father, and confirm the omen of your bird. For for you, unless the soaring bird with empty flight falsely belies the gods, are kept, my boy, the last fates of subdued Libya and a name greater than Carthage." Against him Bogus sings glad omens to the Tyrian king, that the favouring hawk and the birds slain in the cloud portend disaster to the sons of Aeneas and to the race of Venus. Then he is first to hurl, as if a god urged him on and he were privy to the fates, his spear at the foe as its companion. That spear, flying far through the open spaces of the broad field, would have lost its blow for the distance, had not Catus, his reins loosed, while he strives to pluck the glory of the first fight, borne his headlong horse's face into its path. So, growing faint and now about to fall, the cornel shaft found the wound it sought and took its slaughter from the foe, and stood between the temples of the brow it met.

The lines clash, and with a great roar across the plain all check with the rein their horses, reared up high, and then bear them forward of their own will. Risen into the air the steed goes, and flying through the open ground in a swift storm scarcely marks faint traces on the surface of the dust. Before the rest, the swift squadron of the Boii, with Crixus their leader, batters into the foremost and hurls its monstrous limbs against them. He himself, swollen with pride, traced his line from the stock of ancestral Brennus, this Crixus, and dragged the captured Capitol into his titles, and, madman, upon his shield bore the Celts weighing out the gold from the Tarpeian ridge and the sacred summit. The man's milk-white neck glowed with a tawny torque, his garments were striped with gold, his sleeves stood stiff with gold, and his crest quivered with the like metal. With a vast onset the foremost phalanx of the Camertes is struck down and falls, and the close-packed waves of the Boii rush headlong through the crowded ranks: the unspeakable Senones thicken their allied swarms, and bodies, crushed against the breasts of the horses, are rolled over the whole field. The fields swim, and the deep gore of men, the deep gore of horses, swallows the slippery footing of the warring squadron. The heavy hoof finishes off the half-dead with its trampling, and flying about it scatters from the blood foul dews upon the ground, and washes the arms with the wretched men's own gore. The first javelins, boy, of swelling Pelorus, Tyrrhenus, dying you stain with crimson blood, victorious as they are. For while you spur their spirits to battle with the horn and kindle the men anew to wounds with your blast, a barbarian weapon stuck in your panting throat and shut up the hoarse murmur with a deadly wound. But the sound, poured from the dying mouth at its last, wandered through the curved horn over lips now mute.

Crixus slew Picens and Laurus, both not from afar, but Laurus with the sword—to Picens a polished spear, gathered on the banks of the Po, brought death. For while he seeks the byways and plots to deceive with a leftward wheel, the man's spear settled in his thigh and likewise through the panting flank of the flying horse, and gave a double death, the grim thing. The same man, wrenching from the bloody neck of Venulus, lays you low headlong, Farfarus, with the still-warm weapon, and you, Tullus, nursed beneath cold Velinus, a singular glory of Ausonia and a name to be remembered, had the fates granted delay or the Carthaginians kept their pacts; then Remulus, and—once names most renowned in war— the Magii of Tibur and Metaurus of Hispellum, and Clanius, planning with wavering spear a wound.

Nor is there place for the Tyrians for war or battle, but the whole field the Celtic frenzy has filled. The javelins fly vainly for none, and all the steel stands fixed in a body. Here among the trembling, daring a monstrous deed, Quirinius, to whom flight was unknown and who chose, with unconquered mind, in adverse straits to take death upon his breast, fires his horse with the spur and scatters his Gallic darts from his arm, that if a way be given to unbar a passage and to break with the steel through to the king, sure of death he seeks in all his deeds that glory which he could not feel. Down falls Teutalus, his groin pierced, and the earth is shaken beneath the vast weight. Sarmens falls, who, if victor, had vowed to lay his yellow hair and his locks for you, Gradivus, rivalling gold, and the ruddy knot upon his crown. But the Fates, not hearing him vow his unshorn hair, dragged him by it to the shades. Over his white limbs the gore goes steaming, and the drenched earth grows red. But Ligaunus, not slowed by the javelin that met him, rushes in and, facing the man, wheels his sword to meet him, and rising strikes where the sinews bind the supple arm to the shoulder, and the right hand, cut off by the wound, hung dying a little while from the loosened reins, and while it gleams, with a trembling effort it grasps again the strap and, knowing nothing, imitates one guiding the accustomed bridle. Then Vosegus reaps the neck of the turned man, and bearing the helmet hung up with its plume, and the enclosed face of the slain man, hails the gods with the cry of his fathers.

And while the peoples of the Gauls give these dead to the field, the consul, hurrying the squadrons summoned from the camp to battle, was driving them on, and first he was rushing at the foe, high on his gleaming white horse. He draws from every side the choice youth of rich Ausonia, the Marsi and Cora and the glory of Laurentum and the javelin-throwing Sabellian, and the Mars-worshipping man of Tuder from his lofty hill, and the Faliscans clad alike in their national linen, and those whom, beneath Hercules' walls by the silent river, the apple-bearing fields breed, the dwellers of the Anio by Catillus' line, and the Hernican stones, hardened in the ice-cold streams, and the lands of cloudy Casinum used to send. They went into war, the nurslings of the land that rules, a youth condemned by the gods and now never to return. Scipio, where the central whirlpool of the fight devours the columns, drives his horse, and, spurred by the slaughter of his own men, slays as offerings to the dead Labarus and Padus and Caunus and Breucus, scarcely felled by many a wound, and Larus, who rolled his eyes with a Gorgon-like face. You fall too, warlike Lepontius, by a grim fate; for while, fierce, he sets his body in the way to seize the reins, and, standing tall on foot himself, levels with the face of the seated consul, a heavy sword fell into the middle of his brow, and his head, split off, lay upon his shoulders. But Batus, frantic, who wrestles with his horse and blocks the charges with his shield, laid out on the tawny sand by a blow of the steed, his face crushed in by the dashing heels, lost it. The Ausonian leader rages through the troubled plains, as the Getic North Wind, when in victory it has lifted whole the Icarian sea from its lowest depth: the sailor is tossed, scattered over the vast deep with his shattered fleet, and every Cyclad is drenched by the foaming water.

Crixus, since hope was slender and salvation small, . . . arms his mind with contempt of death. His bristling beard glows red with bloody foam, and the gape of the madman's mouth whitens, and his hair is matted with the cast-up dust. He attacks Tarius, who, the consul near, was mixing in the battles, and thunders round the man with fierce arms. That one rolls upon the ground; for the fir-shaft, bringing his utmost fate, pours him forward over his horse's shoulders, and in terror he is dragged along, his limbs bound and tangled to the girths. Long traces of gore the spreading field leaves behind, and the spear-point marks its quivering tracks in the dust. The consul was praising the youth's death and making ready to avenge those noble shades, when through his ears a dread voice came, and he hears Crixus named by the shouting men, though unknown to him by face. His anger rises more violent to close fight, and he fixes his eyes on the longed-for body. Then, urging on his horse with the welcome honour of a stroke to its patted neck, he addresses it: "The common throng and lesser warfare soon, Garganus: the gods call us to greater things. Do you see how great Crixus goes? Even now I set you as your prize that carpet shining with Sidonian flame, a barbarian glory, and you shall be given the tawny reins." So having spoken, with a great shout he summoned Crixus to battle, and demanded combat in the open field. Nor had equal anger failed to kindle the foe, who did not refuse. When the squadrons, ordered, drew back on this side and on that and gave room, and the fight stood in the middle of the plain, as great as Mimas, the nursling of Earth, who in the Phlegraean fields moved his standards and terrified heaven with his arms, so great does Crixus from his half-bestial breast hurl forth his roar, and rouse his wrath with horror-sounding howls: "Has no one survived the burned and captured city, to tell you what right hands the people of Brennus brought to arms against you? Learn now, then," he says, and at once hurls, with its knots and seared oak, the grim beam, fit to shatter even the gates. It sounds with a fearful crash, but, in its over-great cast, improvident, it saved the space of the distant field and flies past the nearer foe. To him the consul: "Remember to carry this to the shades and to your ancestor, how far from the Tarpeian seat you fall, and that to you it was not granted to look upon the Capitol of the sacred mount." Then with knot and light running together he aids the spear, a strain worthy of the man's bulk. It flies through the edges of the many-fold linen and the coverings woven with sinews, and measures the deep breast with its whole point. He sinks down, stretched out in broad ruin upon the fields, and the struck earth groans beneath his huge arms. Not otherwise, on the Tyrrhenian shore, where the mole is built to do battle against the waves and the blind storms beneath, the lofty pier, sounding monstrously, is driven into the sea: Nereus bellows, and the blue waters, parted by the blow, receive beneath their angry surface the rock dashed upon them. Their leader lost, the Celts trust themselves to flight on foot: their one hope and all their great ardour had hung on that one life. And as when a hunter, on the high top of Picanus, rouses the thick coverts, and into the close lairs sends the black plague everywhere through the bramble-tangled wilds, while the fire gathers its silent strength and flame, and the pitch-black summit slowly rolls in murky gloom and twists its clouds with thick smoke: soon the sudden blazes gleam over the whole mountain, there is a roar, the beasts have fled, the birds have fled, and far below in the valley the heifers tremble.

But Mago, when he sees that the squadrons have turned and that the first effort, which alone the nation has, has come to nothing, calls to battle the arms of his men and his nation's cavalry. From every side, bare, they leap to the fray, both bridled and unbridled troops. Now the Italians are borne back upon their rear with reins reversed, now again panic carries the Tyrian squadrons backward, or these bend their rightward circles in crescent curves, or those wind their leftward turns into a horn-shaped sweep. With alternating course they weave their wheeling coils and by the same art, retreating, undo them as they yield. With this same turn the sea, when discord stirs the winds, the North Wind drives and the East Wind drives back, and the mass of the deep they bear now this way, now that, with alternating gusts.

The Sidonian leader flies up, gleaming with gilded purple, and round him Dread and Terror and Fury. And when he raised the gleaming orb of his Callaecian shield and struck the fields with its great light, hope and valour fall, and from the trembling mind the shame of turning the back recedes, nor any care for an honourable death, but flight is fixed, and the gaping of the earth is longed for. So, when the tigress has come forth from her Caucasian caves, the fields are abandoned, and every flock, troubled with maddened look, seeks safe hiding-places: she ranges victorious over the deserted valleys, and now little by little she bares her jaws with drawn-back gape, as if already chewing the bodies before her, and with monstrous maw plots slaughter. Not Metabus, not the taller Ufens escaped her even so, though the one was borne on winged foot, the other by his horse's help at full rein. For the ash-spear, gleaming, sent Metabus down to the shades with its point; Ufens, collapsed with his hamstring cut, the sword cut off, and took with his blood the glory of his speed. And now he had given to death Sthenius and Laurus, and from cold Collinum Collinus, whom green Fucinus in his grotto had nursed and given to swim across his lake. Massicus too becomes his comrade in death, his hurled spear struck home, begotten on the sacred summit of the vine-bearing mountain and nursed by the waters of Liris, which with calm face hides its course and, changing for no rain, glides past its silent banks in a jewelled stream.

Before the front line three brothers were mingling fierce battles, whom in Sidon, blest in her womb amid wars, Barce had borne to Spartan Xanthippus. Greek affairs, their father the leader, the noble name of Amyclae, and the chains thrown on the neck of Regulus by the Spartans swelled their hearts with old renown. They burned to prove their race by war and their father a Laconian by their deeds, and then to visit the cold mountains, Taygetus, and at last, the wars subdued, to swim their fathers' Eurotas and see the rites of Lycurgus. But the god and the Ausonian brothers forbade them to reach Sparta—brothers equal in number, whom harsh Aricia had sent, born in the deep groves of Egeria, matched in age and mind; but no further would hard Clotho grant them to see the lake and altar of Diana. For when, driven against their foes in the whirlwind of battle, Eumachus and Critias and Xanthippus, glad in his father's name, joined their steps—(as lions wage furious wars among themselves and with panting roar fill the squalid fields and the long native huts: swiftly every Moor flees to the hidden rocks and trackless places, and the Libyan wife, checking her offspring's wailing, holds back her children from the breast; those rage grimly, and bones broken in their bloody mouths crunch, and limbs writhe beneath their savage teeth)— just so the youth of Egeria, on this side keen Virbius, on that side Capys, leap forward, and Albanus in equal arms. Sinking down a little, Critias hurls headlong Albanus to ruin, his belly pierced through: but to that one suddenly the entrails, sliding in pitiable fall, filled all his shield. Eumachus then took Capys—but he held with all his weight the covering as though fixed to his limbs; yet the wicked sword struck down the left hand fastened to his shield with a wound, and, not yielding his shield though it was pressed in his own effort, the luckless hand stuck fast among the slipping arms. The last palm remained, two now laid low, to Virbius. As he feigned to draw his steps in fear, Xanthippus falls by the sword, Eumachus by the stiff spear, and at last the fight is evened by a doubled death. Then the blade pierced the breasts of the men in turn, and in exchange, their lives torn away, they laid down the battle. Happy in their death, whom love of kin added to the shades! The coming ages will pray for such brothers, and their glory will be eternally celebrated by a mindful age, if only my songs have the power to carry the day and to see late descendants, and Apollo has not begrudged them fame.

But the consul, with his voice, holds the squadrons scattering over the whole plain, while his voice has strength: "Where do you bear back your standards? What panic, alas, has stolen you from your own selves? If the first bristling lot of the field seemed yours, and to provoke the battle's front, stand behind me, men, and, your terror driven off, only look on! These right hands that you flee were begotten by captive fathers. What hope for the conquered? Shall we make for the Alps? Believe that Rome herself, who bears her walls upon her tower-crowned head, now stretches out her suppliant palms to you. On every side I see the snatching away of children and the slaughter of parents, and the Vestal hearths quenched with blood. Ward off this horror!" After, amid such words, his throat was dulled by the frequent shouting and by the thick dust, with his left hand he seizes the reins, with his right his arms, and thrusts forward his broad breast, and threatens with drawn sword, now himself, now the trembling men, at close quarters, if they do not stand.

While the Father from high Olympus watches these lines, the dangers of the noble consul moved his mind. He calls Gradivus and thus speaks with a father's voice: "The toil of a great-hearted man, my son—who, unless you take up the war, will doubtless be his last—frightens me: snatch from the battle the burning man, and forgetful of himself in his lust for slaughter, halt the leader of Libya; for the wicked one seeks more in the death of one consul than in the whole rout of the falling. Besides, you see the boy who already entrusts the battle to his tender right hand and strives to surpass his years by his deeds and thinks it long to come to manhood through war: let him, you his leader, dare the firstfruits of battle, you his teacher, and let him win this first victory—to have saved his father." So the Sower of the world. But Mars summons his chariot to battle from the land of the Odrysians. Then he takes up his shield that scatters the flames of the black thunderbolt, and his helmet, easy for no god to bear, and his breastplate sweated over with much toil of the Cyclopes, and brandishes through the air his spear sated with blood in the war of the Titans, and fills the fields with his car. With him goes a host of Furies, and the Eumenides together, and the countless shapes of bloody death, and Bellona, busied with guiding the reins, goads the four-horse team with her black whip. A bristling storm is borne from the boundless sky, whirling black globes and turbid clouds, and enfolds the earth. The Saturnian seat is shaken, trembling at the god's coming, and the river leaves its banks when the chariot is heard, and flows back toward its source.

The Garamantian youth had ringed the Ausonian leader with weapons and were preparing fresh gifts for the Tyrian king, the spoils of his arms and the consul's dripping head. He stood resolved not to yield to Fortune, and with a fierce mass hurled back his spears, growing more savage with the slaughter, and now with his own, now with hostile gore, his limbs are wet and drip, his plume is fallen, and as the ring narrows round in its circle, the Garamantian presses with nearer javelins and balances the iron aimed with cruel point. Here the boy, when he saw the weapon fixed in his father's body, his cheeks grew wet, and a sudden pallor seized the trembling youth, and he broke out in a groan toward the stars. Twice he had tried to forestall his father's fate, his right hand turned against himself; twice Mars turned his wrath upon the Carthaginians. Through the weapons, through the foe the fearless boy is borne, and keeps pace with Gradivus' stride. At once the squadrons gave way, and suddenly a broad path appears across the field. Sheltered by the heavenly shield, he reaps the ranks, and lays low upon the arms of the fallen the bodies, and slays the author of the weapon, and many shades before his father's eyes, the longed-for offerings. Then, the spear quickly snatched from the hard bones, bearing his father leaning upon his neck and shoulder, he darts forth. The astonished squadrons, at so great a sight, hold their weapons, and the harsh Libyan yields his place, and all the Iberian yields far and wide, and that signal devotion and youth wrought a wondrous silence on the warring fields. Then from his high chariot Mars said: "You shall raze the towers of Carthage and shall force the Tyrians to terms. Yet in the long age no light so great shall dawn for you, dear boy. Blessing, O blessing on your sacred nature, true offspring of Jove. And still greater things remain, but no better can be given." Then Mars, the clouds and the air traversed, makes for the earth, the sun now spent, and the darkness shut up the weary lines within their camp.

Cynthia was laying night to rest with her downward-sloping car, fanned by her brother's wheels, and from the Eastern sea the rosy flames were rising amid the blue. But the consul, sad, was making for the Trebia and the hills, fearing the plain favourable to the Carthaginians. And now the days were snatched away in marching and busy toil, and broken in mid-stream the bridge floated, its bonds undone, that had carried the Dardanian column across, when the Carthaginian came to the swift waves of Eridanus. And while he seeks the fords and gentle approaches by winding circuits through the byways, and looks for the languid shallows of the pool, sometimes, the alder snatched from the neighbouring woods, he covered the river with a fleet to carry his columns across: behold, the consul was at hand, and held at once the borders of the Trebia, summoned through the long blue sea past Sicilian Pelorus, the offspring of the Gracchi. A clan famous for a great and spirited man, and many an ancestor among the images shone forth with bright titles in war and at home. Nor were the Carthaginians wanting, their camp pitched across the river on the grass. For prosperity stirred their spirits, and their leader, taunting them besides: "What third consul now remains to the city? What other Sicania remains under arms? See, all the bands of the Latins and of the grandsons of Daunus have come together. Let them now strike treaties with me, the leaders of Italy, and demand back laws and pacts. But you, granted your weapons amid the light of war, unhappy in soul, so, so may you live, and to your son once more give this glory; nor in the close of your age be it granted to meet death in war, when the fates shall call. To have fallen fighting is my privilege." Thus he loudly proclaims, ablaze. Then with a light javelin, busy, with his Massylian squadrons he provokes them beneath the very camp and draws out the foe. Nor does the Latin soldier think it right to owe his safety to the rampart, or that the closed gates be battered by the spear. They burst out, and before all flies over the open mound a consul in no way unworthy of the Gracchi. The breeze shakes the waving crests of his Auruncan helmet, and from his shoulder gleams the ancestral glory of his blood-red cloak. With a great shout he calls his columns back, and where the crowd, meeting him, packs its dense ranks, breaking a path he is borne across the field, as a torrent, headlong from the top of lofty Pindus, rushes with a roar into the plains and with a great crash rolls a side torn from the mountain: everywhere, meeting it, the herds and the monstrous beasts and the woods are dragged along, and the foaming wave shouts in the rocky valleys.

Not if the glory of the Maeonian tongue should return to me, and Father Phoebus should grant me to pour forth a hundred voices, could I tell over all the slaughters that the right hand of the great consul, or against him the frenzy of Tyrian wrath, brought forth. Murranus by the leader of Libya, and the leader of the Phalanti by the Ausonian—men skilled in war and old in toil— each laid low the other's, face to face. Murranus stormy Anxur had sent from its mountain, you, Phalantus, the rites sacred to Triton from the snow-white deep. As soon as the consul shone in his splendid raiment, though deprived of part of his sight, with one eye Cupencus, sufficing for the wars, fiercely brandishes his spear and fixes it quivering on the margin of the topmost shield. To him the consul (for anger boils him): "Lay down, wicked one, whatever remains in your fierce face and gleams on your maimed brow." So he says, hurling with a straight whirl the oaken shaft, and sends the grim light through with his whole point. Nor more lightly does the son of Hamilcar rage on his right. To him falls luckless Varenus in his snow-white armour, Varenus of Mevania, for whom the rich teat of the field Fulginia ploughs, and Clitumnus in the broad meadows washes his white bulls in his cold stream. But the gods are grim, and that greatest care, a victim thankless, was reared in vain for the Tarpeian Thunderer. The light Iberian presses on, and lighter the Moor to range about. On this side javelins, on that the Libyan cornel-spears strive to weave the sky with a dense cloud, and as much of the level field as lies between to the banks, so much do the quivering weapons bury, and there is no room in death for the crowded to fall. Allius, set out from Argyripa and the fields of Daunus, a hunter, was ranging over the plain with rough javelins and his Iapygian horse, and borne into the midst of the foe, hurled his Apulian darts with no idle right hand. For him a breastplate bristles with the hide of a Samnite she-bear, and his helmet is fenced with the tusks of an aged boar. But when, as he wrought havoc, as though over the open he ranged the lairs in a wood, or stirred up the backs of beasts on Garganus, on this side Mago, on that as savage saw him likewise Maharbal, as when, with hunger driving them, two bears from opposite crags attack a frightened bull between their twin onslaughts, and rage suffers no sharing of the prey, just so the keen Allius is brought down, his javelin hurled from this side and that: the Moorish yew goes whistling through both flanks. Then the meeting points sounded in the midst of his heart, and it was uncertain to which spear his death should yield. And now, the standards scattered, through the Roman ranks the Carthaginian drives the stragglers to the banks—a pitiable thing— pressing the panicked men and striving to plunge them in the river. Then the Trebia begins new battles in its ill-omened flood for the weary, and rouses its waves by the prayers of Juno. The sinking earth swallows the bodies of the fleeing and, treacherous in its soil, sucks them down in its baffling gulf. Nor is it given to strive and to wrench from the sticky mud the steps sunk deep within: by the tenacious slime the bound footsteps cling fast, and the loosened bank entangles, or with the blind treachery of the marsh strikes them down. And now one over another, rising up through the slippery places, while each man snatches a way for himself over the inextricable shore, and struggles with the rotten turf, slipping they fall and crush themselves with their own ruin.
