That swift swimmer, now just about to grasp safety, while he makes ready and, straining with lifted body, grasps the topmost grass with his hand and emerges from the liquid waves, hangs pinned by a spear hurled into the bank. Here one, robbed of his weapon, clasps the foe with his arms and, mingling death, holds him fast struggling in the shallows. A thousand shapes of death at once. The Ligurian falls in the fields, but the man's face, cast into the river waters, drank in long gasps the bloody stream. At last fair Irpinus was barely swimming out from the mid-flood and calling his comrades' hands with a shout, when a fierce horse, carried by the swift waters and with many a wound, struck him and sank the weary man beneath the surface. Disaster is heaped up by a force of elephants, suddenly seen across the waters, urged on with their turreted backs. For it is swept headlong through the shallows, like a crag torn down from a rent mountain, and drives before its breast the Trebia, which fears the strange thing, and lies upon the foaming channel. Adversity tests men, and through hardship up the steep cliff fearless valour strives toward glory. For Fibrenus, unable to bear losing his death unhonoured and bare of fame, "We shall be marked," he said, "nor, Fortune, will you hide my death beneath the flood. I will try whether there is on earth what the Ausonian sword cannot tame, or the Tyrrhenian spear cannot pierce through." Then rising he casts, and plants in the right eye of the beast his cruel javelins, and leaves the weapon in the wound. With a horror-sounding shriek the monster follows the penetrating thrust of the point, and, mangled, with gore poured forth, lifts its brow and, its driver fallen, turns its back. Then in truth they attack with javelins and frequent arrow, daring now to hope for its death, and through the huge shoulders and the stretched-out flanks the wound comes with its black point. Many a lance stands in its back and on its dark spine, and it brandishes a vast forest with its shaken body, until, the weapons spent in the long contest, it falls and closes the shallows it presses with its great ruin.

Behold, against the stream, though his slowed limbs are held back by a man's wound, the implacable Scipio goes up the river and harasses the foe with countless slaughters. With the bodies and shields and helmets at once of the fallen the Trebia is covered, and one is scarcely left to see the waves. Mazaeus by javelin, Gestar is laid low by sword, then Thelgon, dweller of Cyrene, with a Pelopid ancestor. At him he hurls a pike caught up from the swift flood, and as far as the point, drawn thin by its long stiff iron, projects, he drives it through the gaping mouth. Struck by the wood, the teeth sounded in the wound. Nor was rest sought in death: his swelling limbs the Trebia gave to Eridanus, Eridanus to the waters of the sea. You too, Thapsus, fall, a tomb denied you after death. What did the house of the Hesperides or the groves of the goddesses avail, guarding the tawny boughs on the gold-bearing tree?

The Trebia swelled and raised itself from its deepest pools, and now, fierce, drives forth its whole spring in a flood and hurls all its force. The wave rages with sounding eddies, and a new torrent follows with a roar. The leader felt it, and with kindled anger more violently: "Great penalties, O Trebia, and deserved, will you pay to me, treacherous one," he said: "torn through the Gallic streams I will scatter you over the fields, and take from you the name of river, and stop up the very spring from which you open, nor shall it be granted you to touch your banks and glide into the Po. What sudden madness has made you, unhappy, a Sidonian river?" As he hurls such words, a rising mound of waters struck him and pressed his shoulders with its curved flood. Steep against the opposing mass of the rushing waves the leader stands, and lifted on his shield the rushing river. Moreover, from behind, the foaming wave with a whistling storm sprinkles his topmost crest with spray. To go through the shallows and to set a firm step the god forbids, the earth withdrawn beneath him, and far off the struck rocks sound hoarsely, and the waves, roused to the wars of their parent, do battle, and the river has lost its banks. Then, his hair wet and bound with sea-green leaves, he lifts up his head with a voice: "Do you threaten besides to wipe out my proud penalties and the name of Trebia, O foe to my realms? How many bodies I carry, laid low by your right hand! By the shields and helmets of the men you slay, my course and channel are narrowed and choked. With slaughter, you see, my deep pools redden and are borne backward. Set a limit to your right hand, or fall upon the neighbouring fields."

These things, Venus joined to her, from a high mound was watching Mulciber, hidden in the gloom of a dark cloud, and Scipio, his palms lifted, presses heavy toward heaven: "Gods of my fathers, by whose auspices Dardan Rome stands, did you save me of late from such a death amid so great a battle? Was it thought unworthy that this life be cut off by a brave right hand? Give me back, O son, to dangers, give me back to the foe! Let it be allowed me, in battle, to summon a death that I may approve to my country and my brother." Then, stirred by his words, Venus groaned and turned upon the river the swift might of her unconquered husband. The scattered fire drives flames on every side along the banks, and burning lays waste the shades nursed for many years by the river. The whole grove burns, and Vulcan, poured into the high woods in victory, crackles with loosened reins. And now the fir is scorched in its foliage, now the pine and the alders, now the poplar, standing on its bare trunk alone, has let fall on high the birds wont to dwell among its branches. The greedy flame drinks up the waters drawn from the deepest flood, and, the savage heat pressing on, the dry gore parches on the banks. Far and wide the bristling earth is split into cracks and gapes, broken open with a chasm, and on the pools the deep ashes have settled.

Father Eridanus marvels that his eternal courses suddenly cease, and the mourning choir of the Nymphs filled their innermost caves with stunned wailing. Three times, as he tried to lift his scorched head, Vulcan plunged it back beneath the smoking waves with hurled torch, three times the seized reed bared the god's hair. Then at last his voice was admitted and the vows of one who prayed, and to him praying it was granted to keep his former banks, and at last from the Trebia Scipio called back his weary cohorts to a fortified hill, with Gracchus attending. But the Carthaginian, having venerated the river with much honour, set up grassy altars by its allied waters, not knowing, alas, what greater things the gods were stirring, and what grief, Trasimene, you were preparing for Ausonia.

The peoples of the Boii had Flaminius lately disturbed with arms, and to that man the glory of war was then easy, to crush a nation light in heart and poor in cunning. But it was no equal task to have contended with the Tyrian tyrant. This man, born for the city's fatal harm by left-hand omens, the Saturnian prepares for the weary empire as a leader, and a man worthy of the coming ruin. Then, when the first day of his office and the helm of the country to be guided he seized, and the camp was under his command, as one untaught of the sea and ignorant to handle the deep by art, if he has taken charge of a wretched ship, holds himself the place of the winds, and to every storm gives the vessel to be tossed: the ship is borne wandering on the flood onto the rocks, his own right hand, the helmsman's, driving it— so the army is driven headlong, its arms snatched up, against the peoples of the Lydians and the seat consecrated of old from the origin of ancient Corythus, and the Maeonian colonists joined by the blood of their ancestors to the Italians, their stock intermingled.

Nor does the warning god delay the king of the Africans from his task, worth such great praise. Sleep had hidden all things and was giving forgetfulness to their anxious cares, when Juno, changed into the deity of the neighbouring pool and her wet brow girt with poplar leaves, stirs his heart with sudden cares and breaks the leader's rest with a voice not to be scorned: "O Hannibal, happy in fame and a name to be wept by Latium, if Fortune had created you for Ausonia, destined for the great gods—why do we hold back the fates? Drive off delay. Brief is the Fortune of great favour. As much as you vowed, when you swore the Dardan wars to your father, so much blood from an Ausonian body shall flow for you, and you shall sate your father's shades with slaughter. To us you shall pay your due honours, free of care. For I am that one whom, ringed with lofty mountains, the band sent from Tmolus surrounds—Trasimene of the shady pools." By these warnings he is moved, and the youth, glad in the deity, he straightway carries headlong over the ridge of the airy mountain. Apennine bristled with ice among the slippery rocks, mingling its pine-bearing head with the highest sky. The deep snow had hidden the timber, and on the lofty peak the hoary crest rose to the stars with crusted frost. He bids them go. Sooner does his glory seem to be quenched and to fall, if a stand be made at any mountains after the Alps. They climb the cloudy summits of the sheer crag. Nor does the conquering of the ridge end or soothe their toil: the flats swim, and with rotten ice in the melting waters the trackless fields stand flooded in a miry swamp. And now the leader's bare crown, amid such inhospitable places, is shaken by the cruelty of the sky, while down his face and his cheeks the eye runs. Easy is it to scorn the healers: he believes the longed-for time for war well bought at whatever peril. He spares not the honour of his face, provided he lose not his march, nor does he hesitate to give his other limbs as the price of war, if victory demand it, and he thinks it light enough to see the Capitol as victor, where to make for it and where to strike the Italian foe at close quarters. Having endured such things, at last among the savagery of the place they came to the longed-for lakes, where then in arms he would take ample atonement for his lost sight.

But behold, the senators were at hand, sent from Carthage. No small cause for the journey, nor glad were the tidings they brought. It was the custom among the peoples whom the stranger Dido founded, to seek the gods' favour with slaughter, and upon the blazing altars (unspeakable to tell) to place little children. The yearly urn brought back the pitiable lots, its rites imitating the sacred ways of Thoantean Diana. For him the discordant Hanno, of old hostile, by the custom of the gods sought out, by lot and fate, the offspring of Hannibal. But a nearer fear was from the wrath of the armed leader, and great before their eyes stood the image of his return. This Imilce makes harsher, her cheeks befouled and her hair torn, and fills the city with the clamour of her grief, as an Edonian woman on Pangaeus, stirred by the triennial rite, goes over the ridges and sighs within her breast for the enclosed Bacchus. So among the Tyrian mothers, as if set beneath the torches, she cries: "Ah, husband, in whatever quarter of the world you wage your wars, hither bear your standards. More violent is the foe here, here nearer. You now perhaps beneath the very walls of the Dardan city receive the quivering weapons upon your shield, unafraid, and brandishing the savage torch, carry fires to the Tarpeian roofs. Meanwhile your first home and only offspring, alas, in the bosom of his fatherland, is dragged to the Stygian altars. Go now, lay waste with the sword the Ausonian household gods and toil at forbidden roads. Go, unseal the pacts sworn by all the gods. So Carthage repays your rewards and even now pays you such honours. And further, what piety is this, to sprinkle the shrines with gore? Alas, the first causes of crime to wretched mortals, not to know the nature of the gods! Go, pray for what is just with pious incense, and turn away the cruel rites of slaughter. Gentle and akin to man is god. Thus far, I pray, let it be enough to have seen bullocks slain before the altars. Or if the gods wish the unspeakable, and it is fixed and settled, me, me, who bore him, consume with your vows. Why does it please to despoil the Libyan lands of this offspring? Or were the Aegates more to be wept, and the Punic realms sunk in the deep, if once, by bloody lot, so great a valour of my husband had been snatched away beforehand?" These words, in their wavering fear of gods and man alike, drew the senators to caution, and left it to him whether to refuse the lot or obey the gods' honour. Then indeed Imilce trembled with fear, scarce mistress of herself, dreading the harsh heart of her great-souled husband. Hearing this eagerly, the leader thus then speaks: "What, equalled to the gods, can Hannibal pay you not unequal to so great a gift? What rewards worthy of you shall I find, mother Carthage? Night and day I will bear arms, and from here I will make many a noble victim come from Ausonian Quirinus to your temples. But the boy, the heir of arms and war, shall be saved. Hope, O son, of mine and sole salvation of Tyrian affairs, while Hesperia threatens, remember to contend with the sons of Aeneas by land and sea, while life shall stand. Go on (the Alps lie open) and press on at my toil. You also, gods of my fathers, whose shrines are appeased with slaughter and who delight to be worshipped by the dread of mothers, turn hither your glad faces and your whole minds. For I prepare rites and toil at greater altars. You, Mago, take your stand on the top of the mountain opposite; you, Choaspes, draw nearer to the leftward hills; let Sychaeus lead through the dark places to the barriers and the gorge. But I, Trasimene, with my roving soldiery, headlong will range you over, and seek from the gods the offerings of war. For the god promises in no small things by open pledges which, once seen, men, you may carry back to your native city."

The Sidonian leader had seized the Etruscan hills with hidden soldiery, and through the deep silence of the night had settled in the windings of the woods with concealed arms. But on the left side a lake, overflowing in a vast pool, made wet the likeness of a sluggish sea and far and wide befouled the places nearby with much mud. These shallows, ruled of old by Faun-born Arnus, now, as the day rolls on, keep the name of Trasimene. A Lydian father, the glory of Tmolus, over the long sea had once brought the Maeonian youth to the Latin shores— Tyrrhenus—and had given names to the lands. He first revealed the unwonted murmurs of the trumpet to the nations and broke the idle silences with wars, nor, beyond measure in his vows, did he cherish his son for greater things. But, burning for the boy and stripped of chaste shame (for in beauty you could rival the gods, Trasimene), Agylle, seizing him on the shore, plunged him into her pools, a slippery nymph, that the youth, his mind caught by his first bloom, might warm to no slow arrow of Idalia. Comforting, the Naiads cherished deep within a green grotto the embraces, the youth trembling at the watery realm. Hence the lake holds the name of dowry, and, knowing of wanton marriage, far and wide Trasimene is named for the wave.

And now the dewy night was grazing with its course the black turning-post, nor had the Tithonian wife come forth from her bridal chamber, but stood gleaming on the very threshold, when the traveller would less deny that night had ceased than that day had begun: the consul was pressing on the difficult roads, going ahead of the very standards, and all rushed forward in a mingled mass—the cavalry, the light arms in no separate companies, and the foot-soldiers thrust into the throng, and the camp-followers' crowd, useless for war, filling everything with prophetic tumult, and seeking battle in the manner of those who flee. Then over the lake itself, breathing out a thick fog in blind gloom, far and wide had spoiled all the view for the wretched men, and in the cloak of black night the sky lay foul and pressed among the pitch-dark clouds. Nor did the wiles escape the Carthaginian: he sits, his sword laid by, hidden, and checks the hastening foe with no attacks. He is allowed to go on, and far the shore lies open as if in quiet peace, unguarded, soon to be a place from which there is no return. For under the narrow gorges, the path constricted, it led him into the trap, and twofold destruction pressed the men once received: here the crags, here the waters, hemmed the barrier. But a squadron kept watch from the shady summit of the mountain on the enemy's entrance, ready to have them under its blows as they fled back: just as a skilful fisherman by the glassy waters, weaving a light wicker basket with a wide mouth, ties the inner parts more carefully, and through the middle of the belly gradually narrowing weaves together the pressed tips, and by the trick of the narrowed opening keeps from returning the fish, easy of entrance, that he has drawn from the sea.

Meanwhile, more swiftly the consul kept bidding the standards be driven on, shaken in mind by the whirlwind of the fates, until the horses of the sun, lifting from the sea their flame-bearing chariot, scattered the day. And now, the orb reborn, Titan had washed away the fogs, and slowly the gloom flowed away into the earth, dissolved in the bright clear sky. Then the bird—an ancient auspice, by the custom of the Latin peoples, when they prepare for war and explore the minds of the gods about the outcome—as if foreknowing of grief refused to feed and shunned its food with lamentation. Nor did the bull cease to bellow mournfully at the altars with hoarse sound, and bearing the axe pressed to its neck with wavering neck it left the altar. Even as they strive to wrench up the standards with great effort, foul gore, exulting, burst from the torn earth into the faces of those straining, and the black parent earth herself gave to the wretched men in her bloody lap the tokens of slaughter to come. And besides these, the father of the gods, shaking the lands and the sea with thunder, hurled the lightnings snatched from the forges of the Cyclopes into the Tyrrhenian waters of Trasimene, and, struck by the heavenly flame across the open pools, the lake smoked, and the fires burned amid the waves. Alas, vain the warnings, and vain the prodigies that delay the Fates! Alas, the gods lesser than to contend with the fates! And here a man, excellent of tongue and of proud name, Corvinus, on whose Phoebean helmet the tawny bird, displaying the emblem of his ancestor's battle, perches, himself full of the god, and as terror frightened his comrades, mingles warnings with prayers and begins with these words: "By the Trojan flames and the Tarpeian rocks, by the walls of our fathers, consul, and by the pledges of our children hanging on the outcome of our battle, we beg that you yield to the gods, and await the right time for battle. The same gods will give both fields and a day for fighting: only do not scorn to wait for the gods to favour. When the hour shines forth that shall bring bloody slaughter to Libya, then the standards will follow, wrenched up by no hand, and the bird, undaunted, will rejoice to feed, and the pious earth will spew no blood. Or does it escape you, excellent in war, how much wicked Fortune can do in this place? The foe sits opposite, facing us, but around the wooded ridges threaten ambush, nor on the left does escape lie open through the standing waters, and the gorges stand with a narrow track. If it is your heart's wish to contend with wiles and to draw out the war, meanwhile Servilius will be at hand with swift arms, whose command is equal and whose strength matches his legions. We must fight by cunning. Lighter is the leader's praise that lies in the sword-hand." Such things Corvinus, and the foremost men everywhere added the words of those who prayed, and each, divided in his fear, now beseeches the gods that they oppose not Flaminius, then again beseeches Flaminius not to persist in contending with the dwellers of heaven. The more keenly at this the leader's kindled anger had risen, and, raging at the news that allied forces would not be wanting: "Is it thus," he says, "that you watched me rushing into the wars of the Boii, when so great a plague and a dread mob were pressing on, and the Tarpeian rock again was afraid? What souls then with my right hand, what bodies did I lay low, sprung from the angered earth and scarcely yielding their lives to a single wound! Their huge limbs lay over the fields, and now they press the ploughlands with their great bones. Forsooth, let Servilius join his arms to this late glory, that I may not be able to conquer with the triumph divided, and, content with a share of the honour, fall idle? No doubt the gods warn us. Do not imagine the gods like to yourselves, who tremble at the war-trumpets. Great enough against the foe the augur sword is at hand, and a fair and soldier-worthy auspice it is that the right hand gives to Latium in arms. Or is it settled, Corvinus, that the consul keep himself shut within an idle rampart, while the Carthaginian now seizes the high walls of Arretium, now tears down the citadel of Corythus, hence makes for the Clusian fields, and at last to the walls of Rome unharmed presses his march? Shameful under arms is empty superstition: in the breast of the fighting man the goddess Virtue alone flourishes. By dark nights the columns of the shades stand round me, who roll in the flood of the Trebia and in the waters of Eridanus, an unburied youth."

No delay. Now in the midst of the assembly and beneath the very standards he was fitting on, inexorable to none, his final arms. With bronze and the tawny back of a sea-calf his helmet was guarded, on whose crest, rising up, a triple crest pours out its plumes with Suebian hair: Scylla above, whirling the weight of a broken oar, loomed and bared the savage gapings of her dogs, the noble spoil of Gargenus, which, proud at the slain king of the Boii, the victor had fitted, unmarred, to his head, and bore as a glory into all his battles. He puts on his breastplate: its twisted, woven hooks the scale roughens with raw iron and gold intermixed. Then he takes his shield, which once, splashed with slaughters, Celtic gore had adorned, and in a dripping cave a she-wolf, as though caressing her cub, fondling the boyish limbs, was nursing the mighty nursling of Assaracus toward heaven. Then he fits a sword to his side and a spear to his right hand. His steed stands and fierce frets at the wet bridle, draped with a Caucasian tiger, its body striped. Then, taken up by his horse, where the narrow paths allow, he goes now to these, now to those, and fills them with exhortations: "It is your task and your glory to bear the fixed-up face of the Carthaginian leader through the city, a sight for your parents. This one head, for all of them, will be enough. Let each man recall to himself harsh spurs: 'My brother, alas, my brother lies on the black banks of Ticinus,' 'But my son measures out the deep pools of Eridanus without a funeral.' These things let each say to himself; but he in whom is no fury of private grief, let him truly take up great causes from the common store, things to dig into the breast great wraths— the Alps broken through, and Saguntum that suffered unspeakable things, and those whom it is sin to overpass, the name of the forbidden Iberus, now touching the Tiber. For while the augur and the entrails sought by the fibres and the vain soothsayer delay us, this alone now remains—to plant our camp on the Tarpeian rock."

Turbid, he says these things, and seeing among the close thousands a warrior fitting on his black plumes: "Yours, Orfitus, is the task, yours," he says, "this contest is—who shall bear the spoils of honour, to willing Jove the offering hung from a bloody bier. For why should this glory be brought forth by another hand?" Then, riding past on his horse, when amid the battles a known voice reached him: "Far from here the warlike shout shows you to me, Murranus," he says, "and I see you raging already with Tyrian slaughter. How great a praise comes! But, I beg, these narrow places of the ground, opened by the sword, set free." Then, knowing Aequanus, son of Soracte, outstanding in body and arms, to whom in his father's land is a custom, when the pious Archer rejoices at the kindled heaps, joyfully to carry the entrails three times through the harmless fires: "So may you always tread the Apollonian coals unharmed, and, victor of the heat, bring back to the altars your solemn gifts to serene Phoebus: conceive," he says, "a frenzy worthy of your deeds, Aequanus, and of your wounds. With you as comrade of slaughter and wrath I would not doubt to penetrate the midst of the Marmaridae's phalanx and to burst into the squadrons of the Cinyphian band."

Nor now any longer can he bear warnings and words that delay Mars: that which the sons of Aeneas shall weep for in a long age, together the deadly war-trumpets sounded the signal, and the trumpet broke the air with its terrifying shrieks. Alas the grief, alas the tears, not late even after so many ages! I shudder as at a hanging evil, as if the Tyrian leader were calling to arms. From the lurking hills the Asturian and the Libyan and the Balearian, savage with his twisted sling, burst forth, and many a Mace and Garamantian and Numidian, then—than whom no other swifter brought a venal right hand to battle or approved of hired wars— the Cantabrian and the Vascon with the covering of his helmet scorned. On this side the crags alike, on that the lake, on that arms, and at once a consonant voice presses on, while in turn the shout for the signal spreads round through the hills, the Tyrian ring encircling.

The gods turned away their faces and gave place, not willingly, to a greater fate; Mars himself is stunned at the fortune of the Libyan tyrant, and Venus, her hair disordered, weeps over it, and Apollo, carried to Delos, soothes with his mournful quill the sad grief. Juno alone, sitting on the summit of Apennine, awaits the dread slaughter with pitiless heart.

The first cohorts of the Picentes, when, as if scattered by a burst whirlwind, they saw the columns and Hannibal rush on, attack of their own accord, and seek penalties for the death to come, the victor thrown into confusion—the youth kindled, and as though, the dreaded heaven snatched away, free, sends with their own hands the forestalled offerings. A cloud of javelins is poured with single effort and harmonious daring upon the Carthaginians, and, repulsed, they lower their pierced shields under the curved weight of the weapon. The more keenly at this in turn the Libyan (and the presence of the savage leader spurs him on), each urging the other in his turn, they press on, and with pressed breast drive breast against breast. Bellona herself, shaking her torch and her yellow hair sprinkled with much blood, ranges through the midst of the lines. There hisses beneath the black breast of the Tartarean goddess a deadly murmur, and bristling with deadly song the trumpet drives the frenzied minds into the contests. For these, adversity nurses their wraths, and the raw goad of fortune as it rushes on bids them cast away the hope of safety: those a favouring god and Victory, smiling with glad face, sharpen, and they enjoy the favour of Mars. Lateranus, carried away by a fair love of slaughter, while he follows his right hand, had penetrated into the midst of the foe. When Lentulus, flourishing in equal age, saw him provoking the fates too much in battle and amid too much blood among the hostile bands in unequal warfare, he rouses himself with keen effort and forestalls cruel Bagas, who was already bringing wounds near to the back of the fighting man—swifter than the spear, and joins himself as a comrade to the hard chances. Then eager they gather their arms together, and gleaming from twin brows they flash: their lofty heads shine with matching crests. Driven against them by chance (for who would dare to bear opposing arms, unless one whom the god had condemned to the depths of the Stygian night?), Syrticus, running down from the high mountain, bore broken-off oak-clubs and, fiercely shaking the weight of a knotted branch, burned in vain with a love of double slaughter: "Not here will the Aegates and the shores treacherous to sailors, O youths, and the fortune stirred by new storms without Mars, the sea give you in war. Once victors of the deep, learn what kind of warrior the Libyan is in the midst of the land, and yield your realms to the better man." And at once with the hostile weight of the lopped tree he pressed Lateranus, joining taunts to the fight. Lentulus, gnashing at him in anger: "Trasimene will climb into the high hills sooner than that branch drip with pious blood," and, sinking down with effort, he pierced the flank of the man as he strained, raised on tiptoe. Then hot blood overflows from the black lung through the gaping entrails.

Nor less, with right hands kindled to mutual deaths, in another part of the field the frenzy rages. Tall Iertes beheads Nerius. By Rullus, richest of land, you fall, noble Volunx, nor did the weights shut up in your secret treasuries, nor your palace once gleaming with ancestral ivory, nor the native huts you possessed profit you. What avail things snatched, what to the nations the thirst for gold, never quenched? One whom but now Fortune by her cherishing stuffed full with heaped-up wealth and rich gifts, the boatman will carry naked in his Tartarean skiff. Nearby, the warrior Appius with youthful daring was opening up the field with slaughter, and where valour was greatest and vigour aspiring to none, there he sought his glory. Meeting him Atlans—Atlans from the Iberian shore, in vain the far-off tiller of the farthest sand— strikes his face with a spear, and lightly from the surface of the body the point at its edge tastes the noble blood. The threats thundered, and his violent eyes blazed with new flames. He rages and lightnings through all the throng of those in his way; but the wound shut beneath his helmet commends his warlike limbs with the trickling blood. Then indeed you might see the youth, trembling and striving to hide himself among his comrades, as when before the tigress the doe of Hyrcania, hard pressed, trembles, or, terrified, the dove, seeing the hawk in the cloud, gathers in her wings, or the hare goes beneath the brambles, if in the white air it has felt the eagle balancing its swoop. He strikes the face with his quick sword, then mows off the man's neck and his flashing right hand, and, fiercer with success, changes his foe.

There stood, bearing into the wars a gleaming axe, a Cinyphian, and the wretched son-in-law of Mago, longing to enter the battle before his eyes in hope of praise, Isalcas, swollen at his Sidonian bride and proud of the vain pact of the marriage-torch promised after the Dardan battles. At him fierce Appius hurls his violent wraths, and as he tries to balance the heavy axe at his brow, rising higher he drives the blow above the helmet. But the frail sword is loosed by the strong effort on the Cinyphian bronze, and Isalcas, of no different lot, brushed the boss aside, his useless blow uncertain. Then a stone that he could never have wrenched from the ground, had not grim anger given him strength, Appius hurls, panting, and as the man falls backward in his slip onto his back, he presses him with the mass of the rock and crushes his broken bones. His son-in-law saw him, mingling battles on the joined field, falling, and tears were poured beneath his helmet with a groan, and swift he rushed: the pacts lately given kindle his spirit, and the hoped-for grandchildren. And now he was at hand, and was surveying with his gaze the man's shield and huge limbs, and the nearer light of the gleaming helmet at the front had a little slowed his savage wrath. Not otherwise, hurled headlong down from a shady lookout, the lion, sinking on the plain, draws together his crouched limbs, when he has seen the horns of a fierce bull nearby, though long hunger goad him: now, savage, he marvels at the muscles on the high-rising neck, now at the grim eyes beneath the shaggy brow, and watches him already moving his standards and, the sand scattered, plotting the fight. Here first, hurling his weapon, thus Appius begins: "If you have any piety, do not abandon the pact you struck, and as father-in-law accompany your son-in-law." Swift through the coverings and the delays of bronze the spear stood in his left arm. But against him the Libyan, no words, but burning he balances his spear, the memorable gift of his great brother, which the victor, beneath the walls of Saguntum, having slain Durius, had taken from him, and given to his brother to carry into the battles, a pledge of the renowned fight. The huge weapon, through the man's arms and through his face, aided by the effort of his grief, drove home its deadly blow, and the bloodless hands of the man, as he tried to wrench out the iron, fell upon the wound. On the plain lies a name famous to Maeonia, and a great part of the Italian ruin, Appius. The lakes trembled, and the body shrank away as Trasimene drew in its waters: gasping out his life with bloody mouth he presses the weapon and murmurs against the bitten spear.

Nor of better fate, Mamercus paid the penalty with his whole body, wounded by no foe. For through the opposing ranks, where the Lusitanian dire band roused the battles, the standard snatched with the blood of the slain standard-bearer, he was bearing with great effort, and unhappy was calling back the wavering standards of his men. But the maddened cohort, kindled with proud daring, whatever each carried in his own hand as a missile, whatever the earth offered, scarce passable with scattered weapons, cast at once alike, and many spears found in his body no empty place, his bones pierced through.

Meanwhile the leader of Libya flies up, troubled by anger at his brother's wound, and seeing the gore, whether the point was in his side, whether with its whole weight the weapon had settled, frantic he kept asking his brother and his comrades. And when he learned that the fear of death was far off and the things lighter than his alarm, sheltered by his own shield, headlong from the line he snatches him, and in a camp safe from the whirlwind of battle set him down. Hence more swiftly the healing arts and the help of aged Synhalus he calls. To anoint a wound with the juices of herbs, and to draw out the iron from the body by a charm, and to send sleep to a touched water-snake, this man surpassed all, and his name was thence renowned through the cities and along the shores of the Paraetonian Syrtis. He himself once, Garamantian Hammon the father, of old first had given to Synhalus to know how to soothe by healing the bites of beasts and the heavy blows of weapons. And he then, dying, showed the heavenly gifts to his son, and the son passed on to the honour of his heir his father's arts. Following him then, of no lighter fame, Synhalus, skilled in the Garamantian things shown to him, increased them by his zeal, and with many an image numbered his ancient ancestor, the companion of Hammon. Then bearing his ancestral medicines with a gentle right hand, more swiftly, girt in the custom of twisted cloaks, he soothed with water the wound cleansed of its blood. But Mago, turning over in his mind the spoils and the slaying of the slain foe, drove from his breast his brother's cares with words, and eased the chance with praise: "Spare your fear, my brother. No medicines greater than my own misfortunes will you bring: Appius lies, driven by my spear to the shades. If life should leave me, enough has been done for us: gladly will I follow the foe to the shades."

While these things turn the leaders from the open field and hold them in the rampart, the consul, watching from a high mound the Carthaginian withdrawing from the column, and the dark cloud of war hide itself in the camp, turbid at once attacks the wedges of the trembling men, mournful in soldiery, and with sudden panic loosens the lines already thinning out. Then with fierce voice he demands his horse and rushes into the contests of the central valley. So when Jupiter dashes against the earth a downpour crashing with rattling hail, having heaped up the high Alps now with lightning, now the Ceraunian heights mingled with heaven, together earth and sea and air trembled, and Tartarus itself is shaken, the world stirred, not otherwise upon the astounded Carthaginians fell, in unforeseen whirlwind, an unexpected plague, and a cold horror at the sight of the consul spread beneath the bones of the wretched men. He goes in the midst, and rushing with the sword opens a broad path through the thickest. The shout, with the varied division of voices, bears the frenzy of war to the gods above and beats upon the stars, as when Father Ocean with savage Tethys strikes Herculean Calpe, and into the gnawed entrails of the mountain hurls the whirling sea with barking waves: the crags give a groan, and Tartessus, divided by broad lands, hears the waves broken upon the rocks, Lixus hears it, parted by no small flood.

Before all, by a javelin deceiving silently through the air, Bogus falls, who first at the ill-omened river Ticinus had hurled his swift spear against the Rutulians. He had believed for himself long life and a crowd of grandchildren, deceived by vain signs in the bird. But to break the boundaries of the Fates by augury is granted to no one: he falls amid the weapons, looking up with bloody eyes at the sky, and demands again of the gods the time of his promised old age, now in the midst of death. Nor was it granted Bagasus to exult, or left unpunished that before the consul's eyes he had robbed Libo of life. That glory of laurel-bearing ancestors and his vigorous youth flourished, but the Massylian sword had cut down his head as the down softened his cheek, and with swift death the barbarian warrior had blotted out his green years. Yet to have implored Flaminius, now in his last death, was not in vain. For straightway from the foe was torn away his neck along with his face: it helped to punish the victor by a fierce example and to give back the death he had dealt.

What god, O Muses, in matching words could unfold so many deaths, and to such great shades who could bring laments worthy in song? The young men in the first bloom of life, contending in the glory of falling, and on the very threshold of death the raw deeds of men, and the frenzy beneath the breast pierced by weapons? Foe and foe are laid low in turn by vast onsets, nor is there leisure to despoil and to turn the mind to plunder. The love of slaughter urges, while his brother's wound holds the foe shut up in the camp, and now with javelins, now with the sword he pours forth and rushes—the consul, now seen on horseback amid the thousands of fighters, now on foot in fierce battle before the eagles and the standards. The impious valley flows with streams of blood, and the mounds and the hollow rocks imitate the clash of arms and the breathing of horses.

Mingling the field, bearing into the battles the strength of limbs loftier than human, and at the sight of his fearsome giant body the trembling wings he turned, Othrys the Marmarian: above both columns his huge shoulders lifted his head, and the shaggy hair of his grim brow and his beard, rivalling his locks, shadowed his gaping mouth; on this side his breast, bristling with dread squalor and shaggy with wild bristles, stood up rough. To draw near the man and to bring closer combat no one dared. Like a beast in an open field he was assailed with safe weapons from the column. At last, as he bore his mad face against the backs of the scattered men with a roar, a Gortynian reed, through the silent clouds on its quiet wing, entered his grim eye and turned the man away. At the columns of the fleeing man the consul hurls a javelin from behind, which broke into his bare ribs through the covering, and from his shaggy breast first showed its point. Swiftly he tries to wrench out where he sees the iron rising with its gleaming tip, until, the blood poured out abundantly far and wide, he sank down dying and pressed the weapon into the wound. His overflowing breath blew across the neighbouring field, the dust stirred, and scattered the cloud into the air.

Nor less meanwhile on the mounds and in the woods raged Mars in different places, and over the heights with varied battle the rocks and brambles gleamed, dripping with slaughter. The destruction of the trembling, and the cause of death and bitter carnage, was Sychaeus. He had struck Murranus from afar with a spear, than whom no other, when the wars were silent, more sweetly struck the Oeagrian strings with the quill. He fell in the great wood, and beneath the very death sought his father's mountains and the Aequana fields, happy in Bacchus, and Surrentum, soft with the healthful Zephyr. Sychaeus had added a comrade to the wretched man, and the victor rejoiced in the grim novelty of the fierce battle. For while he follows the scattered men, he had penetrated into a deep wood, and leaning against the blows of an ancient elm guarded his back with the trunk, and in vain Tauranus with his last voice was calling the comrades he had left. The Sidonian point pierced the youth through, and, his limbs pierced through, stuck fast in the wood set against it.

What was it for you, what wrath of the gods, or what dread, sitting in your sinister mind, men? You who, Mars abandoned, sought the help of branches. Not an even counsellor in hard straits, surely, is fear. The harsh outcome convicts by the event the counsels of crooked dread. An aged ilex stretched its lofty branches into the air, inserting above the great shadowy woods its high head among the lofty clouds, the likeness (if it stood in the open field) of a grove, and far and wide held the earth with the black shadow of its leafy oak. An equal oak nearby, having striven through a long age to lift its top beneath the stars with hoary crown, loosened its spreading leaves on its wide-spread trunk and shadowed with its foliage the heights of the topmost mountain. Hither the Hennaean cohort, which Arethusa, your king had sent from the Sicilian shores, not knowing to defend against death its disgrace, and changed in mind by excessive dread, betook itself in rivalry, and climbing in turn pressed the nodding branches with uncertain weight. Soon one above another, while they strive to stand in safety, part of them shaken off (for the rotten fragment of the branches and its age had deceived them, the tree little to be trusted), part hang in dread amid the weapons on the lofty top. Hastening to consume them all, troubled, with one plague, Sychaeus seizes his bronze-bound axe, long since meant for war, his shield laid down, his weapons changed. His comrades' right hands fall to, and with a great crash the tree, struck, groans, sinking beneath the frequent blows. The unhappy throng sways on the shaken trunk, as, when the Zephyr shakes the ancient groves with its blast, the bird, scarce clinging to the whole leaf of the trembling top, is tossed, its nest swaying with it. At last, overcome by many an axe-stroke, it fell, the unhappy oak, a refuge to the wretched and inhospitable, and crushed the men's spread-out limbs in its spacious ruin.

Then other shapes of disaster. Bordering the pine-torches the ilex gleams and is wrapped in swift fire. And now, swelling among the leaves in the dry wood, Vulcan with savage whirlwinds twists the panting globes of flames with their heat and scorches the tops. Nor meanwhile do the weapons cease. The half-burnt bodies of the groaning men fall, embracing the burning branches.

Amid these pitiable contests of men, behold, the consul was at hand, rolling wrath and destruction against Sychaeus. But the youth, in the doubtful crisis of so great a battle, forestalls the outcome, to test it first with his weapon. On the middle of the shield its point stood lightly on the surface of the bronze, and was forbidden to pass through the opposing wickerwork. But the consul does not prepare to trust the fortune of the longed-for slaughter to a hurled weapon, but with the sword he drains his side: nor did the coverings of the raw shield slow him. The unhappy man slips and seeks with bloody mouth the earth, gasping out his life. Then, the cold of Styx diffusing itself through his limbs, the death flowing into his vitals he receives, and composes his eyes in a long sleep.

And while Mars, mingled with various chances, alternates these sad things, now, the camp abandoned, Mago, now the leader of Libya, were hurrying their hastening standards at a swift run, and were eager to make up for the lost time with the slaughter of men and to pay it back with much gore. A mass goes whirling a cloud of dust in a black whirlwind, and the field rises with the sands lifted up, and wherever the leader, bearing his step, turns his tracks, round about a storm driven by a billowing squall rolls and covers the high mountains with gloom. Fontanus fell, pierced through the thigh, Buta through his tuneful throat, and from the pressed-in wound the point looked forth at his back. Him sad Fregellae mourned, manifold in ancestors, him his mother Anagnia wept. Not unlike was your fortune, Laevinus, but your daring not the same. For you do not attempt to clash with the Tyrian king, but a chosen man, Ithemon, a match for the contest, was the leader of the Autololians; whom, his hamstring cut, while you despoil him, with a pitiless whirlwind into your ribs the heavy ash-spear burst, and your limbs, collapsed beneath the blow, fell in sudden ruin upon the foe poured out beneath you. . . . Whom, after the leader of Libya sees exulting in fierce valour (for to him, headlong from the wound, Arauricus, distrusting his light arms, was giving his back), the more keenly at this, kindled to wrath by the fair Mars, and thinking himself worthy to go into the contests hand to hand with the savage man, at him as he draws the weapon from the body he flies, and piercing his breast: "Praiseworthy in toils, whoever you are, by no other right hand was it fitting you should fall. Carry to the shades the glory of your death. Were not your race of Italian origin, you would go off granted your life." Then he makes for Fadus and old Labicus, skilled in war, to whom Hamilcar, having once clashed in the Sicilian lands, had given a famous name in a renowned contest. Forgetful of his years and unmindful of his age, into arms that one indeed went with a raw spirit and most green in his wrath, but vain blows betrayed his old age, cold in war: the idle fire crackled on the empty stubble and gave a hollow flame without strength. Whom, after the leader received him, his ancestral squire pointing him out as proud, the Carthaginian: "The contests of your first battle pay for now here," he said: "Hamilcar, well known, drags you to the shades by this right hand." Then he balances from his ear, hurling the javelin, and pierces him through as he turns himself into the wound. The blood, the point drawn out, befouled his white hair, and ended his long toils with death. Nor less does he behead Herminius in his first arms, accustomed, Trasimene, to drain your lakes with plundering hooks and to draw the nourishment of his father's old age through the lying pools on the hanging line.

Meanwhile, the lifeless Sychaeus upon his arms the mourning Carthaginians were carrying, and bearing his body to the camp. When the leader saw them rushing on with a sad cry, struck in his breast with prophetic grief: "What grief, O comrades," he says, "or what wrath of the gods has snatched him from us? Has the black day, Sychaeus, with hastened funeral, plucked you, burning with love of praise and excessive love of the first battle?" And as, the groan given, the tears of the bearers assented, and the author of the slaughter was named alike to the mourners, "I see," he says, "the fair wound beneath your facing breast of the Trojan point. Worthy of Carthage, worthy of Hasdrubal, you will go to the shades, nor will your best mother mourn you unlike your ancestors, nor, seeing you beneath the Stygian shade degenerate, will our Hamilcar shun you. But let Flaminius, the cause of so sad a grief, lessen my mourning by his own death. This pomp shall follow your obsequies, and impious Rome, too late, will wish it had bought at any price not to have profaned the body of my Sychaeus with the sword."

So saying, he twists the smoking vapour from his mouth, and his wrath drives out the panted murmur from his breast, as when the enclosed liquid overflows with much heat in the kindled waves, and rages when the cauldron is burnt dry. Then headlong he rushes into the midst and wearies Flaminius alone, assailing him. Nor more slowly than the word did that one take up the wars, and nearer Mars had begun to rise, and now each stood joined upon the field, when a sudden crash through the rocks, and stirred all at once— a fearful thing—the hills and the topmost peaks trembled over all their ridges. The woods nod on the pine-bearing summit, and the broken crags fall down upon the columns. Deep within, its caverns wrenched apart, the splitting earth bellows from its depths, and breaks open no small chasm, and far and wide the immense gulf shows the Stygian shades with its wide-gaping jaws, and the shades of the deep dreaded the ancient day. The black lake, lifted into the high mountains and shaken from its ancestral seat, washed the Tyrrhenian woods with unknown spray. And now the same storm and dire plague both laid low and carried off the peoples and the towns of great kings. And besides these, the rivers, flowing backward, fought against the mountains, and the sea turned its waves backward. The mountain abandoned, the Apennine-dwelling Fauns fled to the shores. Yet the soldier kept fighting (alas, the madness of war!), tossed about on the staggering ground, and his trembling weapons, falling as the earth gave way beneath him, he hurled at the foe, until, driven, he turned his wandering course to the shores, his mind bereft, and the Daunian youth was carried into the pools. The consul rebuked their flight (for, snatched away by the whirlwind of the stirred earth, he had fallen): "What then, what, I beg, remains, alas, for the fugitives? See, you lead Hannibal to the walls of Rome, you give to the Tarpeian roofs of the Thunderer torches and the sword. Stand, soldier, and learn keen battles from me, or, if to fight is denied you, learn to die. Flaminius will give to those to come no worthless example. Let not the Libyan, let not the Cantabrian ever see the back of a consul. Alone, if so great a longing and madness for flight is in you, all the weapons alone I consume with my breast, and dying, with this soul fleeing through the air, I will call your right hands back to the battles."

And while he recalls these things and goes to meet the dense foe, fierce in face and mind Ducarius flies up. The man had a clan-name keen, and once, when the bands of the Boii were scattered by his fathers, he bore the ancient wounds of a barbarian mind, and recognizing the proud victor's face: "Are you," he says, "that greatest terror of the Boii? It pleases me to learn this with my weapon, whether blood remains from the wound of so great a body. Nor let it repent you, countrymen, to sacrifice this head to the brave shades: he it was who, standing on his chariot, drove our conquered fathers to the high Capitol. The avenging hour calls." Then at once, with weapons poured from every side, he is overwhelmed, and, covered by the cloud rushing through the air, he left to no right hand to boast that Flaminius had fallen by its own. Nor, the leader slain, was the battle prolonged further. For in a dense column the foremost of the youth, because of the sinister crises of war hostile to the gods and to their own right hands, and reckoning to see the Carthaginian victorious worse than death, more swiftly all upon the limbs of the leader and his prostrate body in a great struggle cast weapons and bodies and, in unhappy war, bloody hands. So, dense with the heap of slaughter, they covered the man as with a tomb. Then, the carnage scattered through the waves, through the woods, and through the valley deep with blood, borne into the midst of the bands, his brother accompanying him, the Carthaginian, among the slain youths: "What wounds you behold, what deaths!" he says, "every right hand grips the iron, and the soldier lies armed, keeping up the contests. These, see, these deaths look upon, our cohorts! On their brows the threats endure, and the wraths stand in their faces. And I fear lest the land which, fertile, breeds great-souled men of such noble nature, has been destined by the fates for it to hold empire, and by these very disasters conquer the world."
So saying, he yielded to the night; and an end to the slaughter the darkness gave, poured in as the sun withdrew.

Now Titan, whom the Tartessian sea had loosed, diffused into night, was yoking his horses on the Eastern shores, and the Seres, first uncovered by the new Phaethon, were seeking again the fleece in their wool-bearing groves, and the foul carnage lay before their eyes, and nearer was disclosed the work of mad Mars: arms and men at once and horse mingled with them, and the right hands of the slain clinging in the wound of the foe, and everywhere shields and plumes and trunks of bodies without their heads, and the sword lay broken on the hard bones. Nor was it lacking to see the eyes of the half-dead seeking the sky in vain. Then the lake foaming with gore, and corpses floating on the surface of the sea, robbed forever of their burial mounds.

Yet not all Italian valour had fallen amid the disasters. A Bruttian, on the huge heap of pitiable slaughter, showing the unequal battle with his pierced body, had scarcely lifted his sad head and was dragging his maimed limbs through the carnage, his sinews slipping apart between, slender of means, leaning on no father or tongue, but harsh with the sword, nor did any man of the Volscian race redeem more years by a great-souled death. As a boy he had longed to add himself to the camp, the down upon his cheek, and to keen Flaminius he had been a man worth note, when the victor in war, the gods more favourable, was overwhelming the Celtic arms. Hence the honour and the guardianship of the sacred bird in every battle: from this his glory nursed the cause of his death. For, certain of death when he could not keep the Carthaginians from the captured eagle, after he had seen the fates sink down and the battle incline in a great ruin, he was preparing meanwhile to hide it and entrust it to the earth. But, overcome by sudden weapons, he laid his slipping limbs upon it and covered it with a feigned death. But when the light, returned from the Stygian night and the wretched sleep, came back, with a spear from the heap of a nearby corpse he raises himself, and, strong with his whole effort, the earth wide, soaked with slaughter and easy to part, with his sword he digs, and, adoring the buried likeness of the unhappy eagle, levels the sands with his languid palms. Then the last thin breath of the weary man passed away into the air, and sent his great soul down beneath Tartarus.

Nearby one could see, demanding for itself a song deserved, the sacred frenzy of valour. Laevinus, from high Privernum, distinguished by the honour of the Latin vine-staff, lay himself lifeless upon the lifeless Nasamonian Tyres: no spear for the man, no sword: in the narrow strait Chance had carried off his arms. Yet in the naked contest grief found a weapon for Mars. With bloody mouth he fought, and the tooth served the turn of iron for his wrath. Now the nostrils are mangled and the eyes befouled by the bite, now the head is maimed, the ears torn away, and the very brow is gnawed away in dreadful fashion, and the gaping mouth flows with blood; nor was there satiety, until the breath should leave the chewing mouth and black death hold the jaws filled.

While sad valour offers such wonders, meanwhile the fleeing wounded throng is tossed in scattered chance, and through the woods, by trackless and blind ways, borne off by stealth with many a wound, they measure the lonely fields through the night. Every sound and breeze terrifies them, and the bird stirred by its light wing. No sleep or rest for the mind. Harshly now Mago drives the stunned men with bitter spear, now towering Hannibal. Serranus, a famous name, your offspring, Regulus, you who, your fame swelling through a long age, will be remembered as one who kept faith with the faithless Carthaginians, shining in his first bloom—alas, by his father's auspices he had entered upon the Punic wars, and his wretched mother and his sweet household gods he was seeking again with sad lot, wounded. No comrade of his survived, and none to bring help to his black wounds: through trackless ways, leaning on his broken spear and snatched away by the stealth of the dark night, he was bearing his silent journey into the Perusine fields. Here, wearied, whatever fates might be given him there, he was knocking at the threshold of a small dwelling, when Marus, unrolling his limbs from the couch, not slow (he was an old soldier of the father, and had handled battles, no deaf to fame), comes forth, the lights renewed at the hearth and at the poor Vesta, holding out his lamp. And when he recognized the face and the man sick with dread wounds and—pitiable to see— his slipping steps propped on the broken-off shaft, his ears already wounded by the rumour of the deadly evil: "What crime do I behold, O born to too much life and too much to bear adversity? You, greatest of leaders, I saw, when with your captive face you terrified the citadel of Carthage, the reproach and the fault of the Thunderer, fall, and I drank in a grief that not even the Sidonian dwellings, overthrown, could drive from my heart. Where are you, gods, see, again? Regulus gives his breast to the iron, and perjured Carthage cuts down the rising stock of so great a house." Then he lays the sick limbs on the couch, and, no novice to bear medicines (for he was practised in wars), now cleanses the wounds with water, now soothes them with juices. Then he binds them, and wraps the wool with gentle touch, and softens the numbed limbs. Then the old man's care is to drive off from the weary man's sad mouth its thirst and to summon his strength with a frugal table. And after these were hastened, sleep at last applies its gifts and pours gentle rest through his limbs. And before the day had risen, Marus presses on the wound's burning: to heal by tried methods, and, having put off his old age, he ministers the welcome warmth with anxious devotion.

Here the youth, lifting his sad face to the stars with a groan and tears at once: "If, not yet hating the Tarpeian heights, you have not condemned the sceptre of Quirinus, look on the last fortunes of the Italians and on Ausonia falling," he says, "father, and at last turn upon the Trojan storms your equal eyes. We have lost the Alps, nor since then is there a limit to our disasters: Ticinus, and Eridanus black with carnage, and you, marked by Sidonian trophies, Trebia, and the tearful land of Arnus. But why do I tell these things? How much heavier, see, the force of evils! I saw the waters of Trasimene swelling with slaughters, and I saw Flaminius falling amid the weapons, the prostrate mass of men. I call to witness, my deities, the shades, that I sought a death worthy then of my father's nobility by the slaughter of the foe, had not the sad fates denied us death, as once they denied it to my father." The old man, striving to soothe by his words the rest of his lament as he heaped it up, speaks out: "By our fathers' custom, bravest one, let us bear whatever hardship is at hand and the bowed-down state of things. By the law of the gods, on the steep path of life, through varied chances the wheel of the age rolls headlong. Enough for you, enough great and published through all the world stand the proofs of your house: that sacred man, inferior to no deity, that father of yours, won high glories by standing against adversity, nor put off any valour before his breath left his struggling limbs. My age had scarcely completed my boyish time, when Regulus in his first years was marking his cheeks with down. I joined him as comrade, and we made allies of all our years, until it seemed good to the gods to extinguish the light of the Italian race, in whose noble breast nurturing Faith had taken her seat and, embracing his mind, held it. He gave us this sword as the equal of great honours and as a reward of valour, and—what you now see grimed with smoke— the bridle (but there is a silver gleam upon them). Nor after such gifts was Marus, as a knight, not set before any man. But the spear surpassed all my honours. Why you see me pour to it the liquids of Lyaeus, it is worth your while to learn the cause.

Turbid, with slow pace, the Bagrada furrows the dry sands, by no river in the Libyan bounds surpassed in spreading its muddy waters more widely and enfolding the open fields with its stagnant shallow. Here, in our zeal for water, of which the land is not lavish, glad we settled along the banks in the savage fields. A sluggish grove nearby, with pale shades, kept a Stygian wood without sun, and a thick breath, bursting through the air, breathed out a foul odour. Within, a dreadful house, and in a curved monstrous cave beneath the earth, a hollow, and sad darkness without light. The horror returns to my mind. A deadly monster, born of the wrath of the earth, whose like scarcely any age of men shall have seen, a serpent, stretched out a hundred cubits long, inhabited the deadly bank and the Avernian groves. The maw of its immense belly and its paunch heavy with venom it sated with captured lions at the spring, or with the herds driven to the river by the sun's burning torch, and with birds drawn through the air by the foul oppression and felled by its breath of corruption. Half-eaten bones lay on the ground, a foul feast, with which, gorged and savage, the flocks laid waste, it had belched in its black cave. And when it had soothed the kindled fires of its glowing feast with the swift flood and the foaming waves, not yet even sunk with its whole body in the river, it would already lay its head on the margin of the opposite bank. Unaware of so great a pest, I was walking, Aquinus the Apennine-dweller and Umbrian Avens my companions: to know the grove and to explore the look of the place was our pleasure. And now, as we drew near, a silent horror penetrated our limbs, and our members stiffened with a hidden cold. Yet we enter, and we pray to the Nymphs and the deity of the unknown flood, and our trembling steps, fearing much, we dare to entrust to the secret grove. Behold, from the entrance and the first jaws of the cave, a Tartarean whirlwind and a breath fiercer than the mad East Wind bursts forth, and from the vast gulf, poured out, a storm arises, whirling a tempest mingled with a hiss like Cerberus'. Terrified by the calamity, in turn we look at one another. The ground resounds, and the earth is moved, and the cave falls in, and the shades seem to advance. With how great serpents the Giants in arms sought heaven, or how great the serpent that wearied the son of Amphitryon in the waves of Lerna, and such as the Junonian snake that guarded the boughs leafy with gold: so great, the earth scattered, beneath the stars its gleaming head, rising, it lifted, and into the clouds first scattered its gore, and befouled the sky with its gape. We fled apart, and, panting, in fear we try to raise a thin cry in vain: for hisses filled the whole grove. But, blind with sudden dread and to be condemned for the deed, Avens (but the fates were dragging him) hid himself in the huge bulk of an ancient oak, if he could escape the unspeakable monster. Scarcely do I myself believe it: with its tightly encircling coils it tore away the mass of the tree, and, wrenched up from the depths, it overturned it from its base and dug it out by its lowest roots. Then him, trembling and calling his comrades with his last voice, it seizes, and, swallowing him in a gulp and in its black jaws (I saw it, looking back), it buried him in its obscene belly. The unhappy Aquinus had trusted himself to the river and the rushing waves, and was now swimming in swift flight. Him it attacked in the midst of the flood, and his limbs, brought back to the bank (alas, an unspeakable kind of death!), it devours.

Thus to me it was granted to escape the dire and lamentable monster. As far as my sick mind allowed, I hasten my step and disclose each thing to the leader. He groaned, pitying the bitter chances of the young men. And as he was fiery for battles and Mars and combats and the foe, and burned with a great love of daring, he bids the arms be seized more swiftly, and the cavalry, proved in every Mars, go upon the fields. He himself rushes, his swift steed goaded by the heel, and at his command the shielded band swiftly follows, and bears the heavy wall-engines, the ballistas, and the spear of immense point, accustomed to move the lofty towers. And now, when the horned hoof, ringing round the deadly hall with its noise, leaps over the grassy field, the serpent, roused by the neighing, rolls out of its cave and hisses out Stygian heats from its smoking mouth: a terrible fire flashes from its twin eyes. But its erect crest overtops the grove and the tall treetops of the wood: its tongue, brandished through the air with threefold motion, flickers, and leaping up licks the sky. But when in truth the trumpets sounded, terrified, on high it lifts its immense body, and, settling on its back, gathers the rest beneath its breast in winding coils. Then into dread war it rushes, and, swiftly unwinding its twisted circles, with straight body the whole mass it extends, and suddenly, near, into the faces of those at a broad distance it comes. Every horse pants, stunned at the serpent, and impatient to be held by the bridle breathes frequent fires from its nostrils. That one, towering above on its swollen neck, nods its head on high to either side. Then, the trembling men, urged on by wrath, now it snatches aloft, now it rejoices to have crushed with its vast weight, pressing them down. Then, their bones broken, the black gore it swallows, and, corruption flowing through its mouth, gaping it changes its foe and leaves their half-eaten limbs. The standards were now giving way backward, and the victor pressed the bands carried farther off, blasting them with its plague, when the leader, swiftly driving the squadron, recalled to battle, urging it on with his words: "Do we, an Italian people, give our backs to a serpent, and confess that Ausonia is no match for Libyan snakes? If an idle breath has conquered us, and our sick mind has flowed away at the sight of its gape, I will go, eager and alone, and will suffice to join hands with the monster." Crying this and undaunted, his spear, swift, he hurls through the void with his lightning arm. It came into the facing brow in no idle whirlwind, the point, and, aided not a little by the strength of the beast rushing on with its ardour against it, settled quivering in the head. A shout is given to the stars, and voices suddenly poured out reached the airy halls. At once the earth-born thing rages with wrath, impatient to give its back, and new to grief, and then for the first time in a long age having suffered steel. Nor in vain would the swift onset have been, the grief goading, had not Regulus, by the art of guiding, his horse drawn aside, eluded it as it pressed, and again, the steed following its circles, by the curve of his bent back, the reins turned aside, swiftly with his left hand escaped. But Marus was no idle spectator amid such things, sluggish in his right hand. My spear was the second in the monster's so great body. And now, and now, with its forked tongue it licked the back of the steed, weary with the contest: I hurled my weapon, and swiftly the savage serpent's battles, pressing on me, I turned upon myself. Then the cohort, imitating me, in rivalry heaps javelins with their right hands, and draws the beast into wrath now this way, now that, until the wall-ballista checked it with its blow. Then at last its strength was broken; nor any longer did its sick spine furnish its accustomed rigour to its efforts, nor its head be lifted, as before, into the clouds—they press more keenly. And now the missile, sunk deep within its belly, settled, and swift arrows snatched away its twin eyes. Now from the wide jaws beneath the vast wound the black cavern breathes out its corrupting gore. And now its last tail, with the javelins cast and the weight of the pole, clings to the ground, yet threatens still with its weary gape, until the beam, driven by the engines, shrieking and with a great crash, shattered its head, and, loosening itself along the long mound of the bank, at last it breathed out into the air a livid mist of venom from its fleeing mouth. A bellowing burst from the sad river, and murmurs poured from the lowest shallows, and suddenly both the grove and the cave and the banks, echoing in the woods, howled mournfully. Alas, with how great losses we soon paid for the sad battle, and how great punishments and what wraths we drained! Nor were the pious seers silent: that we had violated by our hands a servant of the sister Naiads, whom the warm Bagrada nurtures in its wave, they warned us by late perils. This spear was then to us the glory and the prize of the second wound, granted by your father, Serranus, which first drank the blood from the sacred serpent."

For a while now Serranus had been wetting his face with tears and his cheeks, and in the middle of the man's speech he says: "If life had lasted for this leader into our age, the Trebia would not have surpassed its ill-omened banks with blood, nor, Trasimene, would your flood press down so many names." Then the old man: "Great penalties from the Tyrian blood he exacted, and the forestalled atonements of his death. For Africa, drained of men and worn down in her resources, stretched out her upturned palms, when under a dire star spirited Therapne sent a leader to the sons of Agenor. No beauty had the man, and his body lacked grace and a noble front; but in his small limbs his vigour was lively—a wonder—and in effort one to surpass great frames. Now to govern war and to join cunning to the sword and to lead a life easy amid hardships through inhospitable places— not to that one, in whose hands now is the skill of war, would he yield, to Hannibal. Would, O Taygetus sad to us, that you had not hardened this one, this alone, on the shady banks of Eurotas. I would have seen the walls of the Phoenician city fall in flames, or at least I would not have wept the dreadful fates of my leader, and the griefs which, freed by no death nor fire, keeping them, I shall carry into Tartarus. The lines were joined on the fields, and much through the ploughlands Mars seethed, nor was any mind without wrath. Here amid the midst, with deeds to be remembered, Regulus opened the field with the sword and rushed into dangers, and gave no wounds with his deadly right hand that needed to be repeated. So, when a whirlwind, whirling a black globe with shrieking South Winds, carries it, and from a pitch-black cloud threatens ruin hanging over the lands and the sea alike, every farmer and every shepherd on the wooded height and on the sea the sailor trembles, his sails drawn down. But weaving a deceit, where hollow rocks shut in his comrades, the Greek leader suddenly turned the contest and swiftly gives his back in feigned dread, just as a shepherd, providing leisure for his stalls, leads by night the wolves into a pit covered with a thin veil of foliage, by the bleatings of a lamb set there. The glory, torch of an honourable mind, seized and dragged the man, and the deceiving trust in uncertain Mars. He looked not back at his comrades or the bands of his companions, nor at the arms of those following: with a mad love of battle he was now pressing on alone, when suddenly a dense cloud of Laconians from the rocky lurking-places, bent on battle, was poured around, and behind rose the savage might of the men. O day dire to Latium, and a disgrace, Gradivus, to be marked on your calendars! For you and for your city his right hand was born, condemned by sad lot to the chain. Never will I cease from groaning. You, Regulus, the Sidonian prison saw, and you, Carthage, seemed to the gods great enough for this triumph. What punishment, worthy enough, shall follow the Laconians defiled by such warfare?

But the Elissaean fathers, sworn, deliberate to entrust new pacts to their leader, and to send a go-between of peace, demanding the youth bound amid the battles and the captive band to be repaid for our leader. No delay, now there stood in the first waves of the shore a ship pushed off from the dockyard, now the nautical youth either strip oars from the woods, or, the fir cut, renew the thwarts. To these the care to fit the twisted ropes, to those to set the sails on the upright mast. At the curved prow they place the weights of bent iron. Before all, skilled in the sea and helmsman of the keel, Cothon fits the stern and the rudder. The bronze gleam flashes on the deep water of the three-forked beak shining on the sea. They bring weapons too, and against the harshness of the deep varied aid for the moment's need. On the margin of the mid-stern stands one who with his voice may temper the alternate strokes of the sailors and dictate the rhythm to the oars, and likewise, as they are drawn back to the count, applaud the resounding blue with the blades.

After the work was done by the sailors, and the hour gave the course, and the armed ship and the winds gave the deep, all the crowd rushes—mothers and boys and old men. Through the midst of the assemblies and through hostile faces Fortune drags the leader to be gazed at. He bears his eyes against them, his brow at peace, just as when first he reached the Sidonian shores, the helmsman, his fleet brought in. I joined him as comrade, he himself not refusing, and, placed on the ship, I add myself as ally to his sad chances. Filth, and poor tables, and a hard couch, and to contend with pressing evils he thought greater than the foe conquered, nor so noble to have fled adversity by caution, as to have subdued it by enduring. Yet one hope was mine, though well known and long ago that grim faith of his—that if to the wretched it were allowed to touch the city and the walls and his home, the heart of the man could be moved and surely soften at your weeping. I shut up my fears in my heart, and thought there were tears in the man, and a mind like ours amid sad things. When at last we glide to the Tiber-stream of his native land, I kept watching the leader's face, and his eyes betraying his feeling, and I stood fixed, intent with the same gaze. If there is any faith, one, my boy, amid a thousand toils, one even in his native land and in the savage city of Agenor, and one even at the time of his punishment, did I see his face. Through all the cities at once Ausonia went out to meet the captive, and as the crowd overflowed the field, the nearby hills are filled; the Albula roars with its high banks. The Carthaginian nobles themselves strive to recall his pitiless heart to the customs of his fathers, and the honour of the toga was offered him. He stood, amid the weeping senate and the throng of mothers and the poured-out grief of the young men, amid so many groans, unmoved. On the mound the consul stretched out his right hand, and as he first set his footsteps on his native soil, honoured him with a friendly meeting. He drew in his step, and warned the consul to withdraw, and not to violate the highest honour. Hedged round by the proud throng of the Carthaginians and the captive column, he went, and bore his ill-will toward heaven and the gods.

Behold, dragging the twin pledge of her sons, Marcia, unhappy in the too great valour of her great husband, was tearing her squalid hair and her sad garments. Do you recognize the day? Or did it not cling to your tender years? And she, when she saw him near, in dress and in the Carthaginian covering, disfigured, with poured-out wailings, sick, she swoons, and the colour of death seizes her cold limbs. If there is any piety in the gods, may they grant you, Carthage, to see such Sidonian mothers. With quiet voice the father, addressing me, bids me ward off both your embraces and his wife's alike, that one impenetrable to griefs and never bowing his neck to sorrow."

Here the youth, with deep groan and tears arising: "Great father," he said, "than whom no greater deity sits for us even on the Tarpeian citadel, if rights are granted to pious complaints, why did you deny this comfort to my mother and to me, or why, O hard one, did you deny this honour— to touch your hallowed face and to have sipped kisses from your mouth? To grasp your right hand with my right hand was not allowed me? How much lighter would these wounds be, if it were granted to carry to the shades your embraces, venerable one, fixed in my mind. But I recall in vain, unless, Marus (for then we clung together in my first years), his appearance was greater than human. Bristling, descending from his white crown, his hair covered his huge neck, and on his brow, with squalid locks, sat a terrible grace and the venerable weight of his mind. Nothing since has met my eyes like it." Then Marus takes up, and, restraining him from tearing his wounds with lament: "What," he says, "when, his household gods passed by, the hated lodgings and the bitter seats of the Carthaginians he entered? The shields fixed up, and the chariot, and the well-known darts in his small house, the monuments of a great triumph, beat upon his eyes, and his wife on the very threshold cried out: 'Where do you bear your steps? This is no Punic prison, Regulus, that you should flee. The traces of our chaste couch the house keeps, and unstained the ancestral hearth without reproach. Here once and again (what, I pray, of ours has been defiled?) offspring, the senate and the homeland congratulating, I bore for you. This, look, is your dwelling, whence, huge, with shoulders shining with purple, you saw, as consul, the Latin fasces go forth, whence you used to go to war, whither you used to bring back the captured spoils and as victor hang up the arms with me upon the doorposts. I do not seek embraces and the bonds of the sacred marriage-torch, or wedlock: cease to condemn your ancestral household gods, and think it right to grant a night to your children.' Amid these tears, his footsteps joined to the Carthaginians, he shut himself in at the Tyrian threshold and left her complaints. Scarce yet did the bright day survey on the top of Oeta the monuments of the Herculean pyre, when the consul bids the Libyans approach and be summoned.
