Then the temple's threshold we saw him entering. What the senate deliberated, or what words of the man the mourning curia at the last heard, he himself disclosed to us with calm mouth. As he set his steps within, in rivalry with voice and hand they called him to his accustomed seat and the well-known place. He refused, and scorned the ancient honour of the place. But the men, pouring round on every side, no less his right hand sought to grasp, and begged that he give the leader back to his country, by so great a name: that the captive throng could be weighed in his ransom, and that then more justly the Tyrian citadels would burn by that hand which had been bound in chains. Then, lifting his palms and his eyes alike to heaven: 'Giver of justice and right, you who govern all things, and you, no lighter deity to me, Faith, and Sarranian Juno, whom I called to witness my return with a sworn mind, let it be right for me to speak things worthy of myself and to guard the Latin hearths with my voice: I will go to the Tyrians no more sluggish,' he said, 'my faith of return standing and the pact of punishment safe. So cease for me, in the ruin of our affairs, to stretch out honour. By so many wars and so many years we have broken our age. Now too, with chains and a long prison, my strength grows numb in captive old age. He was, and never, while he was, did Regulus rest from the hard service of Mars. You behold a name in a bloodless body. But Carthage, the house of frauds, not ignorant how much of us remains, prepares young men, breasts harsh with the sword, to weigh out the captives against our old age. Go against their wiles, and let the nation, glad to deceive by cunning, learn how much, I being taken, remains to you, Rome. Nor indeed let any peace please, but such as is by the custom of our fathers. The Libyans demand, and gave us these things to report, that, if it please to weigh the war by an equal pact and on fair terms to enroll twin laws. But let me have entered the Stygian household gods before I see the Latins striking such pacts.' Having said these things, he gave himself back now to the Tyrian wrath, and, the grave and faithful warnings not scorned by the senate, the cohort of the Carthaginians was dismissed. It, sad at the repulse and threatening the captive, hastened to its native shores. The crowd, the fathers, follow him, and the field resounds greatly with beatings of the breast and grief. It was their wish to recall him at times and to keep the man snatched away by just sorrow. But his trembling wife, as if standing at a funeral suddenly, when she saw him hastening to enter the ship, with a fearful outcry brought her swift step back to the waves: 'Take me, Libyans, as companion of his punishment and death. This one thing, husband, by the pledges of our womb, this one thing I beg: let it be allowed me, bearing with you whatever toils of lands and sea and sky, to suffer them. I did not send the Amyclaean leader into battle, nor are your chains thrown round his neck by us. Why do you flee a wretched woman all the way to the Carthaginians? Take with me this offspring. Perhaps we shall bend the hard wraths of Carthage with our tears, or, if the hostile city closes its ears, then the same hour shall await you and yours alike, or, if it is fixed to break off life, let us die in our native land. I am here, the last companion of your fate.' Amid these words, the ship, loosed from its bonds, began little by little to move and to depart from the bank. Then indeed the unhappy woman, her mind maddened with grief, cries out, stretching her weary palms toward the shore: 'See, the man who boasts that to Libya and to the wicked peoples and to the foe he keeps faith. Where now, faithless one, are the pacts given to us and the faith promised to our marriage-bed?' This last word then penetrated to the hard ears; the rest the struck oars forbade him to know.

Then swiftly from the river we glide down to the shores of the sea, and we skirt the deep, and with the pine hollowed out we cleave the huge expanse and the immense waves with our curved keel. Shuddering at the mockery of his death, I prayed that the harsh might of the sea might overwhelm us, and that the wicked frenzy of the East Wind might break the ship on the rocks: that death would have been a common one. But to our punishment the gentle Zephyrs, with measured breath, carried us, and gave us to the Tyrian frenzy.

Unhappy, I saw it, and, sent back to my native city, the teller of his punishment, I returned at a hard price. Nor would I now attempt to set forth to you the Pygmalionean race, imitating the rites and wraths of beasts, if the race of men had seen anything greater in the whole world than what the venerable valour of your father brought forth as an example. I am ashamed to add complaints to the tortures which I watched him bearing with calm face. You too, dear boy, cease not to fashion yourself worthy of so great a blood, and check your rising tears. With wood set before them, with matching points, all the wickerwork of the sides is armed, and densely by art is woven, of upright and standing iron in rows, an unhappy goad, and, sleep denied him by this device, wherever, with the time drawn out, sluggish torpor inclined his bent body, they pierce the flesh to the vitals. Cease, O youth, from tears. This endurance surpasses all triumphal cars. In a long age his glory will grow green again; while chaste Faith holds the seat of heaven and the lands, while the venerable name of valour endures, he will live; and a day will come on which, glorious leader, your fates those after you will shudder to hear, by you trodden under foot."

These things Marus, and with sad care he tended again the wounds. Meanwhile, her swift wings drenched with blood, as she had dyed them in the bloody wave of Trasimene, Rumour scattered things true and feigned alike through the City. The Allia and the unspeakable Senones and the captured citadel's face recur to the stunned minds. Grief-bringing Panic shook off the reins, and the storm was increased by their fear. This man rushes headlong to the walls: a horrid voice is borne, "The foe is at hand," and they cast stakes and idle weapons. But other women, growing hoary with torn hair, sweep the high temples of the gods and, late after the deaths of their own, trouble them with prayers. Rest, both the darkness and the day have lost: there lie at the gates, scattered with howling grief, the crowd, and of those returning in a long order the throng watches their steps. They hang on the mouth of the speakers, nor have the glad enough sure faith, and again they delay by asking, and, sometimes praying with their face without voice, they are afraid to hear what they ask. Hence weeping, when ears are struck by a heavier evil, hence fear, if it is denied to know, and the doubtful messenger of the answer holds back. And now, when in near view the bodies of the returning were seen, anxiously glad they pour forth, and on the very wounds they fix kisses and weary the gods above.

Here amid the trembling, venerable in his care, was leading Serranus Marus, and Marcia, who once after her husband's death had not gone out from her house, shunning company, and had endured the light for her children's sake, was rushing into a grief like the ancient one. Suddenly troubled and recognizing Marus: "Glorious companion of great Faith, this one at least you give back to me," she says. "A light wound? Or has the savage point penetrated deep, all the way to our vitals? Whatever it is, so long as Carthage does not snatch him, bound in chains, and renew the monstrous things of his father's punishment, it is welcome, O gods. How often, alas, my son, did I beg that you should not bear your father's wraths and spirit into battle, nor that the sad glory of your warlike father should goad you into arms. The hard punishments of too long a life, of my too long old age, I have paid out. I beg you, now spare, if any deities have fought for us." But, the bitter disaster scattered as if a cloud, the fathers now plan to seek for the weary state help, and there is striving toward the duties of war, and fear is driven off by a graver peril. The greatest of cares was to set a guide over the camp, on whom Latium and the shaken mass of affairs might rest, as the homeland watched its own downfall. That was Jupiter's care—to prolong the time for falling Ausonia and the Italian realms; for the Tyrrhenians and the Carthaginian, swollen with successes, rising on the Alban citadel he had looked back upon, who was preparing to bear his victorious standards against the walls. Then, shaking his head: "Never to you, Jupiter," he says, "O youth, will he grant to cross the gates of Rome and to set your foot within. To strew the Tyrrhenian valleys with slaughters, and to make the rivers' banks overflow with Latin blood, may be right: to approach the Tarpeian hill and to draw near the walls I forbid." Then four times the gleaming thunderbolt he hurled with his right hand, by which all the land of the Maeonians shone again, and, rolling a black cloud through the air, the sky burst open, he shattered it above the columns. Nor was it enough to have turned the Carthaginian back: he gives, with great power, to the sons of Aeneas the mind to lay in a safe bosom the Roman glory, and to entrust the reins of safety to Fabius as their leader. To whom, after he sees the rights of war handed over: "Him never," he says, "shall envy overcome, or popular glory with its flattering dye, no deceitful cunning, no plunder or any other lust. Old in warfare, and with a calm mind able to bear praises and disasters. His genius is equal to the camp and the toga." So the father of the gods, and brings his step back to the stars.

Here, caught in no arms, surveyed by all, and praised by Jupiter, Fabius, wondrously how much he rejoiced, returning, to count back to his homeland the youth which, setting out, he had led with him into battle. Nor did anyone spare his own limbs or his beloved son more keenly, or see with sadder eyes a comrade's blood in war. And that same man, the victor drenched with the foe's blood, sought again the walls with his camp full. A race famous in its stock, and an origin akin to heaven. For long ago the Tirynthian, returning from distant shores, and the fame of the threefold monster and, a sight to wonder at, the captured cattle, drove in triumph here, where the walls of Rome now gleam. Then the Arcadian, so the story goes, was laying out, the Palatium founded among the deserted thickets, the leader, with a poor people, when the royal maiden, overcome by her sacred guest, bore Fabius from a glad crime and mingled the rise of a great seed, an Arcadian mother destined to be among the Herculean descendants. This house armed three hundred Fabii against the foe, gone forth from one threshold; whose fairest deeds Fabius surpassed by delaying, and the leader Hannibal by matching him. So great then, Carthaginian, were you.

While the stricken Latins renew themselves for the wars, troubled by Jupiter and stripped of the hope of battering the walls of Rome, Hannibal made for the Umbrian hills and the fields, where, on the high summit of the topmost mountain, Tuder hangs sloping down its side, and where, thrown out on the broad plains, Mevania breathes out sluggish fogs and sits feeding a huge bull, a gift for Jupiter. Then he pours himself into the Palladian fields of Picenum, rich in plunder, and with roving arms, where spoils invite him, he transfers his ravaging standards, until gentle Campania slowed his pestilent courses and, undefended, received the war into her bosom.

Here, while the leader gazes at the temple and the houses of marshy Liternum, he beholds, gleaming with varied painting, the monuments of a former war fought out by the fathers: for, marked on the porticoes, there remained a long and notable order of events. First, with grim face, Regulus was urging wars, wars to be denied the man, had it been granted to know the fates. But Appius stood as the foremost, war declared against the Carthaginians by the custom of the fathers, and, bound with laurel, he led a just triumph from the Sarranian slaughter. Beside it, a glory of the sea and a naval trophy, a column, bearing beaks, rose in a snow-white mass. The spoils to Mars, and as an offering, Duilius dedicated, the deep fleet of the Carthaginians sunk before all. For him, a nocturnal honour, bright torches and the sacred piper attends after the feasts, and the chaste household gods, distinguished, he sought again with the murmur of glad song. He sees too the last honours of a dead citizen: Scipio was celebrating the funeral of the Carthaginian leader, victor in the Sardinian land. He sees thence the youth rushing on the Libyan shores through their scattered bands; Regulus pressed on, his crest gleaming, and crowded their backs: the Autololians and Numidians and the Moor and Hammon and the Garamantian, their weapons laid down, surrendered their towns. Sluggish on the sandy field the Bagrada foamed with viperous gore, and against the threatening squadrons of its own accord the serpent fought, and waged war with the leader. And besides, cast from the ship and calling in vain on the gods, the Amyclaean helmsman the treacherous hand was sinking in the sea, and late penalties to you, Regulus, Xanthippus was paying by a death deserved on the deep. They had added the twin Aegates rising in the mid-flood: around you might see the fragments of a shattered fleet, and the Carthaginians poured out, floating in the gulf. The possessor of the sea, and with the breeze before him, Lutatius, the victor, was driving the captive ships to the shore. Among these, bound in the joined order, Hamilcar, the father of the leader, drew upon himself, from the image of all things, the faces of all the crowd. But one could see the face of Peace, and the polluted altars of the treaty, and Jupiter deceived, and the Latins dictating laws. The Libyan, with trembling neck, dreaded the drawn axes, and, with palms lowered in order, begging pardon, they swore the pacts in vain. This, from the top of Eryx, Dione watched with joy.

When the Carthaginian had reviewed all these with hostile face, smiling, he proclaims from his slow wrath: "You shall give no lighter deeds of my right hand to inscribe on our roofs: Saguntum captured, Carthage, grant me to gaze on, falling at once by flame and sword; let the fathers pierce through the limbs of their sons. Nor shall a small place hold the conquered Alps: let the victor leap over the steep ridges with his lofty horses, the Garamantian and the Numidian. You shall add the banks of Ticinus foaming with blood, and our Trebia, and the shores of Tuscan Trasimene choked with corpses. Let Flaminius fall, huge in body and arms; let the consul Scipio flee with flowing blood and be carried to his allies on his son's neck. These send among the peoples, and still greater things shall be given. You shall fashion Rome blazing, Carthage, with Libyan torches, and the Thunderer cast down from the Tarpeian rock. Meanwhile you, as is fitting, these (go more swiftly), O young men, by whose right hands such great things are done for me, give to ashes these monuments, and wrap them in flames."
Meanwhile Fabius was the one hope in a fearful hour.

He, headlong, was arming the allies and Italy, sick with her wound, and the warrior, green still in old age for the rigours of toil, was already moving his camp against the foe; but his mind, greater than mortal, looked to no spears, no swords, no spirited horses. Against so many thousands of Carthaginians and their unconquered chief, against so many columns alone he marched, and bore in himself all the arms and men. And had not a sacred force been laid upon the old man, and the resolve to halt by delay the Fortune that fostered the enemy's cause, the last age of the Dardanian name would have passed away. He set a limit to the gods' favour toward the Punic camp, and amid Libya's prosperous wars he fixed an end to her conquering. Swollen with the disasters of Italy, he played the Carthaginian with slow and patient governance. Greatest of leaders, you who guard the again-slipping realm of Troy, the failing fortunes of Latium and the labours of our fathers, who guard the wealth of Carmentis and Evander's kingdom, rise, come, and set your hallowed head, your service done, in heaven.

But Libya's commander, after the new name held sway with a dictator chosen, weighing not in vain how swiftly the Latins had changed their command, was eager to learn what manner of man this was, what his renown, why Fabius should be the last anchor of the weary, whom Rome, after so many storms, deemed a match for Hannibal. The man's years, void of fire, and an old age closed to deceit, vexed and galled him. Quickly he summons one from the captive ranks and demands the leader's descent, his customs, and the labours of his hand. Cilnius, sprung on the Tyrrhenian shores of Arretium, bore a famous name. But an ill-omened hour had brought the youth to the banks of the Ticinus, and, thrown when his horse fell wounded beneath him, he now gave his neck to Libyan chains. He, burning to escape his ills and break off his life: 'It is no Flaminius you deal with, no rash counsels of Gracchus in his hands,' he said; 'this is the race of Tiryns; and had the fates begotten it, Hannibal, on your shores, you would see the empire of the world in Carthage's citadel. I will not lead you through each thing in a long succession. This will suffice: you shall know the Fabii from one contest. The peoples of Veii, breaking the peace, refused to accept the yoke, and war raged with Mars near at hand at our gates, and the consul was summoning men to arms. Levies were forbidden, and a private camp the household of Hercules' line filled. From one house, a marvel, a patrician army went forth in joined arms. Three hundred leaders sprang forth. Under whichever you pleased, under a single commander you could have waged war without fear. But a dread omen met them as they went out: the Accursed Gate's threshold trembled with a menacing, shrilling sound, and the great altar of Hercules' godhead bellowed. They fell upon the foe, and their fierce valour did not suffer the men to be counted, and the slain were more than the soldiery. Often massed in a dense throng, often scattered far and wide through trackless ways, they took their turns, and earning by toil matched merit, with none second to any in valour, they led three hundred triumphs to the Tarpeian shrines. Alas, deceiving hopes and forgetful hearts, and how fleeting is whatever is granted to mortals! That band of men, who, with the Fabian house unharmed, thought it shameful that the public wars be waged, fell together by the gods' envy, sudden arms closing in around them. Yet you have no cause to rejoice that they were slain. There remain as many as can suffice for you and for Libya: one alone could have matched three hundred right hands. So vigorous his limbs, his toil so provident, his cunning sheltered under wary calm. Nor indeed now, hot-blooded as you are, in the prime of life, would you have dug your heel more swiftly into the flank of a battle-horse in the fray, or champed the bit with your mouth.' The Carthaginian, seeing him after these words eager for death: 'In vain, madman,' he said, 'do you provoke our anger and seek by dying to escape your captive chains. You must live. Let his neck be kept in a close fetter.' So spoke the youth, swollen by the gods and by his bold deeds prospered.

But care for the gods was hurrying the fathers and the matrons of Latium to the altars. With eyes brimming in sorrowful faces the women's chorus moves in long array: in order they were dedicating to Juno a robe and the vows they had conceived: 'Be present here, O queen of the gods; a chaste people we pray and we bring, whatever its name be worthy, a throng of Ausonia's daughters, and a fair and venerable gift, which our own hands have woven with needle and golden thread. And while the mothers' fear lessens, this for now, goddess, shall be your veil. If you grant us to drive the Marmaric cloud from our lands, every jewel set in gold shall gleam for you upon a varied crown.' And they worship Pallas too with her own gift, and Phoebus and the armed god and Dione first of all. So great a reverence for the gods is born when affairs are fearful: but in prosperous times few altars smoke.

While Rome proclaims the ancient honours to the temples, already Fabius, advancing with a silent column and, by his art of warfare, seeming sluggish, had closed off every road to fortune and to the foe. To leave the standards was not allowed, and he taught them to obey, that highest glory by which, O Roman, you lift the head of empire to the stars. But when the first standards were well descried far off on the high mountains, and the army gleamed with new arms, the Sidonian's hopes were roused, and the youth grew hot with Fortune's favour. The only thing that seemed to delay his conquest was that the lines had not yet stood firm: 'Onward,' he cries, 'go swiftly, rush to the gates, drive back the rampart with your breasts. As much of the field as parts us from them, so much is left of the foe before the shades. Sluggards are called to war, old men ashamed to fight. Whatever you see, this is the remnant, condemned as useless in the first campaign. See, where now are the Gracchi, where now the thunderbolts of the race of the Scipios? Driven from Ausonia, they did not let their trembling flight cease before terror bore them to the world's farthest bounds and to Ocean. Now each wanders a fugitive, quaking at our name, and keeps to the banks of the Ebro. There is reason too why my glory should grow with Flaminius slain, and why I should be glad to fix upon our titles the still-raw name of a warrior's Mars. How many years my sword has power to take from this Fabius! And yet he dares. Let him dare. I shall see to it he is gazed on no longer in arms.'

Crying out such things, he sweeps the columns on at a flying pace, and, riding ahead on his horse, now with his right hand challenges the foe, now upbraids them with his voice, now, with a spear hurled from afar, he is borne exulting and plays out the semblances of the battle to come: as when the son of Thetis bore to the Phrygian plains the arms of Vulcan, embracing on his shield earth and sky and his mother's sea and the whole world in image. Sitting, a watcher of these vain rages, and lofty on the high ridge of a hill, tames his exultant heart and wearies the broken threats by deferring war, skilled in delay, Fabius; as, under black night, a shepherd in his guarded folds keeps watch over the flock shut in the pens, fearless of sleep: fierce and unfed the savage pack of wolves rages with howling and shakes with biting the barriers that hold firm.

Foiled in his undertaking, the Libyan moves off from there and with slow pace traverses the Apulian fields, and now settles in a valley hidden out of sight, in case it be granted to make his pursuer plunge headlong and to surround him by unexpected trick, now by night he prepares thefts of the road, with shadows concealing the dark way, and feigns a retreat and counterfeits false fears; then swiftly displays his camp abandoned, its booty left, and prodigally invites the foe: as the Maeander roves at large through the Maeonian land, when, doubling back upon itself with winding eddies, it strays. No undertaking is free of guile: at once he turns all things over and mixes them, sharpening his mind for varied attempts, just as the radiance of water, struck by the lamp of the sun, flickers wandering through the house, quivering in a shifting image of light, and beats the ceiling with a trembling shade. And now, raging with grief, in anger he murmurs thus to himself: 'If this man had first borne weapons to meet us, would there now be no names of Trebia and Trasimene? Would no Italians mourn? Would Phaethon's river never have troubled the sea, discoloured with a bloody wave? He has found, while he holds himself in check and we are worn by sitting still, a way of conquering. See how often, as if he came to meet me, he has unbound my wiles by reason and dissolved my snares.' This he muses to himself, when, at midnight, the trumpet was dividing the night, and now the wakeful watch, his ill-favoured lot drawn, the third sentry was going to his arms, his sleep broken off. He turned his march, and leaving the land of Daunus behind him the wasting foe returned by familiar ways to the Campanian shores. But here, when he entered the fields of rich Falernum (a wealthy land, and one that never lied to the farmer), he adds destroying fires to the fruit-bearing boughs.

It is not right, Bacchus, to pass over your honours in silence, though great enterprises call. You shall be remembered, bestower of the sacred juice, whose vines, heavy with nectar, let no presses set a name before the Falernian. In a better age old Falernus furrowed the Massic ridges with a plough, the sword unknown to him. The vine-shoot did not yet weave its shade with green grape on the bare field, nor did they know to sweeten the cups with the juice of Lyaeus, wont to ward off thirst with a spring and pure water. A lucky step and a happy hour brought Lyaeus, journeying to the shores of Calpe and his day's end, to his lodging, nor did it shame the heaven-dweller to enter the small household gods and the humble threshold of the roof. The smoky doorposts received him willing, and after the fashion of a poor age the tables set before the hearth, and the glad host had not perceived that a god had come. But after the manner of his fathers he bustled with grateful zeal and pressed his old age to serve, until—a festal store—now he arranged fruit in clean baskets, now swiftly brought from his well-watered gardens the dewy fare dripping with moisture; then with milk and honeycomb he set off the sweet feast, and with a table polluted by no blood, pure, he brought the gifts of Ceres, and first wiped away every honour of Vesta on every side and cast the offerings into the midst of the flame. That your own juices should be lacking, captivated by this old man's diligence, Iacchus, you forbid. Suddenly, a marvel to tell, the beechwood cups foamed with the juice of the vine, the reward of his poor hospitality, and into the cheap milk-pail flowed reddening wine, and in the cratér hollowed from oak a sweet liquor sweated from fragrant grapes. 'See, take it,' says Bacchus, 'a gift not yet known to you, but one that shall someday spread abroad the name of Falernus the vine-grower,' and no longer did the god lie hidden. Then clusters wreathed his brow, shining with a purple light, and his hair flowed over his neck, and from his right hand hung a goblet, and a vine, slipping down from the green thyrsus, crowned the festal tables with the shoots of Nysa. Nor was it easy, Falernus, to contend with the glad savour, once the cups were repeated for you; now with your foot you stir laughter, now with stammering tongue, and shaken in your temples by your country's Lyaeus, you try to render thanks and worthy reward with words scarcely understood, until Sleep composed your struggling eyes, Sleep, Bacchus, given to you as companion. Hence, when the hoof of dawn first scattered the dews at Phoebus' rising, the Massic flowered far and wide with vine-bearing fields, wondering at its groves and clusters bright in the sun. Beauty came to the hill, and from that time forth wealthy Tmolus and Ariusia with its cups of ambrosial juices and fierce Methymna with its presses yielded to the Falernian.

Such waste did Hannibal then deal, and ranged hostile over the land, and the swords, dry of blood, goaded him on, while Fabius made sport of the leader. And now unholy prayers and a crooked lust for fighting were swelling in the Ausonian camp: bent forward, they were making ready to run down the slope. Grant to fame, grant, Muse, the man to whom it was given to conquer two camps and to master twin frenzies. 'If the fathers had thought our hearts were hot, our temper rash,' he said, 'and that an easy mind is thrown into confusion by shouting, they would not have entrusted the reins of the last extremity and of a Mars given up for lost. The resolve of war, long weighed, stands fixed: I shall conquer by keeping safe those unwilling and pressed by the last fates. Through Fabius it shall be allowed to none of you to fall. If you are weary of the light and have a longing to be the last of the Ausonian name, and it irks you, at such a time, to have made no place famous by fresh disaster and the crash of a glorious ruin, then Flaminius must be called back to you from his dark abode. He long ago, in his haste to rush on, would have given the signal and the omen. Or do you not yet see the headlong, the near-at-hand fates? One victory is enough for the Carthaginian to end the war. Stand fast, men, and feel your leader. When the longed-for moment demands your right hands, then let those fierce words be matched by deeds. It is not, believe me, it is not a hard labour to be borne into battle: one hour, the gates flung open, will have poured all of us out onto the plain. That great thing, granted to those alone whom kindly Jupiter has looked on as they go, that great thing is to return from the foe. The Libyan leans on Fortune, and with a fair wind trusts to drive his ship. Until the breeze drop and the wind, its blast withdrawn, fail the swollen sails, to wait will have served the cause. No Fortune fosters with a lasting embrace. Already how much narrower his force, and in no battle how much of his fame has been worn away! Indeed, among the rest of our deeds it would not lack praise that he, who but now—but to spare my words were better. Already do you demand battle-lines and combats and the foe? O may such confidence, you gods, abide! Meanwhile, the lot of the greater peril shut out, oppose me alone, I beg, me to the whole war.' At these words the fury was broken and the mad arms grew quiet: as, when over the troubled waves Neptune has lifted his calm head and sees the whole sea and is seen by all, ruler of the deep, the savage winds release their fierce murmurs and move no pinions on their brows, then little by little, peace poured over the tranquil waters, the languid waves shine on the silent shore.

The shrewd care of the Carthaginian perceived this, and with the venom of deceit he assails their minds. These few small acres of his ancestral fields Fabius tilled with no many ploughs: the Massic added a name to his vine-bearing clods. From this it pleased him to contrive a plague and to scatter ambiguous occasions of strife in the camp. He spared them with sword and fire, and granted a suspect peace to the place by malign craft, as if the war were being drawn out by a secret compact. This was understood by Fabius, and the dictator saw the Tyrian's wiles raging. But there is no leisure †with grief to fear envy amid swords and trumpets, and to ward off the bites of slander by a doubtful battle, until, as the Carthaginian crept along and, often in vain dragging his camp here and there, scoured for combats, where wooded ridges and crags rise on the rocky summit of the hills, he closed him in with a squadron spread at the partings of the way. On this side the Laestrygonian cliffs pressed from behind with their stony mountain, on that, foul with its watery soil, the marsh of Liternum; nor did the region call for the use of sword or soldier, but, hedged in by the trickery of the place, a sharp hunger pressed them, ready to exact the penalty for wretched Saguntum, and the end of Carthage's arms was near.

Over all the lands and the pools of the wide deep sleep had buried everything, and, the day's toil laid aside, the world was keeping the peace given to mortals by night. But the Sidonian leader's heart, ablaze with cares, and his wakeful fears did not let him drink the gifts of sleep-bringing night. For he raises his limbs from the couch and wraps himself in the tawny lion's hide, on which, flung down upon the grass of the field, he had pressed his bed before. Then to his brother's tent he bears his quick steps near at hand. Nor was that brother degenerate from the warrior's custom: he lay with his limbs propped on a bull's hide and soothing his cares with sleep. Not far off the man's spear was fixed in the ground close by, and a dread helmet hung from the topmost point; but his shield around it, and breastplate and sword and bow and the Balearic javelin together rest upon the earth. Beside him a chosen band, young men tried in war, and his charger cropped the grass with saddled back. When the steps of the one entering had driven off light sleep, 'Hello!' he said (and at once he was reaching his hand for his weapons), 'what wakeful care wearies you, brother, in your fatigue?' And now he had risen, and his comrades stretched out on the turf he recalls, his heel striking, to the duties of the camp, when Libya's leader: 'Fabius drives me through anxious nights, Fabius rouses me into cares, that old age, which alone, alas, blocks my running fates! You see how you are encircled by an armed ring, and the gathered soldier walls you, shut in, in a circle. But come now, since our affairs are straitened, learn further what I have devised. Through the broad fields the seized herds follow, after war's accustomed manner. I shall order dry branches to be bound to their horns and bundles of light brushwood tied to their brows; when the fire, set to them, has spread its heat abroad, that they may leap up everywhere, the goads of pain driving them, and toss the wandering blazes over the hills with their necks. Then, in panic at the strange terror, the trembling guard will slacken his unequal watch and fear greater things by night. If the plan pleases you (the extreme case forbids delay), let us gird ourselves,' he said. With double step they then sought the tents. Huge, his neck laid back upon his shield, amid horses and men and spoils taken by hand and dripping with slaughter, lay Maraxes, and a dreadful cry, as if in sleep he were taking up war, he chanced then to utter, frenzied, and with trembling hand sought, hot, his arms upon the bed and his familiar sword. To him Mago, when with reversed spear, shaking him, he had driven off the warring sleep: 'Bravest of leaders, in the darkness curb your wrath and put off battle till the light. For deceit and secret flight and safe retreats now must the night be used. To bind dry leaves to the horns and to send the herds, set ablaze, into the broad woods, that the opposing companies may open the barriers, my brother makes ready, and to tear away the besieged camp. Let us break out, and let this stratagem persuade Fabius not to vie in guiles.' At this, while the keen youth, glad of the enterprise, made no delay, they hasten to Acherras' tent, whose rest was sparing and his sleep the least, nor was it his way to make his nights equal to his sleep: ever wakeful he tended his fierce horse, and eased it in its weariness by handling it, and soothed its mouth, fretted by the bit. Meanwhile his comrades renew their weapons and the dried gore they wipe from the steel and give edge and anger to the points. What the fortune of the place demands, what the time, and what they themselves intend, they unfold, and they urge him, no sluggish minister of the enterprise, to go. The watchword runs through the camp, and, intent, they show what must be hastened, and each warns his own men: busy fear, urging on those who hurry, presses the alarmed to depart, while the silence is blind and the shadows are at their deepest. Now, the plague set beneath, the brushwood and the fires rise from the high horns. Here indeed, as the mischief swells and the herds toss their sick heads, the flames, helped on, began to grow rich, and the conquering crest of fire to burst through the smoke; over the hills and the thickets (the black destruction drives them) and over the high crags of the rocky mountain are borne, maddened, the panting bodies of the cattle, and, their nostrils beset with fire, the raging steers struggle in vain to bellow. Over the ridges, over the valleys wanders Vulcan's plague, the mischief nowhere standing still, and the nearby shores gleam: as many as the stars a sailor, cleaver of the deep, sees fixed in heaven on a clear night from the midst of the waves, as many as he sees, when with black heat they burn the Calabrian glades for the rich pastures, a shepherd seated on Garganus' peak sees the fires. But at the sudden sight of the flames flitting over the high mountains, those on whom the watch had then fallen by lot shuddered and believed that the very fires roamed with none scattering them, and that untamed blazes fed beneath the hills. Whether they had fallen from heaven, and the Almighty had hurled great thunderbolts with his mighty hand, or whether the luckless earth, bursting from blind caverns, had poured forth its plenty in flames with kindled sulphur, they ask amid their dread. And now they go off, and swiftly with his arms the Carthaginian seizes the throat of the road, and exulting darts out into the open fields. Yet so far had the dictator, vigilant in his art of command, advanced—after the Trebia and the pools of the Tuscan deep— that it might be enough for Hannibal to have escaped Fabius and the Roman weapons. Nay, he would have pressed the routed man's tracks and steps with his camp, had not the sacred rites, to be revered, called him to his country's gods. Then, turned toward the city, he addresses the youth to whom it was his custom to hand over the standards and the chief command and the foremost reins of war, and with these words he forms and shapes him by counsel: 'If Fortune has not yet by deeds, Minucius, taught you to approve my cautious courses, my words will have no power to lead you to true glory or to keep you from evil ways. You saw Hannibal shut in. The soldier and the squadrons availed nothing, nor the legion massed in dense companies. I call you to witness: alone I shut him in, nor shall I delay further. Let me make libation to the gods of the feast and bear the solemn rites: this man, again and again bound, by high mountains or by rushing rivers (only abstain from battle), I shall deliver. Meanwhile (trust one who has tried it, I do not deceive) in a sick state of affairs to have stirred nothing is salvation. Let it be glory to many and let it please them—indeed it is splendid—to lay the foe low with the sword; but let it be your triumph to have kept you safe for Fabius. The camp is given to you full and the soldier untouched by wound: restore these to us (this shall be your glory). Soon you shall see the Libyan lion leaping at this rampart, soon offering you spoils, soon turning his back, looking back the while and brewing his wrath with guile. Close, I pray, your camp, and snatch away all hope of battle. This warning is enough. But if it is not given me to curb your heart for all my pleading, with great right and pious authority, as dictator, I forbid you to take up arms.' So, leaving the camp, he had walled it with his counsels, and was returning to the city.

But lo, with a favouring breeze the Phoenician fleet was cleaving with its beaks the shores of Caieta and the Laestrygonian retreats, and had entered the open harbours, and the whole sea was foaming with many an oar, when, alarmed at the din, from their glassy seats in the cave the sisters of the sea rose together from the deep and see their shores held by hostile prows. Then, struck with great fear, the Nereid throng, amazed, flow swiftly back to their familiar thresholds, where in mid-deep the realms of the Teleboae rise and the pumice seats afar. Huge in a sheer cave Proteus is hidden, and the prophet far and wide flings back the foaming blue against the opposing rocks. After he (well skilled enough in things and fears) had played through various shapes and terrified them with the scales of a black serpent and twisted dreadful hissings, or roared, his limbs changed into a grim lion: 'Tell me,' he says, 'what is the cause of your coming? Whose face has paleness suddenly overrun? Why this desire to know the future?' To this Cymodoce, eldest of the nymphs of Italy: 'You know our fears, O prophet. What do the Tyrian fleets and our shores wrenched from us portend? Are the Rhoetean realms being moved by the gods to Libya? Or shall the Sarranian sailor hold these harbours now? Driven from our native seat, shall we dwell at Atlas and Calpe in the farthest caves?' Then thus, unrolling the recovered beginnings backward, the ambiguous prophet begins and unseals the future: 'When Laomedon's shepherd sat upon Phrygian Ida and, calling back his straying bulls through the bramble-grown wastes with a shrill reed to the dewy pastures, heard, at his leisure, the contest of sacred beauty, then Cupid was driving his mother's chariot of snow-white swans, anxious to guard the season of the strife. A tiny quiver hung from his shoulder, and his golden bow gleamed, and, forbidding his mother with a nod to fear, he showed that he bore a quiver heavy with darts. But another smoothed the locks on his snowy brow, another bound the purple folds of her robe. When thus, sighing, Venus with her rosy lips addresses her comely sons: ''See, the surest witness of your love is at hand this day. Who could believe it, with you safe? Of beauty and of face (what more remains of all things now?) Venus contends. If on you, my little ones, I gave all my darts, charmed with their seductive venom, if your grandsire, who seals the covenants of heaven and earth, stands a suppliant when you wish: let our victory bring back to Cyprus the Idumaean palms from Pallas, let a hundred altars smoke for me at Paphos for the prize from Juno.'' And while Cytherea presses thus upon her winged sons, the whole grove rang as the goddess walked. Now the warlike maiden, the aegis laid aside, and where she wraps her hair in her wonted helmet, yet uncombed, and learning peace in her serene eyes, was going, and to the foretold grove bore the hurried steps of her sacred foot. Elsewhere Saturn's daughter, at the bidding, was entering the woods, about to bear, after her brother's bed, the Phrygian's judgement, the shepherd's scorn, and Ida. Last of all, with shining face, smiling Venus shone forth: all around, both the groves and, deep within, the caves in their leafy crags drew a fragrance, the goddess breathing it from her sacred head. Nor was the judge able to keep his seat, and his eyes fell, overcome by the light of her splendour, and he feared to seem to have hesitated. But the fierce wars of the conquered goddesses bore him across the sea, and Troy was cut down together with its own judge. Then dutiful Aeneas, tossed over lands and waves, set the Dardanian household gods on Italian soil. While the sea-beasts swim in the deep, while the stars shine in heaven, while the sun lifts himself from the Indian shore, here shall be a realm, and to that realm no bounds through the ages. But you, O daughters, while the unmoving thread runs on, flee the ill-omened sands of Adriatic Sason. The Aufidus, swollen, shall be mingled with the sea in bloody waves and drive red billows into the deep, and on a plain once condemned by the songs of the gods you shall fight again, Aetolian shades, against the Trojans. Soon Punic javelins shall shake the walls of Romulus, and the Metaurus shall gleam with the great slaughter of Hasdrubal. Hence that one, born in secret, shall avenge both his uncle and his father's death; then he shall fill the shore of Elissa with flames and tear the Carthaginian away as he scorches the Italian vitals, and shall conquer him on his own shores. To him Carthage shall yield in arms, to him Africa in name, he shall give from himself one to wear out a third war and bring the ashes of Libya, victorious, to the Capitol.'

While in the cave the prophet unfolds these secrets of the gods, already the master of the war and of the horse had stripped from his mind the counsels and Fabius, and was pressing headlong upon the foe. Nor did the Carthaginian fail to feed and nurse the crooked frenzy, and, that with small loss he might lure him to greater battles, he kept giving feigning backs at times: not otherwise than one who, with bait, calls the fish out from the liquid recesses of the deep through the scattered pools, and, when he has seen the light prey now swimming near the surface, draws his captive to the shore with a curving line. Rumour rages that the foe is routed, and that the Carthaginian has found his safety in flight: that, if he might conquer, an end of the disasters was promised, but that valour lacked all sway, and that punishments were stored up for the victors. That the leader would now close the camp and again command the swords to be carried back to their sheaths, that an account in arms might be rendered, and the soldier clear himself why he conquered the foe. So the crowd. And Saturn's daughter too pricked the minds of the fathers with the goad of envy and the favour of the people. Then they decree things unworthy of trust and to be desired by the Carthaginian, which soon, condemned, they would atone at no small peril. The soldiery is divided, and to Fabius and the master of the horse the commands are wholly made equal. The old man saw it, and, free of anger, feared lest his country, ill-advised, should pay great penalties for so deep an error. And then, pondering much within himself, when he returned from the city, having shared out the allied forces, he sets his standards on the neighbouring ridges close at hand, and from a high lookout aloft watches the Roman camp no less than the Punic. Nor was there delay. The madness of Minucius, the rampart broken through, burned with the love at once of destroying and of perishing. When the Libyan on this side, Fabius on that, saw him advance swiftly from the camp, at once the shrewd man's cares were kindled into sudden action: in haste he bids the companies take up arms and keeps his squadrons within the defence of the rampart, the Ausonian; but the leader of the Carthaginians hurls all his forces into battle and drives his columns on with his voice: 'While the dictator is away, soldier, seize the moment of battle. See, a god offers, on the level plain, the contests long unhoped for. Since the chance is given, with the sword wipe off the long rust, and with much blood, men, sate your blades, full of corrosion.' And these things the Delayer weighed from the mound of the rampart, surveying the fields with his eyes, and at so great a peril it grieved you, Rome, to learn who Fabius was. To him his son, bearing arms at his side: 'The wretch will pay the penalties he deserves,' he says, 'who through blind votes seized our fasces for these crises. Behold the mad tribes. Alas, the slippery rostra and the forums glad of empty men! Now let the deeds of Mars match the office, and let the unwarlike decree that the sun must yield to night. At a great price they shall atone for the madness of their error and for having outraged our father.' Then the old man, shaking his spear, his tears welling up: 'With the blood of the Carthaginians, young man, such bitter words must be wiped out by you. Shall I let a citizen be destroyed before my eyes and hands, or, with me looking on, allow the Carthaginian to conquer? Shall I not be acquitted of the fault of not having matched my inferior, if such is my heart? And now, that you may not doubt, son, take this from your aged father and keep it fixed forever beneath your breast: to be angry with one's country is a sin, and no fouler fault is borne by mortals down to the lowest shades. So the elders taught. How great and of what kind you were, Camillus, when, driven from your home and an exile, in your chariot you would have entered the Capitol an outcast—how many bodies of yours, slain, condemned by your right hand, there are! They would have been at peace had not the man's resolve and a mind impenetrable to wrath stood firm, and the realms of Aeneas would have changed their soil with the sceptre, and now you would stand on no summit of the world, Rome. Lay aside my anger, O son. Let us bear allied arms and hasten aid.' And now the trumpets sounded mingled, and the keen onset had dashed the men together.

First the dictator with his hand cast down the barrier of the gate and the high posts, and broke his course into battle. With no heavier mass do Odrysian Boreas and the African wind, mighty to lift the Syrtis, raise their contests of the winds, when, straining against each other, they whirl their raging wars: they pull the strait apart and roll the sea to opposite shores, each his own; the snatched sea follows, with the shrieking squall, now here, now there, and thunders amid the waves. By no means would any honour, the land of the Phoenicians subdued and Carthage falling, have brought as much as the wrong arisen from envy of glory brought. For all things hard at once were conquered by the man: fear, Hannibal, anger, envy, and at one stroke fame and the fortune of the subdued. When the Carthaginian saw them run swiftly down from the high rampart, his rage trembled, and suddenly there fell, with a groan, the hope, presumed for certain, of a ruin past doubt. For he had walled the army round in a dense ring, meaning to drain them, shut in, with weapons hurled from every side. And here the Dardanian leader in his ill-starred contest had already in mind entered the Styx and the eternal darkness (for he was ashamed to hope for Fabius and the man's aid), when the old man, embracing the battle with his twin wings, binds the backs of the Carthaginians with an outer crown, and now, girding the outermost, himself holds in those who were shutting in the line. Greater rising into arms and greater to behold did Tirynthius show himself. His high crests sparkled and, a marvel, a vast vigour came suddenly into his swift limbs: he heaps on his spears and presses the turned foe with clouds of weapons: such as, after his youth, with old age not yet coming on, the Pylian was a ruler in wars in his second age.

Then rushing on, Thurin and Butes and Naris and Arses he gives to death, and Mahalces, who trusted to join hands with him, to whom there was rare distinction and a name won by the spear. Then he lays low Garadus and Adherbes, lavish of hair, and Thulis, surpassing two ranks with his height, who was grasping the topmost battlements on the high mound, these from afar; with the sword Sapharus and with the sword Monaesus and Morinus, rousing the fight with the bronze's shriek, when the death-bringing blow settled on his right cheek, and, running through the trumpet, the blood, driven out by the wound of the pierced jaw, flowed forth with a last murmur. Next to him fell Nasamonian Idmon by the javelin. For as he was slipping over the warm blood and, sick, striving in vain on the slippery ground to escape with his foot, Hannibal lays him low with his charger hurled against him, and as he raised his stricken limbs in alarm from the ground, with the spear pressed more violently he entangled him in the earth and left the weapon in the wound. The cornel-spear sticks in the ground, trembling at the movement of him who lies there, and, fixed, keeps on the field the corpse entrusted to it.

The youth too, made furious by the example of glory— Sulla and Crassus together, and Furnius joined to Metellus, and Torquatus, the better of right hand—were entering the battles, and of one mind wished even by death to have bought the being gazed on by Fabius. Here, wretched, while he snatches his steps back and, his body drawn aside, avoids the mass of the hurled rock, Bibulus is carried backward and, having slipped over a heap of his comrades, where the clasp, its bite loosened by a frequent blow, had undone the breastplate, received in his side and drove deep into his vitals the iron that chanced to stand out from a fixed corpse. Alas, the manner of his death! He escaped the Garamantian weapons and the band of the Marmaridae, only to fall, laid low by an idle point, by a weapon not aimed at his own wounds. He rolls lifeless, and a new pallor mars the comely face of his youth. From his slackened limbs the arms fall loose, and black sleep wanders over his eyes.

There had come to the war from Tyrian Sidon, summoned by the prayer of his descendants, and was bearing allied arms in aid, proud with an Eastern wing of quivered soldiery, the race of Cadmus, Cleadas; tawny gems gleamed in many a place on his helmet and golden necklace, as when Lucifer, renewed by Ocean's wave, is praised by Venus and vies with the greater stars. He himself in purple and his charger in purple, and through all the column the purple, steeped in Agenorean cauldrons, glittered. He, with the horse, now mocking on the left in a circle, now on the right with light wheelings, through trackless ways, Brutus, eager for battle and longing that so famous a name should fall, behind his back pours the swift arrow, declining the fight in the Achaemenian fashion. Nor was the hand condemned, but, sad to tell, in the middle of the chin of the squire Casca the piercing reed stuck fast, and, cutting an oblique wound with its upright point, brought the iron, warmed, to the moist palate. But Brutus, distraught at the dire fate of his friend, the man who had dared much and was scattering into wounds his cruel shafts by the trick of flight, presses no longer with any racing to catch the swift-footed steed, but all the wrath of his breast he commits, grim, to the spear, and the flying weapon from the thong he hurls, and, where the loose necklace had often bared the top of the breast in its swing, he transfixes it with the point. He falls, pierced through, his bow still drawn, and at once his left hand, as he sinks, dropped the bow, his right the arrow.

But Carmelus, the glory of Phoebean Soracte, waged the battle in no such grim Mars allotted to him. For with his own blood Bagrada had now stained the sword, leader and ruler of the Nubian people; now laid low likewise was Zeuxis, the unsubdued stock of Amyclaean Phalantus, whom a Phoenician mother had borne to a famous Laconian. While he fears such things, trusting neither to fight a foe so swift nor then to flight, with fear persuading him, through the thickets, wretched, into the near tops of an oak had crept and was hiding himself in the high shade, Hampsicus, standing on the boughs that trembled beneath his weight. Him, as he long pleaded much and changed the high boughs with leaps, Carmelus pierces through with his spear, as one who lays waste the limed groves with his reed, while he silently strives, the meta built beneath, to reach by degrees the lofty tops of the high grove, and follows the bird aloft with his lengthening reed. He poured out his life, and, with the gore streaming high, his bloodless limbs hung from the bent bough.

And now the fierce Italians were fighting against the scattered and the backs turned, when suddenly with a fearful mass the Moor Tunger bursts forth in terrifying arms. Black were the man's limbs, and dusky steeds drew his lofty chariot, and, all of one colour, with the art of a new dread he matched the leaden backs of the horses: nor had he ceased to set, like raised crests, plumes upon them, and a black mantle covered them: as once the ruler of eternal night, when he fled to his lowest chamber with the maid of Henna seized, drove his chariot black with Stygian gloom. But Cato, his cheeks then sprinkled with the first down, the glory that the Tusculan walls bore on their Circean ridge, once ruled by Laertes' grandson, though he sees the Latins, troubled in face, draw back their slowed step, undaunted himself, lavish with iron heel and loosed rein, kept driving his lingering horse. It refuses to go against the foe, and the steed, scared, trembles, frightened by an empty shadow. Then swift to the fight, borne down from the high back, he presses the wing-footed chariot with his foot and, as it flies, springs upon it from behind. The reins fell suddenly and the goads, and the iron, quivering above his neck, the luckless Moor turned pale, his blood drawn back. He snatches the head with his sword and carries it on the fixed point.

But with savage Mars fierce the dictator breaks through the panting, blood-stained throng. A pitiable sight, he sees the leader, worn with wounds and with much streaming blood, begging his last and shameful prayers. Tears flowed down his cheeks, and he protects the frightened man with his shield, and, spurring his son: 'Bravest of men, let us drive off this disgrace,' he says, 'and for the Carthaginian's mild deeds— that he scattered no fires over our fields— let us pay a worthy price.' Then, rejoicing in his father's art and his goading, the youth with his sword drives off the columns that had encircled the Carthaginian and frees the field, until the Sidonian leader withdrew from the plain: as, with hunger goading, when the warlike wolf has snatched a lamb, the shepherd turned away, and holds the trembling young in its tight jaws, then, if the shepherd, hearing the bleating, should hasten his steps to meet it on the way, now fearing for itself, it casts back the prey still breathing from its deepest teeth and flees, sick, with empty maw. †Then at last the Stygian shadows, which the black tempest had poured around the Tyrians, fled at length. Their right hands were numb, and they denied that they had earned to be saved, and their sick minds swam amid sudden blessings: as those who, pressed by a collapsed ruin, have lain prostrate, when suddenly their limbs are dug out and black night withdraws, close their eyes and fear to recognize the sun by sight.

The old man, glad at these deeds, his soldiers numbered, was seeking again the camp on the hill, on the safe mound. But lo, the youth, reborn now from the midst of death, raising a shout to the stars and in a long array went exulting, and Fabius their glory, Fabius their salvation, they called, vying, and with a great voice named him father. Then he who before had sat apart with the divided companies: 'Holy one, O father,' he said, 'if it is right, recalled to the honour of the light, to make true complaint, why was it allowed us to divide the camp and the men? Why, patient one, did you give the arms which you alone have the power to wield? By this gift, fallen, we saw the eternal shades with much blood. Swiftly bring back here the eagles and the standards you saved. Here is our country, and the walls of the city stand in one breast. And you, Carthaginian, put off at last your known wiles and tricks: with Fabius alone now must you wage your wars.' When he had spoken these words, a thousand altars—a sight to revere— rise hence from the green turf for the hastening men. Nor was it right for any to touch the feast or the welcome gifts of Lyaeus before, having prayed much, he poured upon the table to Fabius the sacred honour.

First of all Fabius had given the sons of Aeneas the sight of the line of Agenor's race retreating. The Roman camp calls him father alone, and Hannibal alone calls him enemy, and, impatient of delay, he roars: that there might be a chance of battle, the man's fates must be awaited, and beneath arms must be prayed for the help of the Parcae. For while this old age breathed, in vain did he hope for the blood of Latium. But now the soldiery was of one mind, and, the standards brought back, the honour undivided, and again and again the same Fabius alone had to be wrestled with: this galled him, sick at heart, with greater cares. By slackening the seething wars the dictator had so wrought, by his art of sitting still, that, with many things, the Tyrian soldier above all became destitute of everything, and, though the end had not yet been gained by battle and by hand, already by war he had conquered the foe. Nay more, of a yielding temper, but fierce at first, the Celts, a boastful race and changeable of mind, were looking back to their homes: they grieved that wars were waged with no slaughter (unwonted to them), and that their right hands, dry of blood, grew dull amid the weapons in a thirst for Mars. Besides these things, inner ruin and the wound of civic envy increased his troubles. Hanno, hostile to the leader's attempts, would not let the fathers send from home any reinforcements, nor aid him with any resources.

This man, torn with cares and dreading the worst of his fortunes, Juno, foreknowing Cannae and lifted up by the future, leads back to hopes of arms and frenzied vows. For she summoned Anna from the Laurentine pools and addresses her with her voice and fills her with coaxing exhortations: 'A youth of your own kindred blood toils for you, goddess, Hannibal, whose name is memorable from your own Belus. Come, go on, and curb the mad surges of his cares. Shake Fabius from his anxious mind. He alone is now girding on his arms to delay the sending of the Latins under the yoke. With Varro his hands must be joined, and with Varro the battles must be sown, nor let him fail the fates in moving the standards. I myself will be at hand. Let him stretch his way at once toward the Iapygian plain. Hither again shall follow the fates of Trebia and Trasimene.' Then the goddess whose home borders the chaste groves of Indiges: 'It is not in my power,' she said, 'to delay your commands. Let it be right, let it only be permitted, I pray, to retain favour toward my ancient fatherland and the great charges of my sister, although among Latin honours Anna's godhead stands.'

Much lies far back in the affairs of things, and antiquity, sunk in dense darkness, is veiled by the windings of the age, why the Oenotrians should call Sarranian deities to a temple, and a sister of Elissa be worshipped in the realm of Aeneas's sons. But, recalled from its source, I will draw the tale tight within the bounds of telling, and briefly unroll old things.

After Dido was deserted by her Trojan guest and her hopes were broken off, into her inmost chambers, frenzied, she hastens to build a black pyre. Then she snatches the sword, resolved on death, the deadly gift of her fugitive husband. Iarbas, scorned in his suit, sets himself over the realm, and Anna flees the warm pyre. Who would bring help to her in her need, with the Numidian tyrant terrifying far and wide? Battus then by chance was cherishing Cyrene with a gentle rule, mild Battus, ready to give tears to human misfortunes. He, when the suppliant was seen, trembled at the fates of kings and stretched out his right hand. And there, while the reaper twice shears the golden ears, her seat was meanwhile preserved: nor was it longer hers to use these resources and Battus. For Pygmalion was now teaching that ruin should be borne across the sea to the wretched woman. So she is driven over the deep, hateful to the gods and to herself because she had not given herself as companion in her sister's last hour, until a deadly whirlwind, pitiable, with torn sails, drove her, tossed about, onto the Laurentine shores. Knowing neither sky nor soil nor the dwellers there, the Sidonian, shipwrecked, trembled on the Latin land. But lo, Aeneas, attended by sacred Iulus, now possessed of his kingdom, was bearing himself with familiar face. Her, with eyes fixed on the ground and fearing much, and then sinking at the knees of weeping Iulus, he lifts up and with a gentle hand leads within the threshold. And when the honour of his hospitality had soothed her misfortunes and the dread of adversities, then his anxious care demands to learn the death of unhappy Elissa. To him thus, drawing out her words with abundant tears, Anna begins, and adds, suited to the time, coaxing words: 'Son of a goddess, you alone were the cause of my sister's kingdom and her life: death is witness, and that pyre (alas, why was it not the same for me then!). After her eyes were torn from seeing you, wretched one, she sat on the shore at times, at times stood, and following the winds the unhappy woman called with a great cry to Aeneas with her eyes, and begged you to suffer her alone to set herself as companion on your ship. Soon, troubled, she carried back her panting course to her chamber, and with a sudden trembling halted, and feared to touch the sacred bed. Then, distraught, now she cherishes the starry likeness of shining Iulus in her embrace, now wholly, all at once, turned to your face, she hangs upon the image and complains to you, and hopes that answers are sent back. Love never lays aside its hope: now her dwelling and her home she deserts and again, frenzied, revisits the harbours, in case any winds with changed breeze should bring you back. The faithless and shameless levity of the Massylian race even forced her down to magic arts. Alas, the sacred errors of the seers! While they call forth the powers of night and promise remedies for new cares, what crime I saw, deceived! She heaped upon the black pyre all the tokens of you and the gifts that brought no good.'

Then thus Aeneas, recalled to sweet love: 'By this earth I swear, often heard by you amid our prayers, I swear by my life, Anna, and by Iulus, dear to you and to your gentle sister, looking back and sick at heart I then left your realms, nor would I have departed from the chamber, had not Cyllenius, threatening great things and setting me with his own hand on the ships, driven the fleet on the deep with the swift East winds. But why (alas, late warnings!), why at such a time did you give an unguarded love leave to rage?' Against this thus Anna begins, scarcely rolling out her panting murmur amid her sobs and with trembling lips: 'To black Jove, for whom the third realm toils, and to the consort of his dark chamber I was preparing strange rites, to lighten the sick mind and trembling heart of my unhappy sister of the marriage-bed; and I myself was dragging dark sheep with my hand, hastening to the visions to be appeased; †for a grim horror in sleep had filled me with dread, and thrice Dido, thrice with a cry had called her own Sychaeus, and, glad, exulting, had shown his face. While I drive these things from my mind, and toward the light, that the visions might prosper, I pray to the heaven-dwellers and am cleansed in the living stream, she, borne with quick step to the silent shore, twice and thrice pressed kisses on the sand where you had stood: then, embracing it to her breast, she warmed your tracks far and wide, as bereaved mothers press the ashes to their breasts. Then headlong, with rapid course and with hair undone, she swiftly escaped onto the high pyre which she had built before with great mass, from whose seat it was granted to see all the straits and the whole city of Carthage. Here, having put on the Phrygian robe and the pearled necklace, after the unhappy woman had drained in her mind that day on which the gifts were first beheld, and brought back the feasts and the tables made festal by your coming, and you, in order, telling the long labours of Troy while she watched through the night, distraught, she turned her streaming eyes toward the harbours: 'Gods of the long night, whose powers death, now pressing, makes greater to us, I pray,' she said, 'be present and gently receive the shades conquered by passion. Wife of Aeneas, daughter-in-law of Venus, having avenged my husband, I have seen the built citadels of our Carthage. Now to you shall descend the shade of a great body. Me too perhaps the man once known to me in sweet love awaits, longing to match his former cares.' Saying this, she drove the sword into the midst of her breast, the sword sought as a pledge of the Dardanian's love. Her companions saw, and through the halls with sorrowful lament they rush together: the house resounds with great wailings. I, unhappy, took it, and terrified by the dread fates, tearing my face with my hand, with frantic course I seek the royal halls and strive to climb the high steps. Thrice I had tried to fall upon the dire iron, thrice I fell back, fainting, upon my sister's limbs. And now the rumour was carried through the neighbouring towns: the chiefs of the Numidians and savage Iarbas prepare arms. Then, with the fates driving me on, I came to the Cyrenaean city. From here the force of the sea drove me to your shores.'

The Trojan ruler had been moved, and had received calm spirit and a quiet mind toward wretched Anna. And now he had driven all grief and all cares from her breast, nor did she any longer seem a stranger in the Phrygian dwelling. Black night with silent slumber had buried all things over both the lands and the pools of the wide deep, when Dido, most sick at heart, with sorrowful face seemed in sleep to pour out these words to her sister: 'In this house, sister, you can indulge in long rest, alas too careless, nor do you see what snares are stretched for you, what dangers stand around you? Do you not yet know the nurslings of Laomedon's land, ill-omened to our race and to our soil? While the heaven shall roll the stars with rapid turning, and the moon shall light the lands with her brother's fire, no peace shall remain between the sons of Aeneas and the Tyrians. Rise, come: already suspicious Lavinia contrives silent snares and turns over a dread crime in her heart. Moreover, that you may not think sleep feigns these things falsely, not far from here, descending from a small spring, Numicus glides and is rolled in a gentle stream through the valleys. Hither, sister, you shall snatch your way and a safe retreat. The glad nymphs shall receive you into their sacred streams, and you shall be honoured as an everlasting godhead on Italian shores.' So having spoken, the Phoenician vanished into thin air. Anna is shaken from sleep, terrified by the strange visions, and fear goes through all her limbs with cold sweat. Then, as she was, her body covered with a thin garment, she leapt from her bed and, going out by the low window, runs through the open fields with nimble feet, until—so runs the tale—Numicius received her in his sandy bosom and hid her in his glassy caves. Day had risen and filled the whole world with its rays, when the sons of Aeneas, having found no Sidonian in her chamber, and, wandering through the field with great clamour, the Rutulian, follow to the banks of the neighbouring river the plain tracks of her feet, and while they wonder among themselves, from its deep the river snatches its waters and its course. Then in the lowest seats the Sidonian was seen to sit among the dark-blue sisters and to address the Trojans with a peaceful face. From that time, honoured in the first days of the year, through all Ausonia she was worshipped with a venerable godhead.

After Saturn's daughter had urged her to the grievous battles of the Italians, she seeks the upper air in a swift chariot, about at last to drink the longed-for blood of Latium. The goddess prepares to obey the goddess, and, seen by none, sought the great leader of the Libyan race. He then by chance, withdrawn from all gathering of men, revolving the uncertain outcomes of affairs and of the war, was drawing anxious sighs with a wakeful voice. To him the goddess thus with friendly words soothes his cares: 'Why, O bravest king of the Sidonian race, do you draw out your grief further with sickening care of leadership? All the anger of the gods now stays appeased for you, all favour has returned to Agenor's sons. Come, up, break off your sluggish delays, sweep the Marmaric forces into battle. The fasces are changed. Already the Tirynthian hero, against the senate's will, has laid down war and arms, and with another Flaminius you must wage your wars. That you may not doubt, the matron of the highest Thunderer has sent me to you. I, an everlasting godhead on Oenotrian shores, am honoured, sprung from the blood of your own Belus. Let there be no delay: snatch up the thunderbolts of war in a swift course. Where lofty Garganus spreads itself into the Iapygian fields (the land not far), hither direct your standards.' She spoke, and lifted her dewy face into the clouds. To her the leader, freshening again at the pledge of promised glory: 'Nymph, glory of my race, than whom no more sacred godhead,' he said, 'is ours, propitious in your appearing, prosper my cause. But I, when I am master of the battle, in the citadel of Carthage will set you in marble temples and beside you will dedicate Dido, made equal by the twin gift of an image.' Having said this, swollen with pride, he spurs his exulting comrades: 'Lay aside your heavy cares and the slow torments of sitting still, soldier fated for Latium. We have appeased the wrath of the heaven-dwellers, the gods return: I announce that here the command of malign Fabius is finished and the fasces changed with a new consul. Now let each man render me his right hand and those great things which, shut out from Mars, you used to promise. See, my country's godhead pledges greater things than those achieved. Let the standards be plucked up, and with a goddess leading let us seek the plain ill-omened to the Trojans by the name of Diomedes.'

And while the Carthaginians, kindled in their breasts, make for Arpi, upheld by the snatched purple of a plebeian office, Varro now rages on the rostra and, hastening to open a place for a vast ruin, brings the fates near the city. And to him belonged a race without lustre and a deaf, nameless ancestry, and immoderately his bold tongue quivered in his tuneful mouth. Hence increased in wealth and lavish of plunder, while he courts the lowest of the crowd and barks at the senate, he raised his head so high in a city shaken by wars that he was the one arbiter of the moment of affairs and of fate, under whose victory it should be a shame for Latium to be preserved. Him, among the Fabii and the names hallowed to Mars, the Scipios, and Marcellus bearing the high spoils to Jove, the blind votes had added as a blot upon the records, and Cannae, that deadly evil, was fostered by canvassing and the Field of Mars, more fatal than the Greek sea. The same man, as a sower of disturbances and skilled to kindle envy, and crooked in the toga, so, feeble in the art of war and unskilled to ply Mars and tried by no steel, hoped with his tongue to attain the glory of the right hand, and from the rostra stirred up wars. So, eager and professing to upbraid Fabius for delay, he carried impudent words against the fathers before the crowd: 'You, whose is the command, I, the consul, demand precepts and the measure of waging war. Am I to sit still or wander on the mountains, while with me the Garamantian and the Moor, scorched of body, divide Italy? Or shall I use the sword with which you gird me? Hear, good dictator, what the Martial commons command: they bid the Libyans be driven out and Rome be relieved of the foe. Are they in haste, who, having suffered very much, a third year burns with tearful misfortunes? Go then, take up arms, men. Delay alone is the short road to triumph. The first day that shows the foe will both undo the rule of the fathers and the wars of the Carthaginians. Go eagerly: with a Latin chain bound about his neck I will lead Hannibal through the city while Fabius looks on.' After he had thundered these things, swiftly he carries arms from the gates and drives off delay: as when, the barrier broken, an untaught charioteer pours out all the reins and, headlong, hanging on the lash with anxious foot, is borne unmatched by his horses: the ill-driven axle smokes, and the discordant reins float on the uncertain car. Paulus saw it (for to him the Field had borne common rights and arms), that affairs were slipping and ruined, the sinister consul sinking; but the wrath of a troubled crowd is fickle, and a scar marked upon his mind curbed the surging griefs in his sick heart. For once, when the Illyrian coast was subdued by the man's youthful arms, envy had barked at the victor with black mouth and tossed him with unfair winds. Hence there was in him fear and a reverence for the harsh commons. But his race, near to the gods, touched the heaven through its high ancestors at the summit: to count his forefather Assaracus back, Amulius was the warrant before him, and Assaracus had Jove, nor would one who had watched him in arms deny his lineage. To him Fabius, as he now sought the camp: 'If you believe your greatest wars will be with the Tyrian leader (unwilling I shall break this utterance from my breast), you are deceived, Paulus. The dire battles of the sons of Ausonia and a foe heavier than your camp await you, or I have learned in vain through much war to foreknow misfortunes. I heard him promise (it grieves and wearies my old age, alas, if any ruins remain that I foresee for it to suffer!) to the leader of so fortunate a Mars that, at whatever hour he should see him, he would take up battle. How near now, Paulus, to the last destruction we are, if the burning Carthaginian has heard this utterance of the consul! Now I believe a battle-line stands ready over the broad fields, and a second Flaminius is awaited beneath the blow. How many men, madman, Varro, will you rouse! Will you (O gods!) you, at once, the arms, you, the field? Will you not first learn and explore by delaying, †what the enemy's manner is? Will you not, what abundance of resources, what nature there is to the ground, what kind of arms there is, search out cunningly, and look upon Fortune, who stands above all weapons? Bring, Paulus, a heart not straying from the right. Why, if it is right for one man to crush his country, should it be wrong for one to save it? The shameless Libyan now lacks in narrow store, and, the heat of war blunted, the loyalty of his allies is loose. Here no friendly house invites him with a native roof, no faithful cities receive him with their walls, and no youth renews itself with equal manhood. Scarcely a third throng of men remains, which comes from the raw Spaniard. Hold fast and, patient, love the remedies of a cautious war. If meanwhile any breeze invite and a god assent, swift draw near to the favouring signs.' To him in turn the consul thus briefly with sorrowful face: 'This devotion shall be wholly with me, and I will bear your mind, unconquered one, against the Carthaginians. Nor does the one reasoning of delay deceive me, by which, while you ranged, Hannibal aged and saw the war settle, crushed. But what is this wrath of the gods? One consul, I think, is given to Ausonia, the other to the Carthaginians. He drags all things with him and madly fears lest, with another consul, Rome should fall. Summon from the Tyrian senate a colleague: he will not wish things so savage. No steed suffices to bear the madman against the foe. He grieves that the darkness of night, which would slow his course, comes on, and goes proud all but with drawn swords, lest any delay slow the battles while the sword is drawn from the sheath. By the Tarpeian rocks and the dwelling of Jove, kindred to us in blood, and by the walls of my fortunate fatherland, which now standing on their own height I leave, wherever the highest safety shall call, I swear I will go, the danger scorned. But if the camp shall fight against me, deaf to my warning, no longer, my sons, will I delay you and the sweet house of Assaracus's race, nor shall wounded Rome see Paulus returning like Varro.' So then with divided mind the troubled leaders sought their camp. But already on the foretold fields had settled the Carthaginian, keeping the Aetolian plains for battle. Never at another time was the Italian land shaken by a greater host of men, by a greater throng of hoofed beasts beneath arms.
