But one breastplate is pierced through with a spear, and clinging to a corslet at times hangs a Moorish reed. At times in mournful clamour they call for their comrades. Here Galba, here Piso, and Curio—not deserving an inglorious death—are wept, and there Scaevola, mighty in war. These on every side, but Paulus equally, like the dire fate of a parent, they mourn: how he never ceased to sing words foretelling disaster and to check Varro's purpose, and how he turned this day so often, in vain, from the city, and likewise how great he was in his right hand. But care for the future presses those whom it grips: some hasten to draw trenches before the walls, or strengthen the gateways' approaches, as means allow, and where the plain lies open to the foe with level entrances, they mimic stags' antlers with fire-hardened branches, and the stake is hidden, a blind weapon in the path of their steps.

Behold, beyond the disasters and the wound past cure, an impious panic and a greater Fury was tossing about the remnants of the war, the bodies undestroyed by the Punic. Across the sea they were making ready Tyrian swords and Punic arms, and to escape Hannibal under a changed sky. The leader was Metellus, not glad in exile from war, yet of a stock with no small name. He was driving his evil-minded heart and degenerate hand to base counsels, and was looking at lands set in another world, where they might hide themselves, lands to which no fame of the Punic name or of the homeland left behind might reach.

When Scipio took this in with kindled mind— he who, as great as when joining fierce battles against the Sidonian leader he stood in the fields, swiftly snatches his sword, and where the men were brewing a shameful evil and final ruin for Latium, breaking the doors, towering, he bursts in. Then shaking his drawn blade with his voice before the faces of the frightened: 'Tarpeian father, who dwell in the temple, a second seat from heaven, and you, Saturnia, not yet changed by Iliac woes, and you, harsh maiden, your breast girt with the Gorgon aegis of your furies, and you native gods, lo, by your own divine powers and by the head, no lighter to me than any god, of my great-souled father I swear: never the Lavinian realm will I leave, nor suffer it to be left, while life remains. Quickly, lo, call the gods to witness: if the walls shall blaze with Libyan torches, no step, Metellus, will you dare to bear onto foreign lands. If you do not pledge this, he whom you dread and whose sleep you break with terror, Hannibal, is here armed. You shall die, nor by any slain of the Punic shall a fairer glory be won.' By these threats the design was struck down. And now, the order given, they bind their souls to the homeland, and swear the dictated oaths to the gods, and cleanse their breasts of guilt.

And while these things, with troubled minds, are done among the Rutulians, Hannibal was ranging the fields and reckoning the grim deeds of his savage right hand, surveying the wounds with his gaze, and with a great crowd thronging about him he offered sweet spectacles to the fierce Punic men. Amid that slaughter, his breast pierced with weapons, half-dead, Cloelius was breathing his life into the air, failing now with a dying murmur, and his face, weary, he scarcely raised by effort on his faltering neck. His horse knew him, and, with ears pricked, pouring out a shrill neigh, dashes Bagesus to the ground, who then was bearing it into the ranks on its captive back. From there, gathering a swift course, over the slippery ground where thick blood stood, and the corpses heaped by slaughter, it flies and halts at the face of its fallen master. Then, bowing its neck and lowering itself on its shoulders, in its wonted way, with bent legs, it offered him to climb upon its back, and trembled with a love all its own. No soldier had vaulted more happily upon that keen horse, whether he were borne back upon its galloping back, his limbs thrown supine, or whether he stood on its bare back, while the swift steed in headlong course carried off the contests of the field.

But the Libyan, marvelling not a little at the horse that matched human feelings in its breast, who that youth might be that fought against the doom of his left side, asks his name and his renown, and at the same time grants a quick death. Here Cinna (for he had turned his arms to the Tyrians, trusting their fortunes, and then went as comrade to the triumphant) said: 'To this man, bravest leader, the lineage is not unworthy of your ears. Once, under kings, that Rome which refuses the Libyan reins, once, under kings, Rome herself was ruled. But indeed, indignant at the throne of the Proud, when she drove out the sceptres, at once great wars came from the house of Clusium. If Porsenna by report has reached your ears, if Cocles, if the Lydian camp— he, girt with Maeonian aid and the Etruscan people, strove to restore through war the kings driven out. Much indeed they dared in vain, and the tyrant pressed, leaning upon the city, the Janiculum. Soon, peace approved, they suppressed their hatreds, and the war was laid down with a treaty, and faith was bound by hostages. Hearts that knew not to grow gentle, O gods! and a race of Italians ready to bear all that is not cruel for the sake of glory: twice six years Cloelia had not yet filled of her youthful body, one of the maidens sent to the king among the Laurentine bands and the pledges of peace, among the virgin throngs. The deeds of men I pass over. She, despising king and treaty and her years and the river, swam across the wondering Thybris, undaunted, breaking the wave with girlish arms. Had nature changed her sex, perhaps you, Porsenna, might not have been allowed to return to the Tyrrhenian shores. But, not to be too long for you, from this youth comes his lineage, and a name to be remembered for a glorious maiden.'

While he unfolds such things, nearby on the left a sudden clamour bursts out. In mingled ruin, among the arms of men and the mangled corpses, they had dug out the body of Paulus from the midst of the heaped slain. Alas, who was he! How unlike him who but now threw the Punic ranks into rout with his weapons, or when he overturned the Taulantian realm, and chains were laid upon the Illyrian tyrant! His grey hair was foul with black dust and dry gore, his beard was caked, and his teeth shattered by the whirling of the wall's stone, and over all his body the wound. When he beheld these things, the Sidonian leader, his joys redoubled: 'Flee, Varro,' he said, 'flee, Varro, surviving, while Paulus lies dead. To the fathers and to Fabius sitting in office and to the people, as consul, tell over the whole tale of Cannae. I will grant you this flight again, if the desire of light is so great, I will grant it to you, Varro. But he whose brave heart, worthy of me and the foe, glowed with no small force, let him be honoured with a last funeral and the honour of a tomb. How great, Paulus, you lie! who, one man, are to me a greater cause of joy than all those thousands. When the fates shall call, such a death I pray for myself, with Carthage safe.'

So he speaks, and bids the bodies of his comrades be given to the earth when next dawn shall redden with her chamber opened, and orders the heaps of arms to rise, to be burned, war god, for you. Then the bidden duties, though weary, they hasten, and with their scattered column lay low the nearby groves: the dark wood resounds, struck by the axe on the leafy ridges. Here the ash and the white-foliaged poplar, lofty, hewn by strong arms, is split, here the holm-oak laid by in the age of forefathers. They roll down oaks and the pine that loves the shores and—funereal grace—the mournful cypress for the pyres. Then in rivalry they weave the funeral pyres, an unhappy office and a gift vain to the slain, until Phoebus plunged his panting horses into the Tartessian pools, and the Titaness, fleeing the sky, drew on the blind night with blackening gloom by her wheel's track. Afterward, when the reins of Phaethon shone with the first fires, and their colours returned to the earth, they set flame beneath, and the bodies, dripping with corruption, they burn on hostile soil. A grim dread enters the mind, the fear of doubtful fortune, and a silent terror wanders through the inmost heart: lest, should the chance of unjust war soon so bear it, they too must lie in this hostile place. But to you, Lord of War, a sacred mountain, built up in a vast heap of arms, was rising to the stars. The leader himself, lifting in his hand a tall pine crowned with flame, called Mars to his vows: 'These first-fruits of the fight and these offerings of glad war Hannibal, victor, burns from the Ausonian name, and to you, Mars our father, not deaf to my vows, the chosen arms of a throng of living men he dedicates.' Then, the torch flung in, the burning fire ravages the blazing mass, and, the gloom broken, its peak driven into the air floods the fields with bright light. From here, swift, he went to the tomb and the funeral granted to Paulus, and vaunted the honour of an enemy's death. They raised a lofty pyre on high, and of soft, green straw they laid out the couches. Gifts were placed upon them, the funeral glory: hated by those who knew it, both sword and shield, and a terror once and a proud emblem, the broken fasces, and the axes captured in war. No wife or children were there, no throng of men joined by near blood, nor, as custom asks, did the ancestral image, going before on the lofty bier, adorn the rites, stripped of all its spoils, and now Hannibal alone was praise enough for honour: with rich purple the shining coverings he casts, sighing, over him, and a cloak inwrought with gold, and addresses him with the last honour: 'Go, glory of Ausonia, where it is right for souls proud in virtue and in deeds to go. For you glory by your death, a noble one, is now won. Fortune still turns our labours about and bids us not know the chances to come.' So the Libyan, and suddenly, the flames crackling on every side, the exulting soul escaped into the airs of heaven.

Then Rumour, its sound swelling, was already reaching the stars, already the seas and lands, and had entered the city first. They despair of the walls: to the trembling people it was enough to have hoped for the citadel alone. For no youth survived, and an empty name of Ausonia stood, without a body, and that the enemy had not yet burst through the gates, they think he idles out of contempt. Already they seem to see the houses burning, the shrines plundered, and unspeakable slaughter of their children before their faces, and the seven citadels smoking. One day mourned two hundred curule chairs overthrown in carnage, and Rome's tottering walls bereft of twice thirty thousand of her youth, drained dry, and this after the Trebia, after the pools of the Tuscan deep, nor with the number of her allies slain in a lighter measure. But indeed, the loyal company of the senate that was left take up their duties by lot. Surveying all things swiftly, Fabius cries to the stunned: 'No room is left, believe me, for delay. Let us make haste, that the foe may not in vain dare to come armed against our walls. Harsh fortune is fed among the fearful by sitting still, and adversity swells through fear. Go quickly, tear down the weapons, O youth, from the temples. Strip the halls in haste and refasten for war the captured shields. We are enough for the homeland, if from our number nothing fear takes from the battle. Let that grim plague be feared on the open plains; never has the Moor, light, exulting with naked body, broken our walls.'

While Fabius sharpens with fear the minds that had failed, a wandering rumour through the walls spreads word that Varro is coming, and floods their breasts with a secret motion: just as, if by chance the master of a wrecked ship should swim alone, saved from the sea, to the empty shores, the uncertain tremble whether to stretch out or withhold their hands to the storm-tossed man, and they hate his very safety, the master surviving when the ship is lost. What ruin remains for the man, who dares to approach the gates and comes as a dire omen to the fearful!

Soothing these laments, Fabius taught that it was base to be angry at disasters, and kept the crowd from wrath. For it was not the part of men to be borne down by adversity, men who inscribe the war god on their race; they could not hide their griefs and demand consolation for sorrow from punishment. But if they would let him reproach, that day had dawned more grievously for him on which he had seen Varro go to the camp, than the one on which he sees him return without his arms. At these words the threats subsided, and suddenly turned their hearts: now they pity his fate, now they reckon the joys snatched from the Punic by two consuls slain. So all the crowd pours itself out now in a long column of welcome, and they testify that they believe it done with great spirit, that, trusting his ancestors and the proud sceptres of the Laomedontiad line, he had not despaired of the city.

No less unhappy, troubled by his guilt and great shame, the consul bore his tottering steps toward the walls, weeping: to lift his downcast face, to look upon his homeland and renew his grief, shamed him. But that, on his return, both people and fathers should offer themselves to him, not to congratulate, but to demand their sons each one, and their brothers, and the wretched parents seemed to be going to tear at the consul's face. So therefore, with his lictor silent, borne into the city, he scorned the honour condemned by the gods.

But the fathers and Fabius, their grief set far away, hasten their cares. Swiftly the chosen young of the slaves are armed, nor does shame, set below safety, shut the camp against deliverance. It is fixed to lead back the realm of Aeneas by whatever hand into the laws of the Parcae, and for the citadel and the sceptres and the honour of liberty to arm even the hands of slaves. The youthful bodies of their own they strip of the bordered robe and gird with unaccustomed arms. The boyish face is shut in a helmet, and the foe is bidden to come of age in slaughter. Likewise, to those who begged that they might ransom the captive crowd with a little gold (and not few were the thousands who prayed), they hardened themselves, to the Punic's wonder, to refuse. So far had it surpassed all crimes and every fault that armed men could be taken. Then it was laid upon them to earn their living far through the Sicilian shores, condemned for having turned their backs, until the foe should leave Latium. Such was Rome then: she for whom, if it stood in the fates to change your ways hereafter, you, Carthage, had better remained.

Now come, what peoples and Sarranian camps the famous disaster on the Iapygian plain turned toward Libya, I will tell. No faith stands long anywhere for mortals when Fortune wavers. They strove openly to join their hands to the Punic, who was breaking the treaties (alas, too quick to lose faith when affairs are wounded!)— fiercer than the rest in keeping his wrath stored up and bold to renew his hatred in time, the Samnite, and soon, fickle and late to feel shame at the deed, the Bruttian, and the Apulian, false with his two-faced arms, then the Hirpinian race, empty and not to be taught repose and unworthy to have broken faith: as if dire contagions of a foul disease were spreading through all the peoples. And now Atella, now Calatia too, drove its cohorts into the Punic camp, fear overcoming right. Then the spirited fickleness of Phalantine Tarentum loosed the Ausonian yoke. Lofty Croton opened her friendly gates and to barbarous commands taught the grandsons of the Thespiads to bow their necks to the Africans. The same madness held Locri too. The shore of the shoaling strand, where Greater Greece guards her Argive walls and is washed, curving, by the Ionian deep, following Libya's glad fortunes and her luck in war, swore, trembling, its battles to the Tyrian war god. And now indeed the Celts, the proudest dwellers by the Eridanus, fell upon the woes of Italy, and old comrades in grief hastened to join themselves with all their force.

But the Celts might be excused this, and the Boian peoples their impious wars: that the frenzy which pleased the Senonian race should please Capua, and that the Dardan walls, from their first founding, should ally with a barbarian Numidian tyrant— who now, when the times have so changed, would believe it? Luxury and the sloth nurtured in mad debauches, and shame consumed by sinning, and honour, left to wealth alone, a disgrace—these tore the people gaping with idleness and the city loosed from its laws. On top of this, a savage pride drove them to ruin. Nor was there lack of strength for their vices. To no people of Ausonia was the measure of gold and silver greater (so then did Fortune favour them); their cloth was steeped in Assyrian poison for the men, and in midday the royal banquets, and feasts caught by the rising sun, and a life smeared with every stain. Then the fathers were cruel to the people, the plebs glad at the senate's hatred, and sedition, striking together the discordant hearts. But meanwhile a more polluted old age was enlarging the reckless faults of the youth. Nor were those whom a base birth and a despised origin of life disgraced, lacking in hoping for themselves and demanding first the commands and the reins of the perishing homeland. Indeed it was an old custom to enliven the banquets of men with slaughter, and to mingle with the feasts the grim spectacles of men contending with the sword, and often over the very cups of the falling, the tables sprinkled with no scant blood.

Approaching these by craft, by which to turn their sick minds more keenly toward the Tyrians, demanding what he was sure Rome would by no chance grant (for he did not wish it granted)— Pacuvius was a name not obscure for its crime— he urges them to demand a share of the highest power, and the fasces in turn, with a consul allied, and, if they should refuse to sit on the divided curule chair, the honour made equal, and to see the two sets of axes, that an avenger of the refusal should stand before their eyes and faces. So a chosen band carries the words at a hurried pace. Virrius, surpassing all in eloquence, stands foremost, but of obscure birth, and second to none in frenzy. When in the gathering of the fathers and the great senate he had poured out the impious counsels of the mad crowd, scarcely whole, and inflamed their ears with swelling words, a harsh clamour bursts from the whole assembly with the united roar of those who refuse; then each man, upbraiding, wearies him, and the temple shakes with the strife of voices.

Here Torquatus, noble for having matched his grandfather's stern brow, said: 'Alas, Capua, bearing such words, have you hardened yourselves to approach the Romulean walls, to which Carthage and Hannibal did not dare bring their arms after Cannae? Does it never pass through your ears, when on the Tarpeian seat the Latins begged for equality, how he who then brought the commands with proud mouth was thrust back—not with words, not with voice, but with a fierce right hand—driven headlong through the temple's threshold in so great a whirling of his rolled body, that, dashed on the cruel rock, with Jove looking on, he atoned for his grim words and paid for impious speech with death? Behold, I am the offspring of him who from the seat of the Thunderer drove out the suppliant and, as consul, defended the bare Capitol with his hand.' Then, seeing the man rave and threaten the eyes with the palms of his hands and prepare to repeat his ancestor's deeds, growing yet harsher in greater stir, Fabius takes him up, gnashing: 'O wholly shameful! The seat, behold, is empty, widowed by war's storm: on whom, I ask, of you do you make ready to set it, and into Paulus's place whom do you give? Or is your lot, Virrius, first and before the others, the senate yielding, and does the purple now summon you and match you with our Bruti? Go, madman, go where you are heading; let perfidious Carthage give you her own fasces.' In the midst of the speaker's heat, unable to hold his fury back longer with a groan, Marcellus cries out grimly from a lightning wrath: 'What patience, and how slow, holds your mind, O Varro, too confounded by the war god's whirlwind, that you can endure, as consul, these frenzied nightmares? Do you not long since drive them, hurled from the temple's threshold, headlong to the gates, and force these half-men to learn what the command of a consul made in our custom is? A youth never sober and soon to perish, I warn you, quickly get gone from the city. Before your walls, as is fitting, the leader, armed, will give the due answer.' Hereupon all rise alike and press the men with a great clamour.

And too the Campanian youth quickly bore their own step from the doors, and Virrius, roused by the grief of so great a rebuff, was turning Hannibal over in his mouth. Fulvius (for the presages of his mind promised him the glory to come, and the image of perishing Capua was even then before his eyes) said: 'Not even if you, victor, drive to Rome the leader of Carthage bound in chains at his neck, will it hereafter be granted to enter the consecrated seats of Quirinus. Make haste, I beg, where your sick mind calls you.' Then, hurried off, they bear back these grim answers of the fierce senate, mixed with threats.

Is it your pleasure, almighty one, that the fates lie hidden sunk in such darkness? A happier age will come one day, when loyal Rome will rejoice in a Campanian consul and, secure, will of her own will restore to her great-souled grandsons the fasces and the arms long denied through wars. Yet this punishment of their proud forefathers will endure: that Capua shall not send her men to the voting before Carthage sends hers. After he had now set forth the senate's words, now its deeds, then Virrius, mixing false with true by craft, sang to the troubled the fatal signal of bloody war. The maddened youth want arms, arms, and Hannibal. The crowd rushes from every side and calls the Punic into their homes. The mighty deeds of the Sidonian youth they celebrate: how he broke the Alps, the partner of Hercules' glory, and crossed at a run the crags that neighbour the gods, how, glutted with slaughter, he closed, victor, the fords of the Eridanus, how the same, victor, troubled the Lydian pools with Roman blood, how he gave the banks of the Trebia to the eternal name of fame, and the same man amid the battles sent both Paulus and Flaminius, the chief men of the state, down to the shades. On top of these they heap Saguntum razed in the first war, and the ridges of the Pyrenees, and the Ebro, and the rites of his father, and the war sworn by the man in his boyhood years. That one man, with so many leaders slain in slaughter, so many routed in the line, stands amid the battles touched by no weapons. When by the gift of the gods it is granted to ally one's hands with this man and be joined by treaty, should Capua, forsooth, endure the pride of a bloodless people and the empty swelling and the lordship of the city, which denies the fasces and equal rights as if to slaves? For truly Varro must be held the worthier of so great a name, since a consul more resplendent in purple flees him.

Boasting such things, they were already making ready to send the band chosen by lot, to join the youth by treaty to the Tyrians. But not the unconquered strength alone within his breast did Decius then lay aside, the glory of Capua. And he, received into the midst of the gathering (for it was not granted to delay), said: 'Citizens, do you go to violate the rights of your fathers and to join in friendship a head condemned at the altars of a profaned treaty? What so great forgetting of the right? It is great, and set among great peoples and men, to show a faith unturned! Now is the time to enter battles for the Rutulians, now to move standards and the line, while affairs are anxious and the wounds demand a cure: that is the place for duty, when good fortune fails, and when harsh Fortune calls us to give aid. For to cherish the glad is in no way the glory of a great spirit. Come here, be present. I know souls like the gods, and hearts never narrow in great misfortunes. They take, believe me, Cannae and the Trasimene shoals and Paulus's memorable death. These are they who with their hands cast out the foe fixed in your walls and snatched Capua from the proud commands of the Samnites. These are they who gave you laws, terror driven off, and held back the Sidicine wars. What allies do you flee? Or whom do you add? I am that Dardan blood, to whom my father left the sacred rites, to whom Capys, kin to great Iulus, left a name drawn down from Jove; shall I, that man, among the half-human Nasamones, and among the savage Garamantian who equals the ways of wild beasts, pitch my tent, mingled with the Marmaric fosterling, and follow a leader for whom now, in place of treaty and justice, there is the sword, and praise drawn from blood alone? Not so, not so; right and wrong are not so mingled for Decius that he could wish for this. With no such great gift has grudging Nature armed us as that the door of death lies open and the power to leave a life that is unjust.'

These vain words Decius hurled to turned-away ears. But the chosen band was making the treaty with the Punic. And now there was at hand, sent ahead to the leader amid the troubling tumult, a numerous cohort of Autololes. He himself with a great column swiftly moved his hastened standards across the plains. And Decius: 'Now is the hour, men, now the time. Be present, while a right hand worthy of Capua, with me as leader, attempts the avenging deed: let the barbarous host fall down. Each for himself, eager, seize this glory. If the foe prepares to approach, offer him gates blocked with corpses and purge the wickedness with the sword. This blood alone, in the end, shall wash the minds stained with the crime.'

And while he proclaims these things in vain, pleasing to none, the harshness of the man and his fierce undertaking being heard, bearing a heart big with much wrath, the Punic was standing at the walls and bids the chosen quickly fetch relentless Decius to the camp. His bristling valour and a breast armed with good faith and the desire of the right and a mind greater than Capua, undaunted by the great peril, stood unconquered, and with grim face assailed the leader's menacing commands with bitter words besides. Him the ruler of Libya, scorning the bearer of so many standards, so many arms, upbraiding, with a great clamour proclaims: 'After Paulus, after Flaminius, am I matched, alas, with mad Decius, who wished to contend with me for the honour and fame of death. Seize (go, hurry) the standards, leaders. Whether the Campanian city lies open to me against Decius's will, I am pleased to learn— to me, who, stirring new wars, found the Alps lying open, rocks thrusting at the sky and trodden by one god alone.' Blood had suffused his face, and from his grim eye flames rose. Then his foaming mouth and the sighs driven from his panting throat rolled a dire murmur deep within. So, borne into the city, the whole senate accompanying him and the crowd alike rushing to gaze on the leader's face, he pours out all his rage and the storms of his wrath.

And too, nearer perils had inflamed Decius's mind, and he saw the time was now at hand when, unarmed, he might surpass the praises of the unconquered leader. No flight, no shut house hid him, but free, as if no Hannibal had entered the city, he had kept his leisure with undaunted face, when, dreadful, a band roused with savage arms attacks the youth and sets him at the feet of the leader, seated on high. Then from above, assailing him with fierce words, the victor thunders: 'Do you alone make ready to prop up rushing Rome and call her back from her death, O madman? Behold, the man who would snatch from me the great gifts of the gods. For Decius, forsooth, an idle one, was I kept, to be conquered—by unwarlike Decius, to whom no woman born on the Agenorean shores of our Carthage would yield. To this man, come (for why should we, great-souled, bear unworthy things?), soldier, fasten the chains he has earned.' He had said these things, and the taunts knew no end yet: as when a lion, borne among the herds, sets himself upon the high necks, and victorious roars monstrously in his wrath, and, heavy, clings with sunk claws, hanging on the neck, gnaws the panting bullock. But Decius, while they bind the chains, says: 'Fasten quickly (for so it befits Hannibal to have entered) the chains, the price of the ill-omened treaty. So a victim fully worthy falls, Decius. For it is not right that you, glad in human blood, should have appeased it by slaying bullocks. See, your hand! See, your treaty! Not yet has the senate-house, not yet the posts of the temples been entered by you: already by a fierce command the prison is opened. Go on, and to such beginnings heap deeds to match. Fame will bear to the shades that you were crushed, fallen in the ruins of Capua.' Nor was he allowed to speak more. His head is veiled in black cloth, and, fierce, he is dragged before the faces of his own.

Then the victor, exulting, his breast calmed at last, glad to look on the city's buildings and temples, carries his serene eyes around and learns each thing: who founded the walls, and how great the youth under arms, how many talents of silver and bronze lie open for war, now what manner of mounted force, now in turn how great the foot-soldiers' force of men. They show the lofty Capitol and tell of the Stellate plains and bountiful Ceres. And now Phoebus with his wearied horses was driving the day to its goal in Olympus, and Hesperus was darkening with shadow gradually poured the chariot hastening to the shores: they set out the banquet in their custom and through the festal city celebrate feasts at tables royally heaped. He himself, deemed worthy of a god's worship and sacred honour, is received on high upon couches of choice and far-shining purple. Not one throng of servants: to some was given the care of laying out the food, to some to tend the hearths, to some to bear the cups in order; and too the larder is built up at fixed places. On the rough table gleam the weights of gold engraved from of old. The flames steal away the night, and with the din of those who move the lofty house murmurs. The Sidonian soldier, unused to the rich table, marvels, and drinks in with wondering eyes the unknown face of proud luxury. He himself eats in silence and condemns such honours to be given to feasts, and that tables should be so easily served by so great a column, until hunger was driven off and the gifts of Bacchus loosed his hard mind. Then at last the gladness was given back to his brow, and the heavier cares laid down from his breast.

Teuthras resounds with his Euboean lyre, a dweller of Cumae, and soothes with songs the ears deafened by the harsh murmur of the savage war-trumpet amid battles. For he sang of Chaos, once a blind mass without a star, no day arising, and a world without light. Then how the god had parted the pools of the liquid deep and set the globe of earth in the midst of the frame; how he had given the lofty Olympus for the gods to dwell on, and he showed the chaste ages of father Saturn. And now he sang of Jove and his glad loves through stealth, and the bridals of Electra, daughter of Atlas, whence was born Dardanus, an offspring worthy of the gods, and how he gave to the Thunderer Erichthonius, a grandson of great stock; hence Tros, hence Ilus, then in the long order of the race Assarcus, and how Capys, less than none in fame or hand, gave his name to the first walls. Together with applause the Sidonian youth alike and the Campanian bands celebrate it. Before all the leader pours libation from the goblets to the honour of the name with august rite; the rest, who follow him, in Bacchus's manner sprinkle the liquor on the tables and the throng grows hot with wine.

Meanwhile, when the Tyrian gathering had dissolved into joys (for I will not, youth not unworthy of being silenced, gladly pass over your beginnings and deny you fame, though your daring, though of great promise, was unfulfilled), one mind, untouched by wine and disarmed by no poisons of drinking from its honour, was rolling in its silent breast the mass of Sidonian battle and slaughter. And, that so sacred a longing might be the more to be marvelled at, born of Pacuvius, he had condemned his father's arts. He, following close behind his father, who, laden with various banquets, was leaving the halls with slow step, after it was given him to disclose his plans and unfold his new attempts, and a free place, the rest of the buildings left behind, lay open at their backs, said: 'Receive counsels worthy of both Capua and us': (and, his toga drawn aside, he bares his armed side) 'this war I make ready to finish with this sword and to bear off, torn, to the Thunderer the head of the Libyan ruler, victorious. This will be that sword which will now seal the treaties polluted by guile. If old age cannot bear so great a spectacle and trembles, weary with years, at deeds too great, then do you withdraw to a safe house and leave me to my own purpose. He whom you believe the highest and match with the gods, Hannibal—O how much greater in name than the Punic will your son now be to you!' From his face flashed a fierce fire, and the man's spirit was already waging the war, when the old man, scarcely now able with sick ear long since to bear the weight of so great an attempt, trembling there sinks down and, fixing frequent fearful kisses on his feet: 'By whatever of life remains, by a father's rights, and by your safety, dearer to me, son, than my own, desist from your enterprise, I beg, lest I see hospitality polluted with blood, and cups filled with bloody gore, and the tables overturned in the strife of battle. Will you—he whom not battle-lines, not walls and cities can withstand, when his nearer brow and eye flash with quivering fire—will you endure those thunderbolts that the man pours from his head, if, at the sight of the sword, he hurls the dire voice with which he turns the columns across the plains? It deceives you, that you think him unarmed among the tables. A majesty eternal, sought by the man in so many wars, won by so many slaughters, arms the leader. If you bring your face near, you will marvel that Cannae and the Trebia, before your eyes, and the Trasimene graves, and the mighty shade of Paulus stand there. What then? In so great a crisis, will the hands of his companions lying near him grow numb? Spare him, I beg, and cease to wish for one whom, victor, you could not survive. Or do the grim chains and Decius not teach you to compose your mind?'

Recounting such things, when he saw the youth blazing with love of greater fame and deaf to fear, he said: 'I ask nothing more; carry your step back to the feast; let us make haste: no longer must you pierce with your hand the breasts of the Sidonian youth that guard the king: test your right hand on this throat. For here is your steel, if you make ready to attack the Punic—through these vitals of mine the steel must be drawn. Do not scorn slow old age. I will set my limbs against you, and the sword denied you to wrench away I will snatch by my death.' Then tears poured from his face, and the Punic, by the great care of the gods, was preserved for the arms of Scipio's son, nor did the fates grant that so great a deed be wrought by a foreign hand. Most fair in his wrath, and worthy to have become master of his memorable venture, how great a praise he lost when the attempt was laid down, for whom merely to have wished so great a thing is glory. Then they hasten to give themselves back to the feast and clear the grimness from their brows, until sleep dissolved the glad banqueting of the men.

The next light was making ready to bring forth Phaethon's horses, its chariot now gleaming swift beneath the topmost waves, and the youth begotten of great Hamilcar long since plies his hard cares. Mago, fierce, is bidden to go to the citadels of Carthage and bear to the fathers news of the leader's deeds. Plunder and captive bodies are gathered, and the spoils stripped from the men in bloody war, the offerings of a war made prosperous by the gods. Another of his cares is dismissed from the Libyan shores— alas, Decius, kept for the leader's slow wrath on his return, had not Jupiter, pitying the youth's undeserved punishment, from on high turned him toward the ancient city of Battus. Here men bearing the Pellaean sceptres of Ptolemy snatched him from his threats, and the bonds were loosed from his neck. And the same earth, guardian of his life, soon afterward received his unviolated bones in a quiet tomb.

Nor meanwhile did the longed-for time escape Venus, to crush the minds of the Punic through prosperity with blind ruin, and to tame their restless hearts with luxury. She bids her sons scatter their deceiving darts on every side with their hands and send the silent flames into their breasts. Then, smiling sweetly on the boys: 'Let proud Juno go and despise us (no wonder, for what are we?), boasting of her deeds with the favourable. She is strong in her hand, strong in her arms: we, with a boyish bow, slowly pour our little darts, and there is no blood from our wound. But come, O my throng, I pray (now is the time), be present and burn up the Tyrian youth with your silent weapons. By embrace and much wine and the sleep of men must that battle-line be overthrown which the sword has not broken, nor fires, nor the war god with reins let loose. Let the leader drink in the luxury that has glided through his vitals, nor let it shame him to have lain propped on a painted couch, nor let him strive against drenching his hair with Assyrian balm. Let that boaster, who would draw out his sleep under the wintry sky, rather choose to spend his nights indoors, and let him lay aside the custom of eating while he sits often on his galloping horse beneath his helmet, and let him learn to give the unwarlike day to wine. Then, dripping after the feasts, let the lyre be welcome, and let him slothful pass the slumbrous nights, or his wakeful ones, beneath our power.' When Venus had said this, the wanton army of cupids applauds and lets itself down from high heaven on snowy wings. The Moorish youth feels the flame-bearing pinions, and alike their breasts grew warm with the scattered darts. They want the gifts of Bacchus and feasts and songs again, melted by the Pierian lyre. No keen war-horse sweats in the open field, no whirled lance through the air exercises their bared arms. Waters softened by flames warm their limbs languishing in sleep, and by wretched goods their bristling valour perishes. The leader himself too, breathed upon by deceiving Cupid, renews the tables with banquets and seeks again the hospitality of the willing, and gradually, faded, puts off his native arts, the hidden arrow corrupting his mind. Now Capua is called a second homeland and, under equal honour, a second Carthage, and the vices that allure shake the genius untouched by second fortune. Nor is there any limit to the luxury and to the life sunk in lust among the Campanians: they heap it up and through various arts of the stage strive to mark out their feasts with shows, as wanton Memphis with its Amyclaean Canopus constantly resounds the Phrygian lotus-pipe to Nilotic strains. † Above all, sweetly, while the Punic rejoices, through their ears now Teuthras pours the song with his voice, now with his plectrum. And he, when he saw the leader of Libya marvelling at the strings sounding under his thumb, beginning then gently to sing the proud praises of the Aonian lyre, moved through his songs a tongue harmonious with the cithara, such as could surpass the swans that leave their life, and chose from many these gentlest themes for the table: 'For the Argive peoples once, wondrous to tell, a lyre was heard, blest, with its tortoise-shell to draw the stone and to set the willing rocks upon the walls. This walled Thebes with Amphion's plectrum, and, the flint summoned to the ramparts climbing of itself, bade the sung towers rise into the immense. Another, ruling the troubled deep with its quill, both held the seals and drew Proteus in every shape and bore Arion on its watery back. Now the lyre, beloved of the Centaur, that on the Pelian crag shaped by song the minds of heroes and the heart of great Achilles, could check the wraths, struck on its string, of either the sea or grim Avernus. But the strings that Orpheus struck by the Riphaean Strymon, heard by the gods above, heard by the shades, shine bright among the stars in a heaven well-earned. Him too his mother, with all the throng of his sisters, the Aonides, accompanying, his mother marvelled at as he sang. Not while he sang did the Pangaean ridges or Mavortian Haemus stand, not at his music the farthest Thrace: the wild beasts came with the woods, the rivers with the mountains, and the bird, forgetful of its sweet nest and its flight laid by, unmoved, hung captive in the air. Indeed, when the Pagasaean ship, the blue waters not yet known, terrified them and forbade them to enter the deep, . . . the sea, drawn by the song, came to the stern of the sacred keel, the cithara enticing it. The pale realms the Bistonian bard and Acheron, sounding with flames, he appeased with his quill, and fixed the rolling stone. O dire Ciconian mothers and Getic frenzies and Rhodope condemned by the gods! Hebrus bore his torn-off face into the sea, both banks following it. Then too, when the swift waves bore the head cut from the neck, suddenly there flashed through the waves the sea-beasts, leaping over the whole deep at the murmur.'

So then Pierian Teuthras with his Castalian song was breaking the men's breasts, hardened by wars. Meanwhile gentle breezes had now brought Mago to the Libyan lands. Wreathed with laurel the ship was entering the longed-for harbour, and over the sea gleamed captive arms from afar, shining on the lofty prow. But rising long since from the broad water, far and wide the sailors' shout filled the resounding shores, and at once, the oars striking against the drawn-back breasts, the sea broke and foamed with a hundredfold lashing. Nor slow does the crowd run out into the midst of the waves to seize the joy, and the throng, lifted up by favour, celebrates in rivalry the new joys with vast applause. The leader is made equal to the gods: him on every side the mothers, him the lesser throng of grandsons, warned to rejoice, and the band of elders, and nearby both people and fathers, deign with the honour of the gods, with bullocks slain. So Mago entered his homeland and the gates exulting with the fame of his brother's praise. Then the senate rushes forth, and the senate-house is thronged with a great gathering of the fathers. Then, having worshipped the gods of his grandsire in the ancient custom, he says: 'I announce a glorious war and the broken resources on which the Italian land relied—I myself no small part of the toils. We fought, the gods favouring our prayers. There is a place that the glory of an Aetolian king marks out, possessed once among the ancient ages by Daunus. The Aufidus surrounds the moist fields with rapid eddy and cuts off the lands with its overflowing pools, soon strikes the Adriatic waves and with great roar drives the yielding sea back into the deep. Here Varro and Paulus, a great name among the Latin names, to whom, as leaders of the state, power was entrusted, the gloom of dark night scarce yet driven off, invade the plain, and with their arms gleaming far and wide of their own accord kindle the light of the rising East. We against them (for keen frenzy drove my brother to the longed-for fight) move the swift standards from the camp. Both the earth trembles, and stricken Olympus bellows. Here the leader hid the river and the plains with the slaughter of men, than whom never did the lands bring a greater commander to wars. I saw, when with savage whirlwind and din Ausonia, routed through the bellowing fields, gave its back to one man. I saw when Varro was carried off on his galloping horse, degenerate, his arms cast aside. Indeed I saw you too, great-souled Paulus, your body pierced with weapons, falling over the slaughter of your comrades. That day avenged Aegates and the lavish servile treaties by slaughter: it would have pleased to wish for no more than the kindly god then granted. If a second light like that should return, you would be the one chief of all peoples then, Carthage, and be worshipped through all lands. These are witnesses of the slaughter, which the proud men are wont to bear on the left as an illustrious sign.' Then is poured before the faces of those who marvel a ring far-flashing with gold, and gives faith to his words, notable for no small heap. Hence, taking up again, 'It remains now,' he says, 'that Rome, already undermined, be turned from her deepest foundations and levelled with the ground. Let us strive: restore the strength drained by so many misfortunes, and let the treasuries lie open, not sparingly, to the hands that we have bought with war. The beast already fails us, the grim terror of the Ausonians, and too the provisions wear out.'

And while he tells these things, turning his face with grim look upon Hanno, whom his swelling glory had long since goaded, crooked man, with bitter envy of the leader's zeal: 'Do we now prove our hands and our enterprises to you? Is it now right that I not serve the Dardan colonist? Or does it please you to surrender Hannibal a second time? You whose breast wells black with the poison of envy and with black gall, won over at last by so many titles, by so many trophies, unhappy man, be silent. Behold the hand, behold the right hand, which you would have given to the Aeneadae to mangle—it has filled both shores and rivers and pools and the broad plains with blood.' So Mago, and no obscure favour fed his spirits. To him, with both envy and wrath goading, Hanno: 'Such taunts of a mad youth I marvel at not at all: he swells with his nature, and you would not be slow to recognize the brotherly heart and the empty venom of his tongue. That he may not believe me changed, ceasing for empty things, I am the author that now we must beg for peace, now, the treaty broken, lay down our wicked arms and beware the deadly war. And indeed weigh for yourselves, I beg, what he brings: no other course is left for us to judge. He begs for weapons, men, gold, fleets, provisions, and a war-beast. Conquered, I would have given no more. We have glutted the Rutulian fields with Dardan blood, and Latium lies in the plains. To lay aside our cares at last therefore, good man, grant as victor, and let it be allowed to sit in our homeland, allowed not to drain our households, often emptied, with the costs of rapacious war. Now, behold, now, I say (let my presages be false, I pray, and my mind be mocked by an empty augury), the deadly day is not far off. I know his savage heart and foresee the wraths born of disasters. You, I fear you, you, Cannae. Lower your standards and even try, come now, and demand peace: it will not be given. That grief, believe me, prepares a greater ruin from his loss, and these treaties the victor will grant sooner than the conquered. And indeed, you who sound such great deeds with proud mouth and blow with a foaming whirlwind on the ears of the ignorant, tell me, lo, that brother of yours in arms, equal to the war god, whom the earth through the ages never bore a leader like for the wars, why has he not yet seen the walls of the Romulean city? Are we, forsooth, to snatch from their mothers' bosom into the foe those not yet fit to carry heavier arms, are we bidden to weave a thousand bronze-bound keels, and is a war-beast to be sought through all the lands of Libya, that Hannibal may prolong his long commands and the armed years, and drag out his rule even into the times of fate? But you (for we are not surrounded by hidden craft), do not despoil your sweet homes, and set a measure to the camps and wealth of the powerful. Peace, the best of things that it is given to man to know, peace alone better than triumphs beyond number, peace able to guard our safety and make the citizen equal—let it be called back at last to the Sidonian citadels, and let the fame, Phoenician, of your perfidy be driven from the city. If so great a lust for arms holds him and he persists in not yielding the swords to the homeland that demands them, I urge that nothing be supplied to his frenzy, and that Mago carry these words to his brother.'

As he was knitting on more (for he had not glutted his wrath by speaking), the clamour of those who willed otherwise troubles him: 'If the glory of Libya, surpassable by no man's arms, Hannibal, is your wrath, shall we abandon the victor at the very goal and not bring aids of wealth, that the envy of one man may hold back the sceptres now all but won?' Then, eager, they grant what the use of war demanded and boast their favour, the man absent, before this witness. Soon it was resolved to carry the same to the Spanish lands, while base malice disparages immortal deeds and does not let the leader's praises grow by their aid.

Now harsh Winter was hiding her icy head, her temples teeming with rains, and her cloudy brow with its south-bearing crest, and gentle Spring with caressing Zephyrs soothed the healthful fields with mild, clear weather. The Punic bursts forth from Capua and shakes the neighbouring lands far and wide with terror sent ahead, as, hidden through the winter while the Riphaean blasts of the north wind freeze, a serpent at last uncoils its limbs from its secret den, and, the day promising warmth, flashes forth renewed and bears its glittering head and breathes out venom from its lifted jaws. But when the standards of the Libyan leader gleamed across the fields, all was deserted in fear, and, dread persuading, they shut themselves at once within their rampart, and, anxious for safety, trembling, awaited the foe at their very walls.

But that vigour was not now in him which, the Alps broken through, had borne arms in and opened roads, and, master of the Trebia, had defiled the Maeonian waves with Italian blood. Soaked with soft luxury and wine, his limbs flowed slack, torpid † by the allurements of sleep. He who was wont to drag out the icy nights, weighed down in his breastplate beneath an unfriendly sky, and often to scorn his tent when the winter clouds rushed down with hail, and not even by night were his shields or swords laid aside, nor his quivers or javelins, and his arms served him for limbs— now the helmet seemed a heavy burden, and the weights of the bucklers greater, and the spears poured down with no whirring.

Gentle Parthenope first felt him renewing the contests, not rich in resources, not despised for valour, but the harbours drew the leader, willing it, and the safe waters that the ship coming from Carthage might seek. One of the Sirens gave her own name (memorable thing) to the walls, Parthenope, daughter of Achelous, over whose sea the songs reigned long, when through the waves she sang a sweet destruction, no boon to the wretched sailors. Now there are gentle ways for the city, and leisure hospitable to the Muses, and an age exempt from heavier cares. Attacking these walls from behind (for the sea had closed the front), the Punic was not able to break through any roads with his whole force, and in vain, inglorious in his venture, he battered the blocked gates, shaking them with the ram. The victor stood before the Greek defences of Cumae in vain, and proved the counsels of his cautious mind by the event, who, after the watery realm of Daunus, through blood had abstained from going to the Tarpeian citadels. 'Behold, you who have boasted that we are slow and know not to add speed to our deeds, because of late it was not granted you to scale the walls of Rome from the battle-line itself— enter, and the feast promised on the Thunderer's seat render to these houses, which a Greek hand defends.' Such things he boasted, and, through shame of fame to come if, balked of his enterprise, he should retreat from the first city, he dared all and sharpened his swords with stratagems. But sudden flames flowed over the walls, and through all the rampart's winding the unforeseen weapons flew through the air. Just as, when the tawny bird of Jove has hidden its young on a rock's height, if with silent effort a serpent has climbed to the summit and frightens it, close, with its gaping mouth, she, assailing the foe with her beak and the claws accustomed to bear the thunderbolts, flies round the circuit of her nest.

At last, wearied, he turned to the neighbouring harbours of Cumae and set himself to provoke fortune with varied movement and to stand against his sinister fame by stirring trouble. But Gracchus, guardian of the city, a defence more sure than the very walls, kept him off and forbade him again to sit before the gates and again to hope for entrance. Helpless in spirit, he ranges and searches all about, borne on his winged horse, and again begins to drive his men with exhortations of glory: 'By the gods,' he says, 'what limit is there to standing before Greek cities, soldier forgetful of your own deeds? What measure will there be? Before the Alps stands, no doubt, a greater mass, and I bid you scale the heaven, battering its crags. Yet, were a second land like that one given, and other cliffs to rise suddenly beneath the stars, will you not go, and bear arms aloft with me leading? Does, alas, the gaping mound of Cumae and its wall still hold you, or Gracchus, who has not dared to be moved from his gates? In a small crisis I see . . . or shall the nations, whatever you have won by toil, think your deeds done by chance? By you, the Tyrrhene pools of the favouring gods, by the Trebia and the ashes of Saguntum I entreat, render yourselves now worthy of your own fame, which you trail, and call Cannae back into your hearts.'

So the leader strove to rouse the minds worn by luxury and frayed by prosperity, and to stay them with words. And here, surveying the approaches, he sees the gleaming temples of the citadel on the ridge, whose first beginnings Virrius then, the relentless leader of lofty Capua, unfolds. 'This which you look upon,' he says, 'is not of our age: greater hands made it. When (so the tale is) Daedalus feared to leave the lands and the realm of the Dictaean king, he found out a way to give no track to one following over the whole world, daring to raise himself into the airs of heaven on an alien wing and to show man flight. Here, balancing his hanging body in the midst of the clouds, he swam through them and, a new bird, frightened the gods above. He taught his son too, beneath the likeness of false plumage, to attempt the ways of birds, and, fallen with the oars of his pinions loosed and his unhappy wings, he saw him beating the troubled straits. And while he gives way to grief, his palms beaten suddenly against his breast, unwitting, alas, he guided his flight with that mourning movement. Here, grateful, in place of his cloud-wandering passage, he founded the holy temple of Phoebus and laid aside his daring wings.'

So Virrius: but the leader counted the idle days passed without war, and was ashamed to stand still. He groans at his reverses, and, looking back at the houses he could not take, makes ready to glut his grief on the city of Dicarchus. Here too now the sea, now the stony mass of the wall hinders his daring and the labours of the defenders. And while a slow toil holds his comrades, striving to break through the hard and barred ways, he himself surveys the wonders of the pools and of the land nearby together.

The chief men of Capua are present: he teaches them whence the warm Baiae take their name, and shows that the pools gave their own names to a companion of the Dulichian ship. But this man records that the names of Cocytus once remained at the Lucrine, and in the midst of the eddy of the sea commends the Herculean path, where the son of Amphitryon, victor over the Iberian herd, split the water. That man shows Avernus, once called Styx by the peoples, its name changed, now mild and famed among the pools: then, bristling with a grim grove and blackening shadows, and feared, it vomited a deadly venom into the sky, poured forth, lethal to birds, and, sacred through the cities by Stygian awe, kept its savage honour. A marsh near to it (the tale is that it opens a way to the waves of Acheron) loosens its dark jaws with a standing whirlpool and opens dreadful chasms of the earth, and at times troubles the shades with new light. But hard by, they tell, the Cimmerian homes lay, dim and through the long age pressed by infernal mists beneath a pallid shadow, and the deep night of the Tartarean city. Then they point out the fields ever panting with sulphur and fire and seething bitumen. The earth, the black vapour welling up, sighing and warmed long with its burnt marrow, boils and breathes Stygian blasts into the air; it labours and hisses fearfully from its trembling caverns, † and at times, struggling to break its hollow seats or to escape by the straits, with a menacing sound Mulciber bellows mournfully and gnaws the torn vitals of the earth and shakes the eaten-out mountains with his murmur. They tell that the Giants, laid low by Hercules' mass, shake the earth thrown upon them, and that with their panting breath the fields are scorched far and wide, and that, whenever they threaten to break the frame set upon them, the sky grows pale. Prochyta appears, allotted savage Mimas, Inarime appears far off, which with its black whirlwind presses smoking Iapetus, as he hurls flames from his rebel mouth and, if ever it be granted him to escape, wishes to renew his wars against Jove and the gods above. The ridges of Vesuvius are shown, and on the topmost peak the crags fed upon by flames, and the mountain laid low in ruin all around, and rocks contending with the fate of Etna. And too he sees Misenus, keeping the Idaean name in his tomb, and Herculean Bauli on the very shore: he marvels at the menaces of the sea and the labours of the land.

When these had been surveyed by the man, returning thence to the lofty walls of the son of Pheres, he lays waste the leafy summits of Gaurus, glad with the joyous vine. Hence he swiftly moves his columns to Chalcidian Nola. Nola sits on the plain, ringed about in a circle with frequent towers, and guards with its rampart the level easy to approach; but Marcellus brought help and aid—one who would give the arms to be defended not to the towers, but would of his own will protect the walls with his right hand. And he, when from afar he sees the Agenorean approach across the plain and a cloud borne toward the walls, cries: 'Arms, the bloody foe is here, take up your arms, men,' and he takes them up. The swift young men stand round and fit to his roaring helm the bloody crests in their custom. Then he resounds, disposing the columns at a quick step: 'You shall keep the threshold of the right gate, Nero; you, turn your cohorts to the left, Tullus, the bright glory of the Volsci, with the ancestral standards of Larinum. But when bidden, through the silence, with a sudden force burst the gates and pour a storm of weapons onto the plains. I myself will be borne, the gate torn open, into the midst, and draw the cavalry's combats.'

And while Marcellus does this, already the Punic were trying to wrench off the bars and, scorning ladders, to break through the walls. Trumpets sounded everywhere, and the shout of men and the neighing, with the clarions and, in the hoarse tumult, the horns, and the arms shaken on their raging limbs. The bitter plague is borne, quickened, the gates flung apart, and the squadrons rush out, poured forth in an unforeseen flood, as a wicked river overflows, its dams broken, as the sea, driven by the north wind, is dashed against the rocks, as the winds, their prison broken, invade the lands. Nor at the sight of the torrent of arms and men can the Libyan stand, cast down from hope. The Dardan leader presses the astonished one, his horse going before, and, leaning his spear on the backs of those who rush, now wearies his comrades with his voice: 'Go on, come, bear forward your steps. The god is kind, the hour is ours. This is the way to the walls of Capua,' now again, turned against the foe: 'Stand. Where are you swept off? Not at the backs of your men, but at you, leader of Libya, do I cry: stand. The plain and arms and Mars are in our hands. I dismiss the cohorts from the slaughter: let us be seen alone. Marcellus, I demand battle.' So the Latin ruler, and the honour of attacking the Barcaean youth in fight, and the prize of the peril, urged him on.

But Juno did not behold these things with a calm breast, and turned him from his enterprise as he rushed to his final fate. He labours to stay the routed and recall them: 'Do we come out such as this from the bosom of Capua and her sinister houses? Stand, O wretches, to whom the highest glory is a disgrace. Nothing today, believe me, faithful awaits you turning your backs. You have deserved that all Ausonia rush upon you, and by savage war you have made it that no hope of peace or life should remain for the routed.' He overcame the trumpets with his clamour, and by the force of his voice, savage, penetrated the ears though they were stopped.

In the arms of Polydamas the young Pedianus waged war, fierce, and boasted of his Trojan seed and lineage and of himself from the Antenorid stock, of no lighter fame in his line, and his glory by sacred Timavus and a name beloved on the Euganean shores. To him father Eridanus and the Venetian peoples in order and the folk rejoicing in Aponus, whether he stirred wars or, peaceful, preferred the Muses and the silence of a learned life and to soothe his toils with the Aonian quill, called none his equal, nor was another youth more known to the war god, nor another more known to Phoebus. He, when, pressing the tracks of the Punic with loosened reins, near him recognized the helmet and the emblem, the spoil of slain Paulus (a boy bore those, glad in the leader's no small gift, Cinyps, Cinyps beloved by the Punic, than whose face none was more pleasing, and on no brow shone more of grace: such as the ivory that the air of Tibur feeds, flashing and ever new, or as the stone that with a wondrous honour of whiteness shines in the ear, brought from the Red waves)— when Pedianus saw him, notable for his crests and his known helmet, gleaming at the rear of the column, as if a sudden image of Paulus had risen before his eyes from the infernal seats and demanded back his lost arms, he attacks, gnashing: 'Will you, most cowardly, bear the coverings of a sacred head, which not without crime and the gods' envy your leader would wear? Behold Paulus.' Then he calls the man to the spectacle of the shades and drives a piercing weapon into the fleeing one's ribs. Then, sliding from his horse, with his right hand he tears off the helmet and the emblems of the great consul and despoils the gleaming youth. All his beauty is loosed by death, and through his snowy limbs goes the Stygian colour and ravages the honours of his form. His ambrosial locks fell, and his violated neck, the throat sinking, sank back upon his marble shoulder. Just as the Cytherean fire, returning over Ocean, when it boasts itself to Venus with its splendour restored, if a sudden cloud invades it, is dimmed and, waning in the black darkness, hides its languishing light. Pedianus himself too, the helmet snatched, astonished stands stunned at the bare face and checks his wrath. Then, bearing back the helmet with a great shout to his comrades, he shook his fierce horse, that bloodied with savage bite the foaming reins. To him Marcellus, turbulent in arms, bore his face to meet him in swift tumult, and recognizing the glory: 'Bravo, O of ancestral valour, bravo, son of Antenor! Now,' he said, 'let us seek the snatched coverings of the Libyan leader, what remains,' and, blazing, with dreadful whirrings he hurls the savage spear. Nor perhaps would he have been baulked of his vow, had not the opposing force of Gestar held the weapon with his interposed body. He, while he protects the leader with arms close by, the heavy spear, thirsting not for his blood, passed through him and, his death changed, fulfilled its mighty threats. The leader is carried off in haste from the crisis of death, troubled, and, raging, takes his course toward the camp.

And now the army of the Punic, immoderate in flight, stretches its headlong step in a contest, their arms turned about. The foe overtakes them with weapons, and one by one glut their long wraths from the disasters, and to the sky in rivalry display their swords bloody, and to the avenging gods. That day first taught what no one would dare believe of the gods, that the leader of Libya could be checked in the contest of war. They drag off chariots and men and the Massylian beast, and bear back coverings torn from the living warriors, and depart, content to have seen the leader's back beneath their spear. Then they match Marcellus in war's glory: he walks with triumph attending, greater than if as victor he bore the spoils to the Thunderer.

Then raging, after he scarcely drove the foe from his rampart, the Agenorean leader: 'When have I washed this stain and with how much enemy blood? Has Ausonia chanced to see my back? Do you, highest of the gods,' he says, 'after the Trebia judge me worthy of so foul a death? And you, youth long unconquered, now, alas, without war, worn down by the goods of Capua—I myself, not degenerate of my deeds, have turned my victorious standards from the Ausonians: to you I gave my back. I saw, when I called you to the wars, you flee no otherwise than from an Italian leader, terrified. What is left to you of your old war-spirit, you who can give your backs while I call you back?' Such things the Punic poured forth. But the Latin squadrons, bearing their spoils, bore themselves toward the walls of Nola with notable clamour.

But Rome, grievously accustomed for long to hear of the fortunes of her own, and never restored by prosperity, when at last news of a favourable battle was brought, is lifted up and rises by this first gift of the gods. Before all, the youth, sluggish for war and fleeing toils, while the war thundered, and who stole themselves away, pay the penalty of their hiding. Then those who, by the sweetness of life, found out wiles and corrupted the treaties sworn to the Punic, they mark out and cleanse the race of its crime. The unhappy counsel of those who meant to leave their native land is punished, and the wicked guilt of Metellus. Such were the hearts of the men. But indeed not even the women cease to match the men in mind and demand a share of praise. Every matron, bearing before herself the ancient glory of her head and hands and the necklaces stripped from her neck, rushes in rivalry and they serve the war. They are not grieved that the men in such a time yielded them so great a lot of praise, and they rejoice to have given place to a deed that will go down through the ages. Then the lofty throng of the senate follows. Into the common store, with great rivalry, private wealth is heaped. To strip their households and to have set aside nothing in secret for the uses of a better life pleases them. The crowd too gathers, without a name. Thus using all her body and all her limbs, Rome, though bloodless, again raised her face to the heavens.

The men carrying responses from Parnassian Cirrha add a sweet hope to the wretched. For they brought glad word that they had heard in the sanctuaries, when the cavern thundered with a sacred voice, and the priestess, now entered by Phoebus, bellowed: 'Loose from your hearts, race of Venus, your heavier fears: adversity, and whatever of hardship remained beneath war, is drained for you. The lighter of your toils remain, and terror without ruin. Only bear to the gods your vows and prayers, and pour warm blood upon the altars, and do not give your backs to your woes. The war god will be present, and the Delian seer himself will turn aside the nearer perils, known ever to have lessened the Trojans' toils. But indeed, but indeed before all let a hundred altars smoke, festal, for Jove: let a hundred victims fall to the knives. He, violent, will drive the grim cloud of war and its savage storms into Libya: you yourselves will behold him shaking the aegis into the battles, the world thrown into tumult.' And after this, proclaimed in the caverns of Parnassus, was brought, and the god's word reached the ears of the crowd, in rivalry they climb to the Capitoline citadels, and prostrate themselves to Jove and honour his shrine with blood; then they sing the paean and pray for faithful responses.

Meanwhile the elder Torquatus, in his accustomed arms, was shaking the Sardinian lands with his country's soldiery. For Hampsagoras, boasting a name from Trojan origin, had called the Tyrians to renewed war. The man had a fair son, not worthy of such a parent, Hostus, on whose gleaming youth relying, he himself, harsh to peace, rekindled his green years, weak though they were, in zeal for the ways of barbarous war. And he, when he sees Torquatus bearing his standards in haste, hurried, and right hands eager for battle approaching, flies out by the deceit of a place he knew, through the hidden trackless glens, and, seizing the foreseen shortcuts of flight, is covered by the thicketed valley and the leafy shadows.

An island, walled round by the wave-sounding deep, is steepened by the waters and, pressed by the eddy, contains its huge lands under the likeness of a bare foot: hence it was first called Ichnusa by the Greek settlers. Soon Sardus of Libya, trusting in his noble blood from Hercules, changed the names of the land after himself. The Teucrians too flowed in and set their compelled seats there, scattered over the sea after Pergama was uprooted. Nor was it a small glory, Iolaus, that you gave to those lands, your column of Thespiads brought with your father's fleet. The tale is that, when Actaeon, his limbs mangled, paid a lamentable penalty for Diana seen in the spring, the parent, astonished at the strangeness of the woe, fled, Aristaeus, across the straits and went to the Sardinian retreats. They say his mother Cyrene showed him the new shores. The land is clean of serpents and widowed of poisons, but grim in its climate and tainted by much marsh. Where it sees Italy, parched on its rocky ridge, it troubles the straits with its crags far and wide, and within cooks the pallid fields too much, the south winds smoking under the Crab. The rest is nourished by the favour of bounteous Ceres.

The land being of this nature, Hostus, eluding Torquatus often through the wooded pathless wastes, awaited the Sidonian weapons of war and his Iberian comrades of the toil. And they, when by the ships' arrival they swelled their courage, no delay: he bursts from his hiding-places, and far and wide the opposing columns bristle, and they seem at length to come together and join step. They seize the open intervals of the spreading plain with their hurled spears from afar, until they reach the tried swords, the most faithful weapons. Then a dire plague: they cut down and fall, and by turns leave their souls on the savage blade.

I could not indeed hope to unfold worthily the countless slaughters and so many grim deeds, in proportion to so great a name of the matter, nor match in words the heat of the warriors. But you, Calliope, grant to my labour that the too little-known deeds of a great man be handed on to long ages, and let us consecrate the honour due to the bard.

Ennius, of the ancient line of King Messapus, was mingling in the foremost ranks, and adorned with the proud glory of the Latin vine-staff his right hand. The rugged land of the Calabrians sent him: ancient Rudiae bore him, Rudiae now a name memorable only for its nursling. He in the first fight (as the Thracian bard once, when Cyzicus shook the Argo, hostile to war, hurled Rhodopean darts, his quill laid by) had made himself worthy of beholding by no small slaughter of men, and the ardour of his hand swelled with killings. Hostus flies up, hoping it would be eternal glory if he should beat down so great a stain, and balances his spear with all his strength. Apollo, sitting in a cloud, laughed at the attempts of his vain enterprise and sent the weapon off afar into the winds, and over this: 'Too much, youth, and of too proud a hope have you drunk. This man is sacred, and a great care of the Aonian sisters, and a bard worthy of Apollo. He first shall sing the Italian wars in illustrious verse and shall raise the leaders to heaven; he shall teach Helicon to resound in Latin measures, nor shall he yield in honour or fame to the Ascraean elder.' So Phoebus, and through Hostus's two temples the avenging arrow runs. By the youth's fall the stricken columns are turned across the fields, and the scattered bands alike give their backs. Then the father, turbid with wrath at hearing of his son's death, groaning a barbarous and monstrous groan, pierces his panting breast and urges his steps to his son's shades.

But the leader of Libya, broken by Marcellus and bruised by the keen fight, had condemned the plains and arms: he had turned to the wretched Acerrae of unequal war. Thence, when he had given over the city to flames and swords, with wrath no lighter nor more sparing he flung himself upon Nuceria and levelled its walls with the ground. Afterward Casilinum, having struggled much against him with the unfair arms of its defenders, with difficulty by craft he unbarred its thresholds and weighed the besieged ones' lives with gold. And now, pouring his columns into the Daunian fields, he bent his fury wherever plunder or wrath had called. Petelia smoked, burned, its roofs overthrown, unhappy for its faith and second to wretched Saguntum, yet once proud to have guarded the Herculean quiver.

Tarentum too had turned its mind to Tyrian undertakings, and the Punic had entered the gates. But indeed in the gleaming citadel, trusting the place, an Ausonian band sat thronged. Here, doing wondrous things, the fleet that lay hidden in the harbour stood (for from the narrow jaws the sea bursts out among the rocks and into a broad recess pours the deep, sundered from the main)— the ships, then, shut in, which had no way to swim out with the citadel set above, by craft he carried beyond the barriers of the sea and bore the keels, transported, through the lands behind. Slippery runners were set beneath on oaken wagons, and the wheel, gliding on the hide of a newly slain bullock, drew the sea-going ship through the grass. And now, driven over the hills and thickets to the shore, the fleet swam upon the deep, coming without a rower.

Meanwhile a messenger fills him, terrifying the straits with the heat of his cares, the keels borne in no usual way, while far off he longs to storm the Oebalian grandsons and first to furrow the lands with naval beaks, telling him the walls of Capua are besieged: the very bars of the gates wrenched off, and all the war rushing on the wretched. Fierce, he leaves his undertakings, and, shame adding wings and wrath alike, with monstrous speed through the nearest lands he flies off and, threatening, is borne to the eager combats. Just as if a tigress, roused by the loss of her cub, darts forth, the Caucasus, astonished, is ranged over in a few hours and the Ganges crossed at a winged bound, until with her lightning course she gathers the tracks of her young and spends her rage on the foe she has seized.

To meet him Centenius, his column scattered, in haste is poured out, ill in daring and ready for perils, but a small glory for Hannibal. For, having discharged the honour of the vine-staff, he had suddenly roused the Latin peasants and thrown the half-armed band to be laid low by the foe. Twice seven thousand sent to death (nor did the column halt), twice seven, which Fulvius, not more skilful with the sword but notable for his birth, led in lawful arms: but equally over the bodies of the fallen, poured down, the way was seized, and the victor, suffering no delay, went on. A funeral alone held back the fame and the name of that man, willing as he was to a merciful mind, with a glad burial. For by treachery, unspeakable, and slain by his host, while he sought a parley and the perfidious promises of the Lucanian race, Gracchus, surrounded by blind craft, had fallen, and the Libyan snatched the praise of burying him.

But now, when the Punic was known to be hastening to the walls, no affair stood in its place: now both consuls were present, headlong, all the force from Nola, and from Arpi Fabius, fresher in years, was bearing his swift arms. Hence Nero, and hence flying Silanus night and day drove on, urging the cohorts to the hastened wars. From every side they gather, and it pleases the leaders alike to set all of them against the one youth. He himself, lofty, sits on Tifata, where a hill stands nearer the walls and from its mounds looks down on the city below. But when he sees, with so many arms surrounding him, the allied gates walled up, and that he is denied both to enter and to burst out of Capua, anxious at the outcome, now he meditates to break by iron the throng of those who block him, now he takes pathless counsels for his enterprise and seeks by craft to draw so many thousands from the narrowed gates and to unbind the ringed walls. So therefore with himself, and thus in his heart he wearies his cares: 'Where, sick mind, do you call me? Shall I again take up perils, unfavoured by the lie of the place, and, with Capua watching, give my back? Or, sitting on the summit of the neighbouring mountain, shall I suffer the allied houses to be cut down before my eyes? Not so did Fabius and the master of the Fabii find me confounded, when I escaped, victor, the hills shut up with Hesperian soldiery, and goaded the bullocks scattered through the fields to toss the fires on their kindled horns. Not all my wiles have yet departed. If it is snatched from us to defend Capua, it shall be granted to surround Rome.'

After these things pleased him, and the resolve held his mind, without waiting until Titan should bring forth his breathing horses with the light from the deep, he drives his men into the column with voice and hand and unfolds his monstrous undertakings: 'Go on, come, conquer every toil, soldier, by your valour, and as far as human strides can stretch themselves, hasten, lofty. You seek Rome. The Alps paved this road, Cannae paved it for you. Come, strike against the walls of Troy your shield-boss, and repay the ruins of Capua: how worth it will have been to fall, that you may see the Palatine and the Thunderer departing from his Tarpeian seat.' Spurred on, they mass their steps. Rome clings to their ears, Rome to their eyes, and they believe, by the leader's skilful acts, this undertaking fitter than if he had led them from the very plain fatal to the Aeneadae. They cross the Volturnus's swift fords in their boat and the last leave behind, to delay the Italians, the keels they have spoiled with fire. Then with nimble maniples they gather the Sidicine fields and Thracian Cales, your homes, Orithyia, named from your son.
