This fire promises you a treaty with the Dardanian race, this fire will give you a kingdom greater than your father's kingdom, and will join your name to the fates of Latium.' So the prophetess; and so clear a marvel stirred the young man's mind: no honours of valour for him among the Carthaginians, while even Hannibal himself was now growing each day more modest in arms.

The Dawn was wiping the clouds from a darkened sky and had scarcely reddened the faces of the Atlantian sisters: he makes for the Ausonian camp, still the enemy's. And when he had borne himself within the rampart, and the Latian leader received him with kindly face, the king begins thus:

'The warnings of the gods above and the answers of my sacred mother, and your valour, O ruler of the Rutulians, most welcome to the gods, have led me here, torn willingly from the Tyrians. If we have often been seen to stand, not slack, against your thunderbolts, we bring you, son of the Thunderer, a right hand worthy of you. Neither has the empty fickleness of a wavering mind subdued us, and a heart that shifts, nor do we chase hope and the prizes of glad battle: it is treachery I flee, and a race forsworn from its very origin. You, since you have ended your battles at the bounds of Hercules, now invade with us the very mother of the war. That man, who for two five-year spans has held the realm of Laurentum, and sets his ladders to the walls of Rome, must be dragged to Libya by fire and sword.'

So the Numidian leader. Then Scipio, clasping right hand in right hand: 'If our race seems fair to you in Mars, it is fairer in good faith. Dismiss from your heart your double-tongued allies. From this great rewards of bright valour await you, Masinissa, and Scipio shall be outdone sooner even in arms than in the zeal of a grateful mind. The other fires you urge me to carry to Libya, time will see to. For such matters are not unconsidered by me, and Carthage wearies my mind.' Then he gives the young man as gifts a cloak distinguished by an embroidered design, and a horse covered with purple, which he himself had taken as victor when Mago was struck down, and had approved its spirit; then a golden bowl and a plumed helmet, from which Hasdrubal had poured libation at the altars of the gods. So, the ally's pact with the king now made firm, he turns his thoughts already to overthrowing the towers of Carthage.

There was a ruler richest in the Massylian lands, nor unarmed in valour, Syphax, whom countless nations sought for justice, and Tethys at the world's last shore. Much land was his, and the swift horse and the elephant, terror of wars, and youth chosen out for Mars. Nor was there any to outdo him in ivory or solid gold, or to dye fleece more brightly in Gaetulian cauldrons. Eager to add these resources, and reckoning the labour should the king turn to the Carthaginians, Scipio bids them set sail upon the deep, and even now his spirit takes up the wars of Africa. But when he had arrived and the keels held the harbour, already Hasdrubal was there, fleeing in a frightened ship along the nearest shore, seeking new pacts for his stricken cause, and dragging the Massylian standards over to the Tyrians.

Hearing alike that the leaders of two peoples had come into his realm, each striving with all his weight and disputing in arms which of them should rule the world, Syphax, high in mind, bids them be summoned kindly into his halls, and lifts himself up with so great an honour for his kingdom. Then, rolling his glad eyes over the faces before him, he addresses the Latian young man, and is first to begin of himself:

'How serenely I receive you, fairest son of Dardanus, and how gladly I look upon you! And how joyfully I recall the face of Scipio! Your form calls back your father to me. For I remember—when I had come to Gades, Hercules' Erythia, to its shores, in my love of the sea and to watch the tides of its waves— with what strange love I gazed upon the great leaders by the neighbouring river Baetis. Then the men brought me gifts, choice spoils, arms, and—then first known in my kingdom— the bridles of swift horses and the bows to which our javelins now know to yield, and they gave me masters of the old soldiering, who would shape my scattered, lawless bands after your fashion for the contests of Mars. But I, when in return I brought what wealth my kingdom held— now gold, now gifts of snow-white tusk— had no power to win with my prayers. Each took for himself only the swords that an inlaid ivory sheath enclosed. Therefore come, gladly greet the entering of our home, and since my fortune brings the Libyan leader over the waves, take in with an easy mind what I shall say. And you who rule the towers of Tyrian Carthage, Hasdrubal, turn your ears, your senses, this way, I beg. How great a storm rushes upon the Ausonian peoples with its torrent of arms, and threatens Latium with its end, and how for twice five savage years now the land of Sicily, now the Spanish shores, drink Tyrian blood— who is allowed not to know? Why then do these grim wars not at last subside, and why do you not lay down your arms of free will? You, Libya, you, Ausonia—remember to restrain yourselves. It will be no disgrace to you, once you have turned to terms, that Syphax was your peacemaker and stood between.' To add more Scipio did not allow, but points to the custom of his people and the judgement of the senate, and bids him drop the empty hope of his undertaking, and teaches him that the Fathers alone weigh these things. This was the limit of persuasion; and what was left of the spent day they turn to the tables and the cups, and when the feast was ended, give their bodies to sleep and loose into the night the hard chains of their cares.

And now Dawn, stepping forth at the first threshold, was bringing a new day to birth for the earth, and the horses of the sun from their stalls were coming to the yoke, nor had he yet mounted his car, but the waters glowed with the flames about to burst forth: Scipio drives his body from the bed and with serene face makes his way to the doors of the Massylian king. It was that king's ancestral way to rear the young of lions and to drive out their rage and anger by feeding the cubs. Then too with his hand he was stroking their tawny necks and manes and handling, unafraid, the fierce mouths of the playful beasts.

When he learned that the Dardanian leader was present, he puts on his cloak, and in his left hand bears the glory, the ensign of his ancient realm. His temples are bound with a white fillet, and at his side, by custom, the sword is fastened. Then he calls him into the house, and in inner rooms the guest sits down with the sceptred king in equal honour.
Then the pacifier of the Spanish land begins first with these words:

'My first and greatest care, the Pyrenean peoples subdued, was to go in haste to your kingdom, O Syphax, worthy of reverence for your sceptre. Nor did the savage sea delay me in mid-passage. We ask of your kingdom nothing steep or dishonourable: join to the Latins a heart of one mind, and come as an ally to our success. The Massylian nations and the land stretched out by the Syrtes, and your ancestral power on the wide plains, will bring you no more glory than Roman valour joined in sure faith, and the honours of the Laurentine people. Why tell the rest? No god, to be sure, is fair to any man who has done harm to Dardanian arms.'

The Massylian heard with glad face and gave his nod, and embracing the man said: 'Let us make firm the favourable omens, nor let the gods be absent from our concordant vows, and let us call with our lips on horned Jove and Tarpeian Jove.' And at once the turf had risen in built-up altars, and the victim stood placed beneath the lifted axe, when suddenly the bull, fleeing the altars, with broken bonds leaped clear, and with its bellowing filled the halls far and wide, and doubling its sighs with a hoarse roar scattered terror through the trembling court. And the fillet, ornament of his forefathers, slipping from his brow with no touch at all, laid bare the king's temples. Such grim signs the heaven-dwellers gave to the realm about to fall, and the heavy omens of a savage fate were at hand. This king, broken in war and torn from his throne— a time will come—he will lead, driving him to the temple of the Thunderer, who now as a suppliant begged for an alliance. This done, Scipio makes for the harbour and gives his ships to a favourable wind, and returns himself to the lands he knows.

The eager nations gathered, and conquered Pyrene sent its various peoples. The mind of all was one: with one accord they call him king and salute him king. For they know this to be the highest honour of valour. But when with gentle face he rejected the gifts as unworthy of an Ausonian man, and in turn instructed them in the customs of his country, and showed them that Rome knows not how to brook the names of kings, then, turned to the one care that remained, with no enemy left to face, he calls together at once the Latins and the host of Baetis and Tagus, and in the midst of the assembly speaks thus: 'Since the favouring will of the gods above has so granted us that the Libyan, cast down from the far edge of the world, should either fall on these plains or, the Hesperian region left behind, range his native sands an exile: now it is my mind to honour the tombs of my own with your soil, and to give peace to the shades that demand it. Favour me with like mind, and turn your ears this way. When the sun's seventh round shall be renewed in heaven, let those strong in arms and the sword, and those who excel in the art of guiding the four-horse chariot, and those who hope to win on foot, and whose zeal is to drive the winds with javelins, be present and contend for the praise of a fair crown. I shall give worthy prizes, famed spoils from Tyrian plunder, nor shall any one leave without a share of my gift.' So with gifts and the desire for praise he fires the throng.

And now the appointed day was here, and the field rang with the countless gathering, and in due order the leader led the mimic funeral rites with welling tears. Every Spaniard, every soldier under the Latin name brings gifts and heaps them on the blazing tombs. He himself, holding cups now full of milk, now of the sacred wine of Lyaeus, sprinkles the altars with fragrant flowers. Then he calls up the roused shades and sings the praises of those men with weeping, and reveres the deeds of the fallen.

Then he betakes himself to the racecourse and begins the first contests, opening with the swift courses of the horses. The fickle crowd surges with a roar like the sea and the rage of those who cheer, before the barriers are yet unbarred, and keeps its eyes on the gates and the thresholds of the horses. And now, when the bolts have sounded at the given signal and the foremost hoof has scarcely flashed from the whole starting-front, a shout is lifted to the sky in a frenzied whirl, and leaning forward, with faces like the contenders, each follows his own chariot, and with a great voice they all speak to the flying horses. The racecourse is shaken by the contest of the spectators, and the ardour has carried off no one's mind: they press their advice on, and steer the horses with their shouting. A tawny ball of sand, rising from the dusty earth, is raised aloft into the air, and covers with a dense fog the paths of the horses and the toils of the charioteers. This man rages with zeal for a fierce horse, that one for the driver. Some are fired by love of country, some by the noble name of an ancient stable. There are those whom glad hope wearies, and a neck new to bearing the yoke. There are those who delight in raw old age, and the horse proven in long years.

Out before all, in his swift chariot through the air, the Galician Lampon flies, and exulting swims across the great expanses and leaves the winds behind his back. They shout together and roar with applause, and believe the greater part of their wish achieved, the boundary forestalled. But those whose care within is keener, and whose knowledge of the course is deeper, condemn strength poured out in the first contest and chide from afar with vain complaints the man who wears out his team by an unmeasured effort:

'Where, where so wildly, Cyrnus, do you rush?' (for Cyrnus was driving) 'Let go the lash and rein in, with measure, your reins.' Alas, deaf ears! He is carried on heedless of his horses and does not think how much of the field is left to run.

Next, distant from the first by as much of the ground as the chariot itself takes up, but next he went, the Asturian Panchates: his brow shone white with the native mark, and his whole foot matched the native white. Great in spirit, his limbs not tall, the grace of his body slight, but then he had made himself wings, and roused he went over the field chafing at the reins: you would think him rising lofty and his limbs growing larger.
His driver, the Spaniard, shone with Cinyphian scarlet.

Third, running with brow level with Pelorus, came Caucasus. He himself was harsh, no horse to love the coaxing sounds of a patted neck, and foaming he loved to chew the iron clenched in his bleeding bite. But Pelorus, teachable to the rein and better at obeying, never swerved aside to bend his car loose, but on the left, hugging the inside, grazed the turning-post, striking for his great neck and the abundance of his mane that played about his throat. A marvel to tell, he had no sire: to the new breezes of Zephyr on the plains of the Vettones his dam Harpe had brought him forth. Noble Durius spurred on this chariot in the field; Caucasus trusted in the old trainer Atlas. Aetolian Tyde, founded by the wandering Diomedes, had sent him: men said he was sprung of Troy's horses, of those that the victorious son of Tydeus by great daring carried off from Aeneas at the waters of Simois. And now, borne nearly to the middle of the field in their contest, they were gaining in the open stretch, and striving to take the lead the spirited Panchates seemed to go higher, above the foremost horses, and to be mounting now, now, the chariot ahead from behind, and with his curved hoof his front foot, striking, was beating against the Galician's axle.

But last went Atlas, yet no slacker than Durius behind: you would think, after the manner of peace, that they ran with brow level and rein in accord. When the Spaniard who went nearest sensed the Galician strength of Cyrnus spent, and that no longer as before did his headlong chariot leap, but his smoking horses were violently forced by ceaseless lashing—as when from a mountain a sudden squall rushes down from on high—stretched out at once up to the necks of his team and hanging over their high heads, he urges on the burning Panchates, that being second he bore the reins, and adds words mingled with the lash:

'Will any man, Asturian, in the contest of the course carry off the palm snatched from you? Rise up, fly, glide over the field swift on your accustomed wings. Lampon shrinks, consumed with panting chest, nor does breath remain to the gasping horse to carry him to the post.' When these words were said, the horse lifted himself, as though then from the first barrier he were snatching the stretch, and leaving Cyrnus far behind his back, who strained to oppose or match his curving steps. Both the sky and the racecourse, struck by the high voices of the spectators, roar. Borne aloft through the air, lifting his neck higher, the victor Panchates exults and himself, the foremost, drags his yoke-mates on.

But last Atlas, last Durius, ply their arts in a circle: now this one tries on the left, now that one presses and strives to come up on the right, and each in turn tries vainly to deceive the other: until, trusting in the flower of his early youth, Durius leaning forward with reins turned crosswise threw his chariot across, and drove the car of Atlas, weak with age, over and overturned—Atlas, justly complaining:

'Where do you rush? What manner of mad contest is this? You labour at a death common to us and our horses both.' And while he cries this out, the axle breaks and he is rolled headlong, and along with him, pitiable to see, his horses are flung across the field, scattered at odds. The victor shakes his reins over the open ground, and Pelorus in the midst of the sand left Atlas behind, struggling and striving to rise, as he fled. Nor was it long to catch the wearied chariot of Cyrnus. Him too, hesitating and learning too late the management of his horses, the swift car flew past at speed. The shout and the voices of those who cheer drive on the chariot, and now even over the back and shoulders of the trembling Spaniard the horse has set his head, and the driver feels his back pressed by the warm breath and grows hot with the foam. Durius bent over the field and sent his team on, spurred by the lash—and not in vain: he seems to match, or even has matched, the yokes that went before, on the right. Then, astonished at so great a hope: 'Pelorus, now, now is the time to show you were brought forth by your sire Zephyr. Let those who draw their name from the breed of cattle learn how far the birth of divine seed excels. As victor you shall give gifts and raise altars to your father.' And had he not been betrayed in too great success and glad fear, with the whip slipping from him amid his words, perhaps he would have hallowed to Zephyr the altars he had vowed. But then indeed, unhappy, as though the crown had slipped from the victor's head, turned against himself in anger he rends his gilded robe down the middle of his breast, and tears and complaints together were poured out to the stars. And now, the lash withdrawn, the chariot obeyed no more. Instead of goads, the empty reins shake upon their backs.

Meanwhile, sure now of the praise, Panchates bore himself toward the post and sought the first prize, held high. Gently along his neck, along his shoulders, the breeze fans his streaming mane; then lifting his soft legs in a haughty stride he triumphs amid a great shout. The gift was the same for all, an axe chased in solid silver, but the rest differing in varied honour. First, a swift horse, no gift to be scorned, the Massylian king's offering, he carried off. Next in valour carried off two cups from the rich Tyrian plunder, bathed in the gold of Tagus. The shaggy hide of a fierce lion and a Sidonian helmet bristling with crests is the third honour. As the last gift the leader summons Atlas— though the elder had sunk down with his axle broken— and gives to him, pitying both his age and the lot of his mishap, a servant in the flower of youth, with a tribal cap added as an honour.
This done, the leader invites them to the glad contests of the foot and fires their hearts with the prizes set out:

'This helmet (with this Hasdrubal terrified the Spanish lines) the first man shall take; and this sword, whose glory is next in the running— this his father stripped from slain Hyempsa. The third shall console his last place with a bullock. The rest of the crowd shall depart content with two javelins each, fierce each one, which their native metal gives.'

The shining boys Tartessos and Hesperos showed themselves together to the crowd's favouring shout. Famed Gades, their homeland, sent these from a Tyrian house. Then comes Baeticus, his cheeks sprinkled with first down: Corduba had given the boy this name from the river, and fostered the glad contests at no small cost. Then, red of hair but with a body of snowy brightness, Eurytus filled all the arena with shouting: Saetabis, reared on a high hill, had brought him forth, and his parents stood by, anxious in their love. Then Lamus and Sicoris, sons of warlike Ilerda, and Theron, drinker of the water that flows under the name of Lethe and grazes its banks with a stream that brings forgetting.

When they, raised on their toes and leaning forward with their chests, their exultant hearts beating with the heat of glory, took their distance at the trumpet, they leaped through the air quicker than arrows poured forth as the bowstring drives them. The cheers and the partisanships are divided, and those who favour them hang on their nails, and each, as is his liking, calls his own man by name, panting. The famous band is carried over the field and leaves no trace marked on the sand it crosses, all in their first youth and graced with golden faces, all light to run and all worthy to win.

Bending to the task, halfway along the course Eurytus had thrust his stride forward and went first, by short margins, yet first, leading the stretch. No less keenly the eager Hesperos presses, and with his first step grazes the prints of the heel that ran ahead. It is enough for the one to be first, enough for the other to hope that he can become first. The more keenly for this they strain their steps and with vigour of spirit drive their bodies on. The very toil increases the boys' grace. Look—running with a light effort and at the rear of the field, after he thought he had gathered strength enough in himself, Theron, towering, pours out his untapped powers in a whirl unlooked-for, and suddenly bursts out and rides past the breezes: you would believe a Cyllenian foot went on its airy course with winged sandals tied. Now these, now those—the people marvelling—he leaves behind, and, lately last, now third in the order of the palm, he harries Hesperos, pressed close upon his tracks. And now not only the man he follows, but the first hope of the crown, trembles, Eurytus, as so great a runner comes on such wings. Fourth by lot of place, but—if the three keep in order the courses they have begun—labouring at his vain effort in vain, Tartessos pressed his brother, with Theron between. And no longer enduring it, Theron lifts himself over the field, afire, and flies past Hesperos, full of wrath. One only was left, and the nearer goal pricked the weary with sharper stings; whatever strength toil had left them— on this side toil, on that the fear piercing the heart— while it was still allowed to hope, each summoned for the short effort: their courses are made level, and they rushed on together. And perhaps they would have earned a double prize with twin palm, reaching the goal at once, had not Hesperos, following Theron's back, savage with vast anger, seized the hair streaming wide over his milk-white neck and dragged it. Glad and exulting at the youth's checking, Eurytus gets clear, and as victor darts to the prizes and bears off the splendid gift of the gleaming helmet. The rest of the band was given the promised gift, and with unshorn hair bound in a green crown each carried off two spears, brandishing their native iron.

From here come the graver contests of men: the sword is drawn for close combat, and the mock images of fierce war are roused. It was not those whom guilt brought, nor the harmful crimes of life, but valour and a fierce spirit for love of praise, that made these men matched in the sword; a spectacle worthy of the war-born crowd, and the image of their wonted toil. Among these were twin (what now have kings not dared? or what crime of kingship now remains?) brothers, who in the vast arena, the spectators damning their madness, joined battle with armed hands for a sceptre. That was the dread custom of their race, and bereaved of the light the brothers sought their father's throne at the hazard of life. They clashed with such spirit as it is fitting men should fight whom the madness for a kingdom drives, and bearing down to the shades hearts glutted at once with much blood they fell. With equal effort the blade, driven through the breast, sank into their innermost parts; their last words were added to their savage wounds; and rolling out curses the dreadful spirit fled into the unwilling air. Nor did the shades suffer peace. For when one pyre with a single flame sought to consume their joined bodies, the impious fire split apart, and the very ashes refused to lie together. The rest of the crowd was given a gift to match their merits, as their valour and their right hand had been. They led away bullocks trained to cleave the earth with the pressed plough, they led away young men used to rousing the lairs of wild beasts in the hunt, men whom Mauretanian plunder gives. Likewise badges of silver and of captive raiment, prizes, and the horse, and the crest rising on its gleaming cone, the spoils and trappings of Libya.

Then they sought glory with the javelin, the last shows of the racecourse, and they vied to beat the limit of the mark: Burnus, strong in his line, whom the bank sent †of the metal where Tagus runs pale, troubled with its gold-bearing sands, and Glagus, famous for outstripping the winds with his arm, and the hunter Aconteus, whose spears no deer was ever able to flee by its most headlong flight, and Indibilis, long glad to wage war for the Latins, now an ally, and Ilerdes, used to catching wandering birds in their cloud with his javelins, both that and a warrior. The first praise was Burnus's, who fixed his shafts in the mark: his gift is a slave-girl skilled to turn white wool with Gaetulian purple. But he whom the next prizes honour, who drove his spear nearest the mark, Ilerdes departed glad, a boy received as his reward, for whom no doe was beyond raising in the course as sport. The third palm was held by Aconteus, distinguished for twin hounds, not fearful to harry the boar with their baying.

When the shout and applause had approved these honours, the leader's brother and Laelius, shining in purple, joyfully call out the great names and the shades of the fallen and hurl their spears together. It pleased them to honour the hallowed ashes and add this glory to the games. The leader himself too, testifying the joys of his mind in his face, when he had matched the loyal hearts with deserved gifts— and his brother carried off a breastplate of layered gold, Laelius swift coursers from the Asturian breed— hurls with great strength a victorious spear, rising as he flung, and declares the honour given to the shades. The spear flying—a marvel to tell—in mid-field, at speed, stopped before their eyes and fixed in the earth, clung fast. Then sudden leaves and branches at its lofty top, and an oak, even as it grew, spreading a broad shade. The prophets, foreseeing, bid him aim at greater things: this the gods showed, this they portended by signs.

At which augury, the Carthaginians driven from the Hesperian shore, the avenger of his country and his house returns to Ausonia, with Fame leading his triumph. Nor does Latium burn with any cares more fiercely than to entrust to the young man Libya and the highest rods of office. But the crowd, unequal in spirit and not lucky in war, with wavering minds—the older men forbade the rash undertakings and shrank from great hazards with cautious dread.

So, when the consul, exalted by the honour conferred, brings his proposal to the Fathers, and begs that the power of destroying Carthage be given him, then, beginning from further back, aged father Fabius opened his lips in this manner:

'I, for my part, could not be feared—sated with both years and glory, with both fame and age now left to me— that the consul should believe I disparage his praises in a contest of envy. My name carries fame famous enough, nor do my deeds, so prosperous, need praise that is new. But to fail my country, while life remains, is sin, and sin to wrong my mind by keeping silent. Do you contrive to lead a new war into the lands of Libya? For there is no enemy lacking to Ausonia, nor is it enough for us to conquer Hannibal. What greater glory is sought at the shore of Elissa? If the spurs of praise drive us, reap this harvest. Fortune has provided you, by a nearer venture, a worthy match. The land of Italy wishes—at last it wishes— to drink the blood of the savage leader. Where do you drag Mars, where your standards? The first task is to quench the burning of Italy. You, going astray, desert the weary enemy, and as a traitor strip bare the seven citadels. Or when you lay waste the Syrtes and the barren sands, will that dread plague not leap upon the now-known walls of the city, and invade Jove, emptied, without manhood, without arms? For how much would he buy your yielding and leaving Rome! And, struck by so great a thunderbolt of war, shall we so recall you from the seacoasts of Libya, as lately Fulvius was summoned from high Capua? Conquer at home, and cleanse with war Ausonia, that mourns her dead through three five-year spans. Then stretch your march to the far Garamantes and contrive Nasamonian triumphs. The straitened Italian state now forbids such undertakings. That father of yours, who—no sluggard—added a name to your race, when as consul he was making for the banks of the Spaniard, recalled his soldiers and was the first, of his own accord, to set himself against Hannibal descending eagerly, the Alps once crossed. Do you, as consul, prepare to depart from the conquering enemy, and to pluck the Carthaginian away from us, of course, by this cunning? If then he sits still, unafraid, and does not follow you into Libya and your arms, with Rome taken you will condemn your improvident counsels. But suppose he, thrown into confusion, turns his standards and follows the sails of your fleet. He will surely be the same Hannibal, the same whose rampart you saw from the city's walls.' So Fabius, and the band of elders murmured assent with one voice.

Then the consul in reply: 'When long ago the leaders, great-souled, were slain by a twin death, and the whole land of Tartessus, possessed, had passed beneath the Sidonian yoke, with no man turned—I confess it—to Fabius, nor to any whose heart holds the same opinion, for help, in my earliest years I met the cloud of war and alone set my head against the falling sky, and turned all things upon myself. Then the aged band thought the war ill entrusted to a boy, and this same prophet sang of rash undertakings. I give thanks and praise to the gods, beneath whose power we are the Trojan race: that boy, that futile age, those unwarlike years, that Scipio, not yet ripe for arms, unhurt restored the Spanish lands to the sons of Troy, drove out the Carthaginians, and following the farthest paths of the sun to Atlas, banished from the Hesperian world the name of Libya, and brought back his standards from †the gold no sooner than he saw Phoebus, around the steaming seas, loosing his car on a Roman shore. The same man won over kings. Now Carthage remains the last labour of our deeds. This Jupiter, sower of eternal time, warns. Behold, old age trembles in Hannibal, or he feigns sick fears with a lie, lest the title of having brought an end at last to long ruin should be ours. Surely now our right hand is tested, and we have increased its strength in our flourishing years. Do not, then, fashion delays, but let this lot run its course to wipe out the shame of the old defeats— a lot the gods kept for me. The glory of being unconquered is fair enough for cautious Fabius, and the Delayer by sitting still won everything. Neither Mago nor Hanno, nor the son of Gisgo, nor Hamilcar would have turned his back on us, had we slackly dragged out our battles behind a closed rampart.

Could the Sidonian boy, with his manhood scarcely budding, reach the Laurentine peoples and the Trojan walls and yellow Tiber with its sacred flood, and could he prey on Latium in a long war: and shall it irk us to carry our standards to the lands of Libya and harry the Tyrian homes? The shores lie open wide, safe from danger, and the land stands quiet in rich peace. Let Carthage at last be afraid, accustomed as it is to being feared, and let it understand that we have arms to spare, though the fields of Oenotria be not yet free of Hannibal. That man—whom you yourselves, with your caution and your counsels, made an old man in Latium, who lavishly through a third five-year span draws our blood— that man I shall turn, trembling and afraid too late, back to the burning seats of his country. Or shall Rome see the shameful footprints of the Agenorean right hand on her walls:

shall Carthage, untouched and secure, hear of our toils in the meantime, and make war with its gates open? Then indeed let the shameless enemy batter our towers again with the Sidonian ram, if he has not first heard the temples of his own people crackling with Rutulian flames.'
The Fathers, kindled by such words, and the fate calling them, assented to the consul's speech, and praying that it might be fortunate for Ausonia, granted leave to carry the war across.

That a foreign foe might withdraw from Ausonia's lands, the old oracles of the prophetic Sibyl had decreed that the mother of the gods, sought from her Phrygian seat, must be consecrated within the walls of Laomedon's city: that the godhead, brought over, should be received by him who, chosen out of the whole council of the Fathers, lived as the best man of the present age. Behold, a name better and greater than triumphs! And now she was here, sought out, with the Latian ship bearing Cybele, and before all, while the great senate gave way, Scipio hastened to meet the summoned rites, who, son of the uncle chosen for the African wars of the leader, shone with the many likenesses of his ancestors. And he, when from the far-off sea he received the coming godhead, a suppliant, with his palms, and lofty led the ship to the mouth of the Tuscan Tiber's resounding stream, then women's hands came beneath, to draw the tall alder up the river by fastened ropes. Round about the bronze rang with shrill, hollow chimes, and together the drums contended, resounding with their hoarse beat, and the half-male choirs who keep chaste the twin-peaked Dindyma, who revel in the Dictaean cave, and who know the ridges of Ida and the silent groves. Amid these roars and vows in glad uproar the sacred barge stood still, refusing to go on though the ropes were drawn, and on a sudden shoal stuck fast, unmoved. Then from the middle of the ship, with a great cry, the priest:

'Forbear to touch the ropes with polluted palms, and far from here, I warn you, far from here, whoever you are, unchaste, take your steps, nor mingle in our holy toil, while it is enough to have warned you in the goddess's name. But if any woman is strong in a modest mind, if any stands sure of her own untainted body, let her, even alone, take up the holy task with her hand.'
Here Claudia, drawing her name from the ancient line of the Clausi, ill credited by the people's unfair report, with palms and eyes turned to the ship speaks out:

'Mother of the heaven-dwellers, godhead who create for us all the gods, whose offspring govern by their allotted lot the earth and the sea, the stars and the shades of the realms below, if our body has been violated by no crime, come, goddess, as witness, and set me free with an easy keel.' Then, untroubled, she takes the rope, and the roaring of lions seemed suddenly to be heard, and through the air, struck by no hand, the goddess's drums sounded a graver note. The barge is carried forward, head down (you would think winds drove it), and outstrips the woman who draws it against the opposing waves. At once a greater hope soothes the breasts of all, that an end to arms at last, and an end to perils, was coming.

Scipio himself, eager, departing from the Sicilian land, hid the sea far and wide with his ships driven forward, having appeased the sea's godhead with a bull for victim, and the entrails, cast out, floated on the blue waves. Then, gliding from the seat of the gods and through the pure upper air, the armour-bearing birds of Jove before his eyes began to point out the sea-ways and to lead the fleet. Their clangour gave a glad augury. Then following their flight, gone before under the clear cloud, only so far as the eyes of watchers keep them, not in vain, in sight, they held the treacherous shores of the Agenorean land.

Nor slack, with so great a storm coming on against herself, had Africa, under a great name, made ready a fearful mass, the king's resources against them, and Massylian arms, and Syphax was the one hope of the Libyans and the one terror of the Laurentines. The plains alike and the receding valleys and the shores he had filled with the Numidian used to deck his horse with no woven cloth, and through the air dense clouds were hiding the sky with hissing javelins. Forgetful here of the right hand he had given and the pact joined at the altars, and of the tables as witness and the rights of a guest, of law and good faith together, changed by a base love, he had broken them, and won a marriage-bed at the price of his kingdom. There was a maiden of surpassing beauty and famous father, daughter of Hasdrubal, and when he had taken her to his lofty chamber, as if kindled by the first torch and the wedding-pine, the son-in-law turned his strength to the Carthaginians, and, the bond of Latian friendship dissolved, carried over his dowered arms.

But it was not the least of cares to the Ausonian leader to have warned Syphax, and his envoys threaten: let him stand by his kingdom, reckon with the gods, keep the guest-pact: far off would the marriage be, far off the Tyrian wedding, set amid the lines of the Dardanians. For in blood, if he refused, his obedience to a too soft and easy husband would have to stand, and the loves of his blazing chamber.

So the Latian leader warned, mingling threats, but in vain. For his wife had stopped his deaf ears. And so, harsh against warnings that strove for nothing, he calls his swords, and, calling the chaste altars of the broken pact to witness, busily stirs up Mars by various art. The camp, roofed over with light reed and marsh cane, such scattered huts as the Moorish shepherd loves, he attacks, the shadows guarding his theft of arms, and in the silent night scatters hidden fires. Then, when the gathered flames began to spread the swift plague and to bear themselves with a great noise through the rich fodder, the flames range out openly into the air and drive the smoke before them with a flying light. The hostile pest goes through the whole camp with a whirlwind, and Vulcan with panting roar devours the dry feeding, and the fires stream from every tent. By most the fire is felt before it is seen, as they are roused from sleep, and the flames invade the mouths of many who call for help. On every side the conquering Mulciber flows, and with his swift embraces seizes arms and men: the pest overflows, and half-burnt the camp flies through the topmost clouds in whitening ash. With a vast leap, mournfully crackling, the blaze flies wide about the very tents of the king, and would have swallowed the man, had not a guard, in fear at the disaster, snatched him, praying unavenged, from sleep and his bed.

But soon, when the Massylian and the Tyrian leaders had joined their forces behind a common rampart, and the manhood summoned from the kingdom had eased the wounds of that ill-starred night, wrath and shame, and his wife, a third fire, gave him monstrous spirit, and the barbarian, his face scorched by the camp's flames, and himself with no covering scarcely snatched from the foe amid the trembling bands, gnashed and threatened: but that by no daylight could Syphax, not in clear day, nor with the sun looking on, be conquered by any man. Such things the frenzied king had boasted, but already Atropos was closing his breath and allowing no more, and hastening the thread of his swollen tongue. For when he sprang from the camp, like a turbid river which, dragging woods and rocks headlong through trackless ways, rolls on and loosens its banks with a foaming flood, riding before all on his horse he draws his columns on with his voice. Against him the Rutulian's busy band, and the army, lofty, rushed when they saw the king far off, snatching up their arms, and each to himself: 'Do you see? Do you see how in the front line the Massylian leader hovers, demanding battle? My right hand, make this glory ours. He has profaned the altars of the heaven-dwellers and broken the chaste leader's pact. Let it be enough that he escaped our camp once, when it was burned.' So each in silence, and they pour their spears in rivalry. First the flying spear lodged in the horse's nostrils breathing fire, and reared the beast up, his mouth bloodied, as he beat the air with his lifted hooves. The fierce horse crashed down, and tossing his pierced limbs with the spear-point, this way and that, betrayed his rider to the foe. They rush in, and as he struggled in vain to flee and to lift his weary frame, with the weapon drawn back from the wound they seize him; then bonds for the man, and manacles—shameful— were added, and (a lesson never to trust glad fortune) they bound his sceptre-bearing hands with a tight chain. He is led down, cast from the high summit of his kingdom, who but now beneath his feet had seen the lands and sceptres and the open shores down to Ocean, and the sea obedient to his nod. His kingdom's resources laid low, the Phoenician columns are mown down, and Hasdrubal, hateful to Mars and known for flight, turns his back in haste, his daring condemned.

Carthage stood, her limbs lopped off on every side, leaning on one man, and Hannibal, though absent, by his name held back the mass that fell with so great a crash. That sole resource the last extremities of their state bid them rouse, weary and in need of help and aid; here in fear they flee for refuge, after they see themselves deserted by the power of the gods. No delay: the keels, driven on, furrow the salt waters, to call him back and bear him their country's charge, warning him not to look, slow, on no citadels of Carthage left standing.

The fourth Dawn had brought their ship to the shores of Daunus, and fierce dreams were troubling the leader's mind. For while, heavy with cares, he took his rest by night, he seemed to see Flaminius and Gracchus, to see Paulus, all at once rush against him with drawn swords and drive him from the Italian land, and the whole host of shades from Cannae and from the waters of Trasimene was going, driving him into the sea. He himself, longing for flight, sought to escape to the known Alps and, embracing the Latian earth with both arms, clung to it, until a savage force from the deep thrust him off and gave him to the swift gales to carry away.
With these visions, the men bearing the charge come to him in his sickness, the envoys, and lay open his country's last perils:

how the Massylian arms had fallen, how on his neck the chains the ruler of Libya had borne, and, death denied, was kept as a new show for Jove; how Carthage labours, with frightened Hasdrubal, who had held the reins of state, shaken by more than one rout. They themselves, grim to tell, had seen, when two camps burned in the silent night, and Africa shone with criminal flames. That a headlong young man threatened, while the Carthaginian held the Bruttian shores, to strip with black fires the country to which he might return, and his own famous deeds. When these things were said, and the disasters and fears lay bare, they pour out tears and worship his right hand as a godhead.
He heard them, fixed with a grim gaze, and with sick care silently weighed within himself, turning it over, whether Carthage were worth so much. Then thus he speaks:

'O dread destruction to mortals! O envy, never enduring that anything should grow or that great praises should rise! Long since I could have overthrown and razed Rome and levelled her with the ground, led the captured nation into slavery and laid laws upon Latium. While they deny the leader the cost and the arms, and to renew his maniples worn by success with a fresh levy of recruits, and while it pleases Hanno to cheat the cohorts even of grain and food, all Africa is wrapped in flames, the Rhoetean lance batters the Agenorean gates. Now the glory of his country, now her sole support is Hannibal alone, now the last hope lies in our right hand. The standards shall be turned, as the Fathers have decreed, and together both the walls of our country and you, Hanno, we shall save.'

When he had thundered this out, he drives the tall ships from the shore and, groaning much, moves his fleet over the sea. No one dared assail the backs of the departing, nor call the man back: all seem to grant that he should leave of his own will, you gods, and at last set free Ausonia. They pray for winds, and to see the shores bare of the foe is enough: as when the South Wind checks its fierce blasts and, departing, gives back the sea, the sailor with a modest vow meanwhile does not ask for friendly breezes, content to be rid of the South, and reckons a quiet peace enough in place of an easy passage. All to the deep the Sidonian soldiery had turned their gaze on every side: the leader kept his eyes fixed, intent, upon the Italian land, and the tears flowed and wet his face, running in silence, and he heaved frequent sighs, no otherwise than if, driven out, he were leaving his country and his sweet home, and were dragged, a grim exile, to alien shores.

But when, the winds poured into the sails, the ships began to go on and little by little the mountains to sink in the distance, and there was now no Hesperia and nowhere now the Daunian land, here, gnashing within himself: 'Am I in my right mind, and now unworthy of this return, who ever tore myself from the bounds of Ausonia? Would that Carthage had blazed, set to the torch, and that the name of Elissa had rather fallen. What? Was I then in my right mind, who did not carry the burning weapons from Cannae into the Tarpeian temples, and drag Jove from his throne? I would have scattered fires over the seven hills, emptied by war, and given to the proud race Ilium's destruction and the doom of their forefathers. Why, further, should these things gnaw me? Now, now, who forbids me to fall on them with the sword and turn my steps again to the walls? I will go, and, retracing the monuments of my camp, where the known road calls, I will return to the waters of the Anio. Turn your prows toward Italy, wheel the fleet about: I will see to it that Scipio is recalled to a Rome under siege.'

When Neptune from the deep looked out upon him, burning with such furies, and saw the ships turned toward the shore, the father, shaking his sea-blue head, heaved the waters from the bottom and stirred the swollen sea beyond the shores. At once he rouses winds and rains, and from the rock the Aeolian storms, and hides the sky in clouds. Then, working the inmost realms with his three-pronged weapon, he drives Tethys from the west and from the east and stirs all the head of Ocean. The seas rise foaming, and at the dashing of the waters every crag trembles. First, lifting himself from the seats of the Nasamones, the South Wind, cloud-bringing, laid bare the Syrtis, the wave snatched away. There follows, bearing on high with black wings, the North Wind, the torn-off flank of the sea. Black he thunders with discordant blast, and the East Wind snatches a part of the deep. Hence the burst poles roar back, and hence the frequent flashing of lightning, and the implacable heaven rushes upon the fleet. Fires and storm-clouds and waves and the wrath of the winds agreed together, and darkness laid night upon the sea. Look—a squall, twisted by the South and coming from the stern, bellows in the yardarm (and the harsh shriek of the cordage whistles) and, like a mountain in the blackening deep, breaks over the leader's trembling face a wave. Rolling his eyes to sky and sea, he cries out:

'O happy brother, made equal to the gods by your fall, Hasdrubal! whose brave right hand in arms won you a noble death as you fought, and to whom the fates granted to grip the Ausonian land in your last bite. But to me, on the plains of Cannae, where Paulus, where those noble souls fell, it was not allowed to give up my life, nor, when I carried fires into the Capitol, to go down to the shades by Tarpeian Jove's bolt.'

While he mourns so, the wave, driven by warring blasts, rushes against both flanks and held the ship beneath the black ridges of the sea, as though plunged in a whirlpool. Soon, struck high by the black eddies of the surging sand, the ship returned to the airs of heaven and hung above the waves while the wind held it poised. But the South Wind, by a hard lot, drags two biremes onto the rocks and the bristling crags—pitiable and grim. The prows crashed at the impact. Then on the sharp reef the hull, its joints burst, sounded as it broke apart. Here a varied sight before their eyes: there swims over all the sea, among the arms and helmets of men and the reddening crests, the treasure of flowering Capua and the Laurentine spoils of the leader, set apart for the triumph, the tripods and tables of the gods and the images vainly worshipped by the wretched Latins. Then Venus, terrified at the face of the heaving sea, addresses the king of the sea with these words: 'This is enough of wrath for now, father: enough of threats for greater things. Spare the rest, I pray, to the deep, lest bitter Carthage carry off this glory, that no war could surpass— to have brought forth such a head—and that the Carthaginians needed the waves and all the deep for the death of the sons of Aeneas.'
So Venus. And the swollen waves of the flood subside.
. . . and against the opposing camps they drive the meeting bands.
The leader, old in arms and skilled to kindle hearts with praises, was maddening their minds to wrath with fiery exhortation and burning their breasts with the flames of glory:

'You bring me the dripping face of slain Flaminius, the leader: I know your right hand. You, first against the blows of mighty Paulus, rush, and fix your sword in his bones. For you are borne the spoils of warlike Marcellus, and Gracchus, falling, drenched your sword for you. Behold the hand that, when you battered him, warlike Appius, on the lofty wall of high Capua, struck him down dying, hurled headlong from the rampart by a spear. Behold another thunderbolt of the right hand, by which the noble name of Fulvius took more than one wound in his breast. Set yourself here in the front line, you to whom in arms the consul Crispinus fell. Do you accompany me through the foe, who—I remember—at Cannae, most glad in your wrath, bear the face of the leader Servilius transfixed upon a stake. I see your blazing eyes and your face, fearsome no less than your very sword, bravest young Carthaginian— such as I saw you when, in the savage stream of Trebia, you clasped in your huge arms and plunged to the bottom the tribune struggling in vain. And you, who first at the cold waters of the Ticinus dyed your iron with the blood of Scipio the father, finish what you began and give me back the son's blood. Should I dread the very gods, if they come to battle, when, squadrons, I have seen you trample ridges bordering the sky, flying over the highest Alps, when I see the plains of Argyripa, that took fire with your sword and your hands, broad as they are? Will you go more sluggishly now for me, you who first hurl your weapon at the Dardanian walls, and are not ready to yield to my glory? Should I goad you, you indeed, who, when I stood against the lightning and the storm-clouds and the thunders and the wrath of the highest godhead, bade me endure the noises and the empty clouds, and made for the lofty Capitol before your leader? Why should I urge you on, by whom Saguntum was destroyed in famous war, whom the beginnings of the war ennoble? As is worthy of me and of you, defend, I beg, the past praises of your right hand. By the gods' own favour, and by conquering, I, an old man, after my country has tottered for thrice five years, and the home not seen in so long an age, and my son, and the face of my faithful wife long since, trusting in you, I seek again. No other battle remains now for Libya, no other battle remains for the Dardanians. This day, fought out by us, receives its master for the world.'
So Hannibal. But the Ausonian soldiery, impatient of the words that held them back, as often as the leader had begun to open his lips for speech, kept demanding the signal and the fight.
When the father of the gods saw his sister watching this from afar in an airy cloud, and her face grieving under his keen gaze, he spoke thus with friendly voice:

'What gnawings of the mind devour you? Let me know, wife. Does care for the Carthaginian leader's fate and for Carthage trouble you? But consider with yourself the frenzies of the Sidonians. Against the race and the fated kingdom of the Teucrians—what end, I ask, sister, will there be for a rebel people, the treaties broken? Carthage herself has borne and drained no more of evil and of toil than you have undergone, tried for the sake of the Cadmean race. You have stirred up seas and lands, and let loose a fierce young man upon Latium. The walls of Rome have trembled, and for twice eight years Hannibal has been first of the human race. It is time to compose the nations. We have come to the end, and the door of war must be closed.'

Then Juno, a suppliant: 'Neither, striving to change these things whose day is fixed, have I settled in the hanging cloud, nor do I seek to call back the lines or to prolong the war. What you can grant—since my favour languishes and my first love has fallen now—against the threads of the sisters I ask nothing: let Hannibal turn his back to the foe, as you please, and let the ashes of Troy reign in Carthage. This I beg of you, by the mutual pledges of our twin love, both as sister and as wife: that you let the great-souled leader swim through the perils, and grant him his life, and not suffer him, captured, to bear Ausonian chains. Let my walls stand, even bruised by ills, the Sidonian name broken, and let them be kept for my honour.'
So Juno, and against her Jupiter briefly thus began:

'I grant a respite to the walls of lofty Carthage, as you wish. Let them stand by your tears and prayers. But hear, wife, how far it is allowed me to indulge you. No long fates remain to the city, and a leader of like name shall come who shall overturn from the foundations the citadels now saved. Let Hannibal too, as you ask, draw the airs of heaven, snatched from the battle. Here he will wish to mingle the stars with the sea and to fill the lands with returning arms: I know the man's heart, teeming with war. But let this be the law of our gift: let him not, hereafter, see the realms of Saturn, nor seek again, ever any more, Ausonia. Now bear him off, snatched from the death that presses, lest, if he mingles fierce battles on the wide plains, you be unable to withdraw him from the young Roman's right hand.'

While the Almighty fixes the fates of city and leader, the lines fall on the fight and challenge the stars with their shout. At no other time did the earth see weightier peoples, or, of those who moved their country's arms, greater leaders contend. The high reward of the hazard lay in the midst: whatever the sky covers on every side. The Agenorean leader went, gleaming in purple, and lifted high his lofty head with the nodding plume of his red crest. A savage terror from his great name goes before him, and his sword flashes, well known to Latium. But against him Scipio shone with burning scarlet, showing forth his fearful shield, on which he had engraved the dire battles of his father and of his uncle together, their living likenesses: his high front belched a vast flame. Under so great a force of weapons and of men, in the leaders alone stood the hope and the victory of all. Indeed, as favour or fear sways most men, they believe that, had Scipio been born on Libyan shores, the sceptre would have come to the descendants of Agenor, and, had Hannibal been born in an Ausonian seat, they doubt not the lands would have been under Italian sway.

The airs shuddered, the spears quivering in a swift whirl, and drew a horrid cloud across the sky. Then the sword, and the lines nearer, and face brought close to face, and eyes blazing with dire flame. There is laid low the throng that scorns danger, which flung itself headlong against the first spears, and the earth unwilling drank the blood of its own people. Hot in temper and hot in years, Masinissa bears his huge limbs into the front squadrons of the Macedonians and flies about the field with his winged javelin. No otherwise, when he fights, does the blue-painted dweller of Thule hem in the close ranks with his scythe-bearing war-car.

The Greek phalanx had massed its bands in its native fashion and stood, penetrable by no spears, with theirs locked together. Forgetful of the pact, Philip had sent these to war after the treaty, and was warming up the shaken city of Agenor. The soldiery grows thin, loosened by many a wound, and, with bodies laid low, opens wide-spreading paths among the weapons. The Ausonian band breaks in with the weight of ruin and unseals the Greek perjuries.

Rutilus slays Archemorus, Norbanus slays Teucer (and both Mantua their mother had sent forth in their budding age), the right hand of warlike Calenus cuts down Samius, and Selius cuts down Clytius—Clytius, vainly swelling at the name of Pella, his homeland: but the glory of Pella availed not to defend the wretch from Daunian weapons.

Fiercer than these, the Latian Laelius laid waste the Bruttian standards, taunting them: 'Was the land of Oenotria so to be loathed, that over harsh seas and through mad waves you fled with Tyrian oarsmen? But to have fled was enough. Do you over and above seek to drench alien lands with Latian blood?' Saying this, he forestalls Silarus, who was planning battle with his spear. The flying lance sat deep beneath his throat and at once, driven home, closed the ways of life and voice together.

Caudinus is laid low by Vergilius, Amanus by bitter Laus. The faces of the men and the look of their arms, well known, and the voice attuned to one tongue, kindle their wrath. When the son of Hamilcar saw them baring their backs in flight, crying 'Stand, and do not betray our race,' he comes up and turns the battle with his right hand: as in the heat-bearing plains of the Garamantes the Paraetonian serpent, teeming with venom, fed on the burning sand, rears its neck and over the air far and wide twists its surging length, drenching the clouds with foul slime. At once he hinders Herius, who bore a wound on his deadly spear, flying before him—Herius, to whom the Marrucine house and famous Teate gave a noble name. And as the foe strove hard and stood erect for praise, his eager hand sat at the hilt's very end, and the wretch sought his brother with dying sight, when the young Pleminius comes up, and, stung by the bitter death, flashes his savage sword before his face and with a great cry, threatening, demands his brother back. To him the son of Barca: 'If indeed it pleases you to give back the brother, I do not refuse. Only let our pact stand:

call Hasdrubal back from the shades. Shall I ever lay aside my bitter hatreds against the Romans, or let our hearts grow soft, and spare a man whom the Italian land has borne? Then let my brother drive the hostile shades from his eternal seat and banish me to a shared Avernus.' So he speaks and, with the whole weight of his shield, where the ground, slippery with his sliding brother's blood, betrayed his footing, lays him flat and overtakes him with the sword. Falling, Herius stretched out his palms, and embracing the prostrate man, with their deaths joined eased his griefs. Then the Libyan falls on the struggles of the mingled crowd and, rushing, turns the enemy's backs the whole length of the line, as when thunders mingled with lightnings terrify the world and the high house of the highest father totters: all the race of men trembles on earth, and before their very eyes the dread light flashes, and Jupiter is believed to stand present, man by man, over the stricken, his fire aimed.

In another quarter, as though the field's only struggle were there where Scipio, driving on, mingled grim Mars, the harsh fight under a varied image of death gives many forms. Here one lies prostrate, the sword driven home, here another, pitiable, groans, his bones shattered by a stone, and others, to their shame, fear flung face down in flight, while the valour of these gave their breasts, fronting, to Gradivus. The Rhoetean leader himself presses over the slaughter, as by the cold Hebrus higher Mars shakes his car and looses the Getic snows with hot blood, glad in the carnage, and the war-bearing axle, shrieking under its weight, breaks through the ice driven on by the North Winds. And now, ranging in grim ardour, he goes against every bravest name with the sword. Renowned through the world for famous slaughters, the youth fall wide among the weapons: those who seized your walls, Saguntum, and made the wretched ruins, the beginning of the unspeakable war, those who polluted your sacred lakes, Trasimene, and the Phaethontian pools with gore, and whom such confidence carried, that they went to plunder the throne and house of the king of the gods: they are slaughtered hand to hand in one destruction, and yield up their lives—they who bore off the secrets of the gods, profaned, and first unbarred the Alps, denied to human steps. The line, full of this terror, rushed back in haste, dead with fright: no otherwise than when the Vulcanian plague pours itself into the roofs of a city, and the swift wind fans the fires and scatters the flying flames over the gables, the stunned crowd bursts out in sudden terror, and there is panic far and wide as in a captured city.

But when it wearies him to dawdle, hunting the scattered fights of men and held in a lighter combat, it pleases him at last to turn all his strength against the cause of the war and the author of their woes. While Hannibal alone remains, even if fire be set to the walls of Carthage and all her armies fall slain, no profit is won for Latium. But, if that one man fall, all the arms and men of the Agenoreans will be for nothing. So, ranging the field, he turns his eyes about and searches out the leader. It pleases him to bear his step into the supreme contest, and he longs to meet the man, with all Ausonia watching. Lofty, with a fierce shout, he calls him out, taunting his foe, and demands fresh battles.

When Juno heard these cries, terrified lest they reach the Libyan leader's undaunted ears, she shapes a Latian likeness and quickly lifts it with gleaming crests, adds the shield and plumes of the Roman leader, and lays on its shoulders the honour of a gleaming cloak, gives it the gait and bearing of one rousing battle, and grants it bold movements without a body. Then a matching likeness of a false horse, an empty image, to be guided swiftly through trackless ways at speed, is given to the warlike shade for the show of a contest. So before the Carthaginian leader's eyes, the Scipio feigned by Juno exults and of itself brandishes its weapons. But the Carthaginian, glad at sight of the Latian commander before his face and hoping at last for great things at closer range, swiftly sets his nimble limbs upon his horse and hurls his spear against him in a hastened whirl. The winged image turns its back and, fleeing, flies over the field and passes through the lines. Then indeed, as victor and master now of his high prayer, the Carthaginian bloodies his horse with the iron heel and harshly shakes the loosened reins:

'Where do you flee, forgetting to yield to our realm? No hiding-place is yours, Scipio, in the Libyan land.' This he says, and with drawn sword follows the flier, until he led the baffled man over a long stretch into fields far apart, away from the contest of the fight. Then suddenly the deceiving phantom withdrew into the clouds. The lightning leader: 'What god,' he says, 'has set himself against us with hidden power? Or why does the same one hide? Does my glory so stand in the gods' way? But you will never tear away from me—whoever you are, you who stand, a favouring heaven-dweller, by Ausonia—you will not snatch my true foe from me by your arts.' Then, in a fury, he turns the reins of his goaded horse and made for the field, when suddenly, collapsing in the trembling of a hidden plague, the bulk of the horse falls, and breathed out from its panting chest, into the clouds, the life that Juno's care had claimed. Then indeed, impatient: 'This is your second, your fraud, you gods,' he says: 'you do not deceive me. The rocks should have hidden me sunk in the sea, and the deep and the waves should have swallowed me! Was I kept for this death? My standards, followed by those to whom we gave the omen of battle, are cut down, and absent I hear the groans and voices and the words of men calling on Hannibal. What Tartarean torrent will atone enough for our sins?' Even as he poured this out, he looked at his own right hand and seethed with the love of death.
Then Juno, pitying the man, turns into the face of a shepherd and comes out suddenly from the shadowy woods and addresses him as he ponders his inglorious fate:

'What cause has driven you, armed, to come into our woods? Are you making for the hard battle, where great Hannibal subdues with arms the remnants of Ausonia? If you delight to go swiftly and short cuts are welcome to you, by a near path I will lead you into the midst.' He nodded and loads the shepherd's breast with lavish promises, and tells him the Fathers of lofty Carthage will repay him greatly, nor will he himself give the lighter share. Headlong, and clearing the nearest ground with a vast leap, Juno leads him round and, deceiving him as to the lie of the roads, keeps hidden a safety unwelcome to him who would not have it.

Meanwhile the Cadmean band, deserted and afraid, sees no Hannibal anywhere, nowhere the known struggles of the savage leader. Some believe him fallen by the sword, some that he condemned the line and yielded to the gods' frown. The Ausonian commander presses on and drives the routed over all the field. And now the very citadels of Carthage tremble: all Africa is filled with wandering terror, the columns driven back, and rushing in headlong flight without a battle they bend their stunned courses to the farthest shores and, fugitive, are scattered onto the Tartessian coasts; some sought the homes of Battus, some the streams of Lagus. So when, conquered at last by a blind force, Vesuvius vomited up to the stars its fires fed through the ages, and the Vulcanian plague was spread over sea and land, the Eastern Seres saw—a marvel to wonder at— their wool-bearing groves grow white with Ausonian ash.

But at last, on a nearby mound, queen Juno halts the weary leader, whence all the face and the black traces of the battle appear, brought close to his eyes. Such as he had seen the field of Garganus and the marsh of Trebia and the Tyrrhene shallows and the river of Phaethon surging with the slaughter of men, such, pitiable to see, opens the dire sight, the maniples laid low. Then Juno, troubled, revisits the seats above. And now the enemy drew near and came up the mound, when the Carthaginian to himself: 'Though all heaven, its frame dissolved, fall upon this head, and the lands gape open, you will abolish Cannae, Jupiter, in no age, and you will depart from your realms sooner than the nations be silent of the name or the deeds of Hannibal. Nor, after this, do I leave you secure of me, Rome; surviving my country, I will live for you in the hope of arms. For though you now excel in battle, my foes only abide: it is enough and more for me that the Dardanian mothers and the Italian land, while I live, should fear me and know no peace in their hearts.' So he is swept off, mingled with a few of the fleeing, and the high mountains thereafter he seeks, back the way he came, and safe lurking-places.

Here was the end of the war. At once the citadels are opened to the Ausonian leader, now of their own will. Their lawless rule was taken away and their arms, and their laws cut down, and their proud resources— their might broken—and the elephant laid aside the towers it bore. Then the tall ships, a savage spectacle for the Carthaginians, received the flaming brand, and in a sudden storm the seas blazed, and Nereus took fright at the light.

Master of glory that shall last through the ages, the commander, first to bear the surname of the conquered land, secure in his command, seeks Rome again across the blue and rides into his ancestral home in a lofty triumph. Before him Syphax, seated on the litter, a captive, kept his eyes downcast, and golden chains held his neck, here Hanno and the noble Phoenician youth by race and the chief of the Macedonians and the swart bodies of the Moors, then the Numidians, and the Garamant known to Hammon when he ranges the sands, and the ever shipwrecking Syrtis. Next, lifting her conquered palms to the stars, Carthage went, and the image of the Spanish shore, now grown gentle, Gades, the world's end, and Calpe, once the bound of the praises of Hercules, and the Baetis, wont to bathe the horses of the sun in the sweet water of its stream, and, thrusting her leafy peak to the stars, the mother of wars, fierce Pyrene, and the ungentle Ebro, when together it dashes into the sea the rivers it has brought. But nothing held minds and eyes more than the sight of Hannibal's image, fleeing over the plains. He himself, standing on the car, adorned with gold and purple, offered his martial face for the Quirites to gaze on, such as Liber, descending from the perfumed Indians, drove his vine-wreathed car with a tigress bridled; or as, when the mass of the Giants was finished on the Phlegraean plains, the Tirynthian strode on, touching the stars. Hail, unconquered father, not to yield to Quirinus in praises, nor to yield to Camillus in deserts: nor indeed, when she recalls you sprung from the stock of the gods, does Rome lie in calling you the offspring of the Tarpeian Thunderer.
